NOTE: Niwot's well-known community events (the summer Rock & Rails concert series, the Great Niwot Duck Race, Enchanted Evening) are widely referenced locally but I could not confirm current-year details from a primary source — verify dates and current status with the Niwot Business Association before naming them on the page.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: the putting green, and the money that pays for it. Castle Pines is where this client's stated ambition actually lives — $191,229 median household income, $895,500 median home value, 77% detached, still growing — with the Village at Castle Pines next door at a $1,453,400 median home value and a top-coded $250,001 household income, zero renters, and a Jack Nicklaus course that has been the neighbourhood's organising fact since 1981. Water conservation is NOT the lead here; these households are not price-shopping their water bill. The lead is a private backyard putting green built by someone who can talk about how The Ridge's large rolling Weiskopf greens run versus the Nicklaus greens at Castle Pines Golf Club, and match stimp and contour to what the customer actually plays. Water is the supporting argument, and it comes with a specific design move no competitor is making: CPNMD pays the batch's highest sod replacement rebate at $3.00/sq ft residential and $2.50/sq ft commercial-HOA, and requires roughly 50% ColoradoScape plant material — so the smart Castle Pines design is a hybrid, synthetic green or play area carried by xeric beds that capture the rebate, rather than a wall-to-wall turf conversion that captures nothing. Close on the two things that prove local knowledge: the city is not the Village, and wildfire is a real conversation here that deserves a real answer rather than silence. Castle Rock next door argues with a turf ordinance and no rebate; Parker argues with worn-out tract lawns; Castle Pines argues with greens, grade, pines and price point.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No Castle Pines municipal ordinance on artificial turf was found; the city's site surfaced no landscaping or turf regulations and directs enquiries to the Municipal Code and Community Development — CHECK THE CODE DIRECTLY before asserting the city is silent. HOA coverage is effectively universal across the Castle Pines North filings and total within the Village at Castle Pines, which operates its own covenants and architectural control. The governing law is therefore state law plus covenants. SB23-178 bars HOA guidelines from prohibiting nonvegetative turf grass in the backyard of a single-family detached home, requires at least three preapproved front-yard garden designs, requires an option that is at least 80% drought-tolerant plantings, and bars unreasonably requiring hardscape on more than 20% of the landscaping area — attached homes sharing a wall and condominiums excluded. With 77.2% of the city's stock detached (85.3% in the Village), that statute covers the great majority of homes here. SB24-005 has since 1 January 2026 prohibited artificial turf on commercial, institutional and industrial property and on common interest community common property, exempting athletic fields of play — so HOA common-area work is off the table in both the city and the Village. Practical sequencing for a Castle Pines job: statute protects the backyard, but the HOA's architectural review still governs materials, colour, edging and drainage details, and the front yard remains the HOA's call.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: Castle Pines North Metropolitan District (CPNMD), 7404 Yorkshire Drive, 303-688-8550. 2026 schedule: outdoor watering permitted THREE days a week through September, days assigned by address parity (the district publishes the day pairs in a downloadable PDF graphic rather than in text). Water waste including runoff, overspray and leaks is prohibited. New installations should avoid watering between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. Exemptions: drip irrigation anytime; hand-watering of trees, shrubs and gardens with a shut-off nozzle; system testing and maintenance; COMMUNITY SPORTS FIELDS; and new sod or plants for 21 days, but not during July or August. The district recommends cycle-and-soak: water 5-10 minutes, allow 30-60 minutes of absorption, repeat 2-3 times. REBATES — THE BEST IN THE BATCH, and the district flags them as 'INCREASED': Sod Replacement Rebates up to $3.00 per sq ft residential and up to $2.50 per sq ft commercial/HOA. Also $100 per WaterSense smart irrigation controller, up to $5 per rotator nozzle (replacement only), rain sensors at up to 50% of purchase price to a $50 maximum, a residential Rachio discount that itself qualifies for the $100 controller rebate, $25 off Garden In A Box, $100 per high-efficiency toilet to a maximum of three, and $10 per water-efficient showerhead. CRUCIAL NUANCE: unlike Castle Rock, CPNMD publishes NO explicit artificial-turf exclusion — but it does require that landscape designs contain a minimum of roughly 50% ColoradoScape plant material. A turf-only conversion therefore will not qualify, while a hybrid design pairing a synthetic play area or putting green with xeric beds plausibly could capture the rebate on the planted half. That is a genuine, specific, sellable design strategy and the highest-value thing on this page — but the client must ring CPNMD and confirm it before putting it in writing.
facts.soil_and_yard: Ponderosa pine foothills at 6,559 ft, the highest and most wooded of the five, with rolling to genuinely steep lots and real grade to manage. Douglas County expansive-clay and heaving-bedrock country: bentonite and montmorillonite clays that swell up to 20% by volume under pressures exceeding 30,000 psf, cracking flatwork and slabs, plus the heaving bedrock the Colorado Geological Survey studies specifically in Douglas County and maps as a Dipping Bedrock Overlay District, with several million dollars of documented damage since mid-1980s development. WILDFIRE IS A LIVE LOCAL CONCERN AND SHOULD BE ENGAGED, NOT IGNORED: the City has an approved Community Wildfire Protection Implementation Plan, partners with South Metro Fire Rescue, publishes a Wildfire Resistant Plant List curated by South Metro, and participates in Douglas County's Slash Mulch Program. I found NO explicit rule about artificial turf, combustible materials or mulch placement in the city's wildfire materials, and no stated defensible-space distances — South Metro Fire Rescue's Preparedness Division (ReducingRisk@southmetro.org, 720-989-2271) is the authority to ask. A page that acknowledges the wildfire question honestly will read very differently from one that pretends it does not exist, in a community that thinks about it every summer.
facts.housing_stock: 5,119 housing units, median year built 2005. 77.2% single-family detached (3,952 units) — the second-highest detached share in the batch — 9.2% 1-unit attached, 12.6% multi-unit; 79.3% owner-occupied. Population 11,036 at the 2020 census, estimated 15,583 by 2025, so unlike Lone Tree or The Pinery this place is still growing hard. Median home value $895,500. Median age 44.4. Elevation 6,559 ft across 9.594 sq mi — the highest of the five, and it shows in the ponderosa pine and the grades. The stock is essentially the Castle Pines North master plan built out from the late 1980s through the 2000s in named filings — BellMont, Forest Park, Glen Oaks, Hidden Pointe, The Retreat, Daniels Gate — with newer construction continuing south and east. Lots are generally larger and more sloped and more treed than Castle Rock or Parker tract product, with mature ponderosa on many of them. LOT SIZES ARE CHARACTERISED FROM PATTERN, NOT MEASURED — verify against parcel data before publishing figures. HOA coverage is effectively total. THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS MOST ON THIS PAGE: Castle Pines the CITY is not Castle Pines VILLAGE. The Village is a separate unincorporated CDP immediately south — 1,839 units, median year built 2001, 85.3% detached, 92.8% owner-occupied with essentially zero renters, median home value $1,453,400 and median household income top-coded at $250,001. It rebranded to 'The Village at Castle Pines' in 2018. Conflating the two will mark the page as an outsider's work instantly — and the Village is the single richest turf prospect in this entire batch.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $191,229 (ACS 2024) — second-highest in the batch and roughly $46,000 above Castle Rock, $58,000 above Parker and $67,000 above Lone Tree. Median age 44.4; roughly 85.4% White, 3.4% Asian, 6.8% Hispanic or Latino. Established, older-skewing, family and empty-nester affluent, overwhelmingly owner-occupier. Directly adjacent, the Village at Castle Pines runs a $1.45 million median home value on a top-coded $250,001 household income with zero recorded renters. Together the city and the Village are the closest thing in Douglas County to the 'upper echelon, the Cherry Creek types' the owner named as the target for $10-12/sq ft. This is the batch's premium market, and it is not close.
facts.golf: VERIFIED: The Ridge at Castle Pines North — Tom Weiskopf design, public with membership pass programmes available, in the city, in the foothills of the Front Range with views to Pikes Peak and downtown Denver, described as roomy fairways, sculpted bunkers and large rolling greens, and recognised by Golf Magazine, Golfweek and Golf Digest among Colorado's top courses. VERIFIED: Castle Pines Golf Club — Jack Nicklaus design, founded by Jack A. Vickers, opened 1981, private, and the residential community grew around it; it hosted The International, a PGA Tour event, from 1986 through 2006. IMPORTANT SITING FACT: Castle Pines Golf Club is in Castle Pines VILLAGE, the unincorporated CDP, not in the city of Castle Pines — get this right or lose credibility with exactly the customer you want. NOT VERIFIED IN THIS SESSION: whether Castle Pines Golf Club has hosted or will host the BMW Championship (the disambiguation page I reached carried no venue history). Confirm before publishing any tournament claim beyond The International.
facts.commercial_targets: Buffalo Ridge Elementary and Timber Trail Elementary — school athletic fields are the protected category under SB24-005's athletic-fields-of-play exemption, and CPNMD separately exempts community sports fields from its watering restrictions, which gives a school or district a clean dual rationale. The Ridge at Castle Pines North — practice greens, range tee and short-game area work at a publicly accessible Weiskopf course. Coyote Ridge Park improvements and the city's park design project, both live municipal procurement. Castle Pines Golf Club in the Village, for practice-facility work, is the prestige reference job in this batch if it can be won. DO NOT pitch HOA common areas: SB24-005 has prohibited artificial turf on common interest community common property since 1 January 2026, and both the city's filings and the Village are common interest communities. No named daycare or pet business in Castle Pines was verified in this session — the nearest confirmed pet-turf prospects are Camp Bow Wow Castle Rock and Camp Bow Wow Parker.
facts.landmarks: The Ridge at Castle Pines North golf course and its Front Range and Pikes Peak views. Castle Pines Golf Club and the Village at Castle Pines immediately south — Jack Nicklaus, 1981, home of The International 1986-2006. Coyote Ridge Park, currently undergoing improvements. The city's ongoing park design project. Buffalo Ridge Elementary and Timber Trail Elementary. The I-25 corridor and the ponderosa ridgeline the city is named for. Rueter-Hess Reservoir recreation, managed by Douglas County, is nearby. Castle Pines was Douglas County's first new city since 1995: approved as the 'City of Castle Pines North' by popular vote on 6 November 2007, incorporated 12 February 2008, and renamed the 'City of Castle Pines' by voters on 2 November 2010 — a detail residents remember and outsiders always get wrong.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: the shade under the pines — then the Stage 3 restrictions, then the statute. Three facts stack here that stack nowhere else in the batch. First, the yards: a median build year of 1994 on large, heavily treed ponderosa lots means thirty-year-old bluegrass dying under a canopy that has closed over it, with pine-needle litter and irrigation systems installed in the Clinton administration. That is a 'grass will never grow there again' job, not a water-savings job, and it is the emotional lead. Second, the water: Pinery Water is at DROUGHT STAGE 3 with mandatory restrictions from 1 May — by a wide margin the most severe of any provider serving this batch, where everyone else is at Stage 1 or has declared no stage at all — so unlike in Parker, the scarcity argument here is genuinely true and locally felt. Third, the customer: 96.6% detached, 95.1% owner-occupied, median household income $194,446 (the highest of all five places, above even Castle Pines city), median age 46.1 and near-zero turnover — meaning almost every household both holds the SB23-178 statutory right to nonvegetative turf grass in the backyard regardless of what the covenants say, and can comfortably afford the $10-12/sq ft tier for a product they will still own in fifteen years. The page should also be candid that this is a CDP, not a town: no city hall, no municipal code, county rules and HOA covenants instead — which itself signals that whoever wrote the page actually knows the place. Compare the neighbours: Parker leads with worn-out tract lawns at volume, Castle Rock with a municipal turf ordinance, Castle Pines with putting greens and price point, Lone Tree with the fact that half its housing is not detached. The Pinery leads with mature-tree shade on big lots and the harshest water restrictions in the entire service area.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: NO MUNICIPAL ORDINANCE EXISTS — The Pinery is unincorporated, so Douglas County regulations govern, including the county's geologic-hazard and Dipping Bedrock Overlay District provisions. Day-to-day landscaping control sits with the homeowners association and its covenants and architectural review, and I COULD NOT REACH A PINERY HOA SITE to read those rules; the domain I tried did not resolve. That is the single most useful missing piece for this page and should be obtained directly from the association — the architectural-control guidelines will govern materials, colour, edging and visibility from the street. What is certain is the state overlay, and here it lands harder than anywhere else in the batch: SB23-178 bars HOA guidelines from prohibiting nonvegetative turf grass in the BACKYARD of a single-family detached home, and expressly excludes attached homes sharing a wall and condominiums. Because 96.6% of The Pinery's housing is detached single-family, effectively the ENTIRE community holds that statutory right — the highest coverage rate of the statute of any place in this batch (against 77.2% in Castle Pines, 73.7% in Castle Rock, 70.0% in Parker and just 40.7% in Lone Tree). The statute also requires the association to preapprove at least three front-yard garden designs, to allow an option that is at least 80% drought-tolerant plantings, and not to unreasonably require hardscape on more than 20% of the landscaping area. SB24-005 separately bars artificial turf on common interest community common property from 1 January 2026, so association common areas are closed while private backyards are protected.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: Pinery Water and Wastewater District, 5242 Old Schoolhouse Road, Parker CO 80134, 303-841-2797. THE MOST SEVERE RESTRICTIONS IN THE ENTIRE BATCH BY A DISTANCE: the district is at DROUGHT STAGE 3 with mandatory restrictions beginning 1 May. For comparison, Castle Rock Water is at Stage 1, Southgate is at Stage 1, Northern Douglas County is at Stage 1, and Parker Water publishes no formal drought stage at all. A mandatory watering schedule is assigned by customer address; the specific day and hour rules were not retrievable from the pages I could reach, and the district's drought-information page returned a 404 — GET THE CURRENT STAGE 3 SCHEDULE AND PENALTIES DIRECTLY FROM THE DISTRICT before publishing, because this is the page's central factual claim and it must be exactly right. INCENTIVES: the district lists a sprinkler consultation programme, a turf replacement programme, and Garden In A Box, which it describes as a past partnership with Resource Central spanning six years. Rebate AMOUNTS are not published, and there is NO STATEMENT either way on artificial turf eligibility — verify by phone. The working assumption, consistent with every other provider in this batch, is that artificial turf does not qualify.
facts.soil_and_yard: The most distinctive yard conditions in the batch, and the reason this page writes itself differently. Ponderosa pine country at 6,067 ft on large, heavily treed lots with a mature canopy that is now thirty-plus years past the community's 1994 median build date — so deep, permanent shade over ground that was originally sodded in full sun, plus continuous pine-needle litter and acidic duff. Grass does not come back under that canopy no matter how it is watered, which is a fundamentally different sales conversation from Parker's worn tract lawns or Castle Rock's ordinance cap. Slope and drainage vary lot to lot rather than following a graded subdivision pad. Underlying it is the same Douglas County ground as the rest: expansive bentonite and montmorillonite clays swelling up to 20% by volume under pressures exceeding 30,000 psf, cracking flatwork and slabs, and the heaving-bedrock hazard the Colorado Geological Survey maps in Douglas County through its Dipping Bedrock Overlay District, with several million dollars of damage recorded since mid-1980s development. As unincorporated county land, county building and geologic-hazard requirements apply directly here rather than a town's. Wildlife pressure — deer, turkey — is routine on these lots and worth addressing in the product spec.
facts.housing_stock: HONEST CAVEAT FIRST: this is an unincorporated CDP with no town hall, no municipal code, no municipal website and no reachable local news source, so the ordinance, landmark and golf research below is genuinely thinner than for the other four — I have flagged every gap rather than filling it. The demographic and housing data, by contrast, is the most distinctive in the whole batch. 4,017 housing units — the smallest count here — but 96.6% single-family DETACHED (3,879 units), just 2.4% attached and 1.1% multi-unit, and 95.1% owner-occupied against 4.4% renter. Median year built 1994: a decade older than Castle Pines (2005), Parker (2004) and Lone Tree (2004), and thirteen years older than Castle Rock (2007). Population 11,311 at the 2020 census, up only 7.5% from 2010 — effectively built out and static, in a county defined by growth. Occupancy 97.4%, homeowner vacancy 1.1%. 79% married-couple households, 36.4% with children under 18, nearly 18% aged 65 or over. Median home value $791,100. The community was platted around The Pinery Country Club in ponderosa pine country, and the lots are correspondingly large and heavily treed — commonly half an acre and up, materially bigger than Parker or Castle Rock tract lots. LOT SIZE IS CHARACTERISED FROM DEVELOPMENT PATTERN, NOT MEASURED; ACS carries no lot-size variable and there is no municipal GIS to check. Verify against Douglas County parcel data before publishing acreage figures. Governance is by homeowners association and covenants rather than a town.
facts.who_lives_there: THE BATCH'S BIGGEST SURPRISE: median household income $194,446 (ACS 2024) — the HIGHEST of all five places researched, above Castle Pines city ($191,229), Highlands Ranch ($159,307), Castle Rock ($145,197), Parker ($133,369) and Lone Tree ($123,741). An unincorporated CDP with no city hall is the richest per-household place on this list. Median age 46.1, the oldest of the five. 87.4% White, 8.1% multiracial, 7.3% Hispanic or Latino, 1.8% Asian. 79% married couples, a quarter of residents under 18 and 18% over 65 — so both established families and long-tenured empty-nesters. Elevation 6,067 ft, 10.4 sq mi, sitting between Parker to the north and Castle Rock to the southwest with Colorado State Highway 83 running through the centre. The customer profile is exactly right for a premium product: high income, near-total owner-occupancy, low turnover, older, and staying put long enough to care about a fifteen-to-twenty-year installation rather than the cheapest bid.
facts.golf: The Pinery Country Club is the community's namesake and organising feature — the neighbourhood was developed around it — but I COULD NOT VERIFY its details in this session: the domains I tried did not resolve, and the Wikipedia article on The Pinery contains no golf information at all. Number of holes, public or private status, and founding date all need direct confirmation before publication. Adjacent courses in Parker and Castle Rock are within a short drive. Given the income profile and the golf-community origin, the private-putting-green market here is likely strong, but the page should not name course details it has not checked.
facts.commercial_targets: GENUINELY THIN, and it should be treated as a residential page rather than forced into a commercial one. There is no municipality, so no town recreation centre, no municipal fields and no city procurement. Schools serving the area are Douglas County School District, but no Pinery-specific school was named in the sources I could reach — check DCSD's school locator for the assigned elementary, middle and high schools before naming any. The Pinery Country Club is the obvious commercial prospect for practice-green and short-game work once its details are verified. Homeowners association common areas are legally closed to artificial turf under SB24-005 as of 1 January 2026. No daycare or pet business in The Pinery was verified; the nearest confirmed pet-turf prospects are Camp Bow Wow Parker at 10325 S Progress Way, (720) 605-2364, and Camp Bow Wow Castle Rock at 500 1st St, (720) 901-2958. The commercial section of this page should be short and honest rather than padded.
facts.landmarks: THIN AND PARTLY UNVERIFIED — say so rather than padding. Confirmed: Colorado State Highway 83 (Parker Road) runs through the centre of the CDP, which sits between Parker to the north and Castle Rock, the county seat, to the southwest; elevation 6,067 ft across 10.4 sq mi; the ponderosa pine canopy that gives the community its name. The Pinery Country Club is the community's organising landmark but its details are unverified (see golf). Bingham Lake is locally associated with the community but I could NOT verify it in this session. Rueter-Hess Reservoir sits nearby to the north, on the Parker side. For a page like this the honest move is to lean on what is genuinely checkable — the pines, the ridge, Highway 83, and the country club once confirmed — rather than assembling a list of landmarks a local would not recognise.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE NEW-BUILD BACK YARD: 'You just closed on a house in Sterling Ranch and the back yard is builder dirt — and you can't touch it until the Design Review Committee approves your plan in writing.' Sterling Ranch is the only place in this batch where the whole market is FIRST landscape rather than replacement, and where the customer is already actively shopping. Build the page around three things nobody else in the batch can claim: (1) DRC-first process — written approval before any work starts, plans drawn to the Code of Rules Guidebook, and the explicit promise that the installer is on (or working to get on) the CAB's own APPROVED LANDSCAPERS LIST of contractors 'familiar with our community standards.' Naming that list on the page is the single highest-trust move available in Sterling Ranch. (2) The new-construction ground truth: compacted construction fill, imported subgrade, builder rough-grade that must be preserved, and CAB/County chase drains running through the yard — a turf base built on a five-year-old production lot is a drainage engineering job, not a carpet job, and getting it wrong on a house still inside warranty is expensive. (3) Fit the community's own identity instead of fighting it: Sterling Ranch runs Colorado's first community-wide rainwater harvesting program through Dominion Water, meters and monitors every home, and publishes a Denver Botanic Gardens plant list. Frame turf as the part of the yard that stops consuming, sitting inside a water-wise design that uses that plant list — that is how you sell here, not with a drought-fine scare, because Sterling Ranch has no published mandatory restriction to scare anyone with. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Roxborough Park is three miles away and is a 1970s-2000s retrofit market under an Aurora-imposed ban on new sod; Stonegate is a 1990s retrofit governed by a rear-yard-only covenant; Castle Pines Village is a $1.45M estate market priced by a water budget; Meridian is commercial. Sterling Ranch is the only one where the yard has never been landscaped at all, the buyer is 35 with two kids, the deadline is now, and the gatekeeper is an approved-vendor list.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Sterling Ranch Community Authority Board (CAB), 8220/8155 Piney River Avenue, 720-661-9694, partnered with seven Metropolitan Districts. THE OPERATIVE RULE: 'Any change to the exterior of the home or on the lot must be submitted to the Design Review Committee and WRITTEN APPROVAL OBTAINED BEFORE ANY WORK IS STARTED' — and the DRC documents explicitly cover 'landscaping, play or sports equipment' among outdoor projects. Residents are bound by the Sterling Ranch Code of Rules Guidebook and the CAB has adopted formal non-compliance and enforcement procedures. Critically for a contractor: the CAB publishes an APPROVED LANDSCAPERS LIST — 'Updated list of landscapers who are familiar with our community standards' — and runs HOMEOWNER LANDSCAPE CLASSES through the year teaching residents the design review process and requirements. There is also a Community Standards Toolkit and a Sterling Ranch 311 issue-reporting system. HONEST GAP: I could not retrieve the DRC guideline documents themselves (they sit behind the CAB's document centre), so I could NOT verify whether Sterling Ranch's written standards permit, restrict or limit artificial turf, or whether they impose a front-yard/rear-yard split like Stonegate's. That must be confirmed with the CAB before the page states a rule. SB24-005 also restricts new artificial turf on common interest community property (athletic fields of play exempt), which bears on CAB common areas and park projects.
facts.water_and_rules: Dominion Water and Sanitation District (dominionwsd.org, established 2004) is the wholesale water and wastewater provider across a 33,000-acre area of north-west Douglas County, and built a water treatment facility inside Sterling Ranch. It broke ground on the Chatfield Basin Water Reclamation Facility in August 2025. Water is assembled through partnerships with Denver Water, Aurora Water and Douglas County systems, with a closed-loop system including a diversion and regional treatment facility on the South Platte and sources up to 85 miles away. Sterling Ranch runs COLORADO'S FIRST COMMUNITY-WIDE RAINWATER HARVESTING PROGRAM, managed by Dominion — a genuinely unique, checkable fact. Homes have advanced water metering and monitoring plus smart irrigation controls, and home orientation is used to cut demand; the community states it 'uses significantly less water than other Front Range communities.' Sterling Ranch partnered with DENVER BOTANIC GARDENS to publish a curated drought-resistant plant list for residents. CURRENT STATUS (checked 2026-09-07): I found NO published mandatory drought stage or day-of-week watering schedule for Dominion/Sterling Ranch — unlike Roxborough (Stage 1, 2 days/wk), Stonegate (Stage 1, 3 days/wk, no Wednesdays) and Cottonwood next door (Stage 2). Say that honestly rather than inventing a restriction. TURF REBATE: none found at Dominion or the CAB; the state CWCB Turf Replacement Grant Program stopped accepting applications March 2025 and funded living water-wise landscape only. So in Sterling Ranch the water story is IDENTITY, not restriction or rebate — the community sells itself on conservation, and a homeowner installing turf is joining that story rather than dodging a fine.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 5,709 ft — the lowest of the five — on the transition bench between the plains and the foothills, west of Chatfield and immediately below Waterton Canyon and Roxborough State Park. Douglas County soils here carry the Front Range expansive bentonite/montmorillonite clay risk the Colorado Geological Survey describes, and the CGS specifically names 'inadequate management of surface drainage and planting vegetation next to the foundation so irrigation water enters the soil' as a landscaping-caused damage mechanism — an argument that lands unusually hard on a five-year-old house still inside its structural warranty. The dominant NEW-BUILD site conditions: heavily compacted construction subgrade and imported fill that drains poorly and settles unevenly; builder rough-grade that must not be altered; construction debris in the top layers; CHASE DRAINS installed by Douglas County or the CAB (the CAB publishes a dedicated Chase Drain information page) that any base excavation has to respect; and narrow side yards and tight rear setbacks that make access and spoil removal the real cost driver. Slopes are moderate — nothing like Roxborough's or Castle Pines Village's grades.
facts.housing_stock: THE NEWEST HOUSING STOCK IN THE METRO — construction began in early 2016 and has not stopped. 3,400 acres planned for eventual ~33,000 residents across NINE VILLAGES over a roughly 20-year build-out, with about 40% open space and two wildlife corridors. Providence Village, the first village, holds just under 800 homes plus a recreation centre, church, school, civic centre and several parks; Ascent Village and Parkvale are also underway. NINE production and semi-custom builders are selling simultaneously: David Weekley, Lennar, Lion Residential, Pulte, Richmond American, Sheffield, Taylor Morrison, Tri Pointe and Trumark. Homes from the $400s. Consequences that matter for turf: tight, narrow, small back yards on modern production lots (frequently 1,000-2,500 sq ft of usable rear yard, many far smaller on paired and alley-loaded product); yards handed over raw or minimally landscaped at closing; compacted construction subgrade; and chase drains installed by Douglas County or the CAB that the CAB publishes guidance about. Ranked Colorado's #1 best-selling master-planned community and #35 nationally. HOA prevalence 100% — every lot sits under the Sterling Ranch Community Authority Board and one of seven metropolitan districts. HONEST DATA GAP: the 2020 census recorded only 1,789 residents and 5.529 sq miles, and Sterling Ranch has no usable ACS income or home-value profile (DataUSA and Census Reporter both return nothing) because the CDP is too new and growing too fast. Do not publish a median income figure for Sterling Ranch — use builder pricing and Douglas County context instead, and say so.
facts.who_lives_there: Median age 35.5 with 29.3% under 18 and only 7.2% aged 65+ (2020) — the youngest FAMILY population in the batch and the opposite end of the life cycle from Castle Pines Village's 53.9. First-time and second-time move-up buyers from $400s upward, heavily dual-income, drawn by new construction, fibre (Colorado's first 1 Gig community, fibre to every home) and trail access. The behavioural fact that matters: these are people who just closed on a house, are inside a landscaping deadline, have a mud pit for a back yard, and are actively shopping for a contractor RIGHT NOW. No other place in this batch has that concentration of in-market intent.
facts.golf: No course inside Sterling Ranch. Immediately adjacent, sharing ZIP 80125: Ravenna Country Club (8285 Dante Drive, Littleton — private, family-owned, Golfweek top-100 residential course ten years running, set against a 70-million-year-old red sandstone ridge, with fitness/pool amenity 'La Bella Vita') and Arrowhead Golf Club (10850 Sundown Trail, Littleton — Robert Trent Jones Sr. & Jr., par 70, semi-private through the red rock fins). Also nearby: Deer Creek Golf Club and the Ken-Caryl courses. The golf angle in Sterling Ranch is a backyard practice green in a small new-build yard for someone who plays Arrowhead or Ravenna — a compact 200-400 sq ft green, not an estate installation.
facts.commercial_targets: THE APPROVED LANDSCAPERS LIST is target number one — getting onto the CAB's published list of 'landscapers who are familiar with our community standards' is worth more in Sterling Ranch than any advertisement, and the CAB's homeowner landscape classes are a standing speaking opportunity. Beyond that: the nine builders' MODEL HOME PARKS (David Weekley, Lennar, Lion Residential, Pulte, Richmond American, Sheffield, Taylor Morrison, Tri Pointe, Trumark) — a model-home putting green or turf back yard is a permanent showroom in front of every prospective buyer in the community. The Overlook Clubhouse and Ranch Social outdoor areas. Prospect Park (all-abilities surfacing is a natural synthetic application). Burns Regional Park pickleball court surrounds. Schools: John Adams Academy (tuition-free classical charter, already open in Sterling Ranch, K-8 expanding toward K-12), Primrose School in Providence Village (early childhood — a prime pet-and-play turf buyer), 'Elementary School 51 in Sterling Ranch' (DCSD, under construction, opening 2027 in Providence Village for up to 750 students Pre-K-5), plus Coyote Creek Elementary, Roxborough Primary and Intermediate, Ranch View Middle School and ThunderRidge High School. Sterling Ranch Community Library (2027). CAB common areas and the seven metro districts' parks.
facts.landmarks: Providence Village (the first of nine villages) with its civic centre, church and parks. Ascent Village and Parkvale. The Overlook Clubhouse (fitness classes, weights, swimming). Ranch Social — the community café with coffee, remote work and happy hour. Prospect Park, an all-abilities inclusive recreation space. Burns Regional Park pickleball courts. 30 miles of internal trails and ~40% open space with two wildlife corridors. Immediately adjacent: Roxborough State Park, Chatfield State Park, Waterton Canyon and the Colorado Trail. Titan Road and Rampart Range Road. Colorado's first 1 Gig fibre-to-the-home community. Sterling Ranch Community Library, opening 2027 in Providence Village.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE REBUILD YARD. Superior is the only place in this batch — and one of very few in the whole metro — where a large, identifiable share of homes are 2022–2026 new builds standing on lots that were scraped to bare dirt after the Marshall Fire took 398 structures, 393 of them homes, with Sagamore wiped out entirely and only seven historic houses left standing in Original Town. Those owners have already spent their insurance money on the house, are exhausted by four years of construction, and are staring at a compacted, debris-laden, builder-graded rectangle where the developer's sod is already thinning. That is a fundamentally different conversation from Erie's brand-new production lot (never had a lawn, owner has never watered it) and from Niwot's 40-year-old shade-killed yard. The page should be about BUILDING A YARD ONCE, PROPERLY, ON GROUND THAT HAS BEEN DESTROYED — excavation depth, what to do with compacted fill and buried construction debris, drainage away from a new foundation on expansive Laramie clay, and finishing the job in one season rather than three years of failed sod. Second, and only second, the water argument: Superior is at Stage 0 with restrictions lifted as of 30 April 2026, so scarcity is NOT the urgent hook here the way it is in Left Hand Water District territory — do not manufacture panic, sell permanence. Third, the legal hook: SB23-178 means the Rock Creek HOA cannot stop a detached-home owner putting nonvegetative turf in the BACK yard, which pre-empts the single biggest objection in a town where nearly everyone is in an HOA. *** COMPLIANCE WARNING — DO NOT LET THIS PAGE CLAIM ARTIFICIAL TURF IS FIRE-RESISTANT OR FIRE-SAFE. *** Synthetic turf melts and can ignite under ember attack. Making a fire-safety claim to a community that lost 400 buildings in a wind-driven ember storm would be false, cruel and a serious legal and reputational exposure. Lead on rebuild and permanence; say nothing about fire. WHY IT DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Erie next door leads on a named rebate that excludes turf; Superior leads on rebuilding from bare ground. Louisville shares the fire but not the Sagamore-scale total loss. NOCO OVERLAP: LOW — Superior is unambiguously Denver-metro/southern Boulder County and reads as the safest town in this batch to build out under the Timeless brand.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: TWO STATE LAWS DO THE HEAVY LIFTING HERE AND THEY CUT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS — this is the single most valuable thing on the page. (1) SB23-178 (2023) — a unit owners' association MAY NOT prohibit xeriscape, NONVEGETATIVE TURF GRASS, or drought-tolerant landscapes as ground cover on a unit owner's property. Specifically, association rules must 'not prohibit the use of nonvegetative turf grass in the backyard of a unit owner's property,' must not unreasonably require hardscape on more than 20% of the landscaping area, must allow an option of at least 80% drought-tolerant plantings, and must not prohibit vegetable gardens front, back or side. CRITICAL SCOPE LIMIT: this applies ONLY to single-family DETACHED homes — not attached single-family/townhomes, not condos. In Rock Creek that means roughly 60% of homes are protected and the 13% townhome / 27% multifamily share are NOT. (2) SB24-005 (2024), effective 1 January 2026 — local governments may not allow the installation of nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF, or invasive plant species on commercial, institutional or industrial property, common interest community property, street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors. EXEMPTION: 'athletic fields of play.' Residential single-family yards are excluded from this prohibition. NET EFFECT FOR THE CLIENT: HOA COMMON AREAS AND COMMERCIAL SITES ARE NOW LARGELY OFF THE TABLE FOR NEW SYNTHETIC INSTALLS IN COLORADO; residential back yards are legally protected; athletic fields remain wide open. The whole commercial strategy for this site needs to be rebuilt around athletic fields, indoor sports facilities and residential.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: Town of Superior municipal water utility, supplied from Northern Water allocations (Colorado-Big Thompson). Current status: DROUGHT STAGE 0 — no mandatory savings required. Voluntary restrictions were implemented 30 March 2026 and LIFTED 30 April 2026; the Town says it is actively monitoring snowpack and supply projections and may implement additional or mandatory restrictions. Voluntary guidance stands: water before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m., avoid frequent sprinkler use. Superior adopted a Drought Mitigation Plan on 22 June. REBATES: Superior partners with Resource Central for Garden In A Box, free 'Slow the Flow' sprinkler evaluations, lawn replacement incentives, and a Water Efficiency Rebate Program. DOES ARTIFICIAL TURF QUALIFY? Superior does not publish an answer — but the neighbouring Town of Erie's equivalent 2026 program states flatly that 'Artificial Turf is not eligible for this rebate,' and Boulder's Resource Central lawn replacement is defined as conversion to water-wise PLANTS. The honest, defensible line for the page: synthetic turf is almost certainly not rebate-eligible in Superior, do not imply otherwise, and sell on metered water savings instead. Verify by calling the Town at 303-499-3675 before publishing any rebate claim.
facts.soil_and_yard: Superior sits at 5,522 ft on the Boulder-Weld coalfield. Bedrock is the Laramie Formation — sandstone, mudstone, clay and coal — over Pierre Shale, which is the classic Front Range expansive/swelling-clay package. Practical consequences for a turf install: heavy clay subgrade that holds water and moves seasonally, so base depth, positive drainage away from foundations and proper compaction are not optional. UNDERMINING IS A REAL, MAPPED HAZARD HERE — the Colorado Geological Survey's EG-09 documents the Boulder-Weld coalfield with plates for mining extent, depth of cover, pillar locations, probable extracted coal thickness and a subsidence inventory, and notes that 'land development has encroached on the undermined area.' CGS also cautions that absolute predictability of subsidence is not possible from surviving records. The Marshall Fire rebuild lots add a second soil problem on top: scraped, heavily compacted, construction-traffic-worked ground, often with buried debris and lime/ash-altered chemistry, which is exactly the ground where a builder's sod fails and where a properly excavated turf base actually outperforms. Yards are flat to gently sloping — no mountain grades.
facts.housing_stock: Three completely different housing products inside 3.97 sq mi, and the page has to treat them separately. (1) ROCK CREEK / ROCK CREEK RANCH — the master-planned bulk of the town, development began 1987 and ran hard through the 1990s, 2,804 single- and multi-family homes. Mix per the master HOA: roughly 60% single-family detached, 13% townhome/duplex/triplex/fourplex, 27% multifamily. These are 1990s production two-storeys on modest platted lots — usable but not large back yards, typically fenced, flat, sod-and-sprinkler as originally delivered. Now 30+ years old, meaning original bluegrass sod on 30-year-old irrigation. (2) ORIGINAL TOWN SUPERIOR — the pre-1900s coal-town core; tiny, irregular historic lots. Effectively erased: after the Marshall Fire 'only seven of the historic homes survived.' (3) DOWNTOWN SUPERIOR — 21st-century mixed-use, 405 urban flats and townhomes plus 51,000 SF retail and a 270,000 SF life-sciences/R&D campus; near-zero private yard, courtyard and balcony work only. Overlaid on all of it: the Marshall Fire (30 Dec 2021) destroyed 398 structures in Superior — 393 residential, 4 commercial, 1 public — and Sagamore was completely destroyed. So a large, identifiable share of Superior's stock is 2022–2026 new construction sitting on lots that were scraped to bare, compacted dirt. HOA prevalence is very high — Rock Creek Master HOA covers common-area grounds, exterior/roof maintenance, insurance, snow removal and weekly trash/recycling/compost.
facts.who_lives_there: Affluent, highly educated, young-family professional. Median household income $157,909 (2023) — the highest in this batch by a wide margin and roughly 1.6x Erie's. Median home value $795,500 (2023). Population 13,361 (2024 est), 13,094 at the 2020 census. Median age 36.8 — young, family-forming. 77.1% hold bachelor's degrees against 46.4% statewide. Racially: 72.6% White, 13.7% Asian, 10.5% multiracial, 8.1% Hispanic/Latino, 1.1% Black. The Asian share is notably high for Boulder County and tracks the tech/Broomfield-corridor employment base. This is the closest thing in this batch to the client's stated '$10–12/sq ft, upper echelon' target — and unlike Cherry Creek, these buyers are engineers who will read the spec sheet, ask about infill, drainage rate and warranty, and compare three quotes. Price on substance, not on prestige.
facts.golf: No golf course inside Superior. The page must borrow from neighbours, which is fine because they are minutes away. COAL CREEK GOLF COURSE — 585 West Dillon Road, Louisville CO 80027; public, 18 holes, 4,825–7,017 yards, par 72, associated with the City of Louisville; the nearest course and the one a Superior resident actually plays. OMNI INTERLOCKEN GOLF CLUB — Broomfield, immediately south-east. COLORADO NATIONAL GOLF CLUB — Erie, 2700 Vista Parkway, public, home of the CU men's and women's golf teams. No golf-course-lot residential community inside Superior itself, so backyard putting greens here are sold as a home amenity to golfers, not as a 'my lot backs the 7th fairway' product the way they would be in Vista Ridge (Erie) or at Boulder Country Club (Gunbarrel).
facts.commercial_targets: STRONGEST LEAD — WILLIAMS TURF FIELD, the Town's existing synthetic field, explicitly described as a 'synthetic crumb rubber playing surface.' Crumb rubber is falling out of favour and these fields have finite life; this is a named, checkable replacement/renovation prospect, and SB24-005 exempts athletic fields of play so it is legally clean. Other Town athletic assets: Superior Commons Athletic Field (2250 Creek View Way — soccer, rugby); West Multi-Purpose Field; Community Park (1350 Coalton Road — baseball, soccer, football); Scanlan Baseball Field; Stewart Baseball Field; Autrey Park (1830 Honey Creek Drive — 6 pickleball courts, disc golf); Founders Park (601 W. Coal Creek Dr — basketball); Wildflower Park (3151 S. Indiana St — basketball); North Pool tennis courts (4). SCHOOLS (Boulder Valley SD): Superior Elementary, Monarch PK-8, Monarch High School, plus Eldorado PK-8 nearby. Note Monarch High is the area's flagship athletics program. COMMERCIAL/OTHER: the Downtown Superior life-sciences and R&D campus; Superior Marketplace retail; Rock Creek Master HOA common areas — BUT flag that SB24-005 now bars new artificial turf on HOA common-interest-community property and on commercial/institutional/industrial sites, so HOA common areas and retail centres should be pursued only for repair/replacement of existing installs, not new ones.
facts.landmarks: Superior Community Center; Superior Civic Space; Downtown Superior and its central plaza (51,000 SF retail, 405 flats and townhomes, a 270,000 SF life-sciences/tech/R&D campus); Superior Marketplace; Original Town Superior; the Coal Creek Trail; 788.2 acres of town parks and open space; Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport immediately adjacent (a long-running source of noise disputes — a genuine local sore point a resident will recognise instantly); and, unavoidably, the Marshall Fire burn scar and the Sagamore rebuild. Elevation 5,522 ft.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE GOLF, THEN WITH PERMIT FLUENCY. This is one of a handful of places in America where a homeowner can say 'I want a green that rolls like Cherry Hills' and mean the course down the street that hosted three U.S. Opens, two PGA Championships and the 2014 BMW Championship - on neighbouring lots that are 1 to 2.5 acres by zoning right. The page should be an unapologetically bespoke, top-of-range putting-green page, and it is the single best page on the whole site for the $10-12/sq ft repositioning. The second beat is the one no competitor will write, and it is what separates this page from Greenwood Village's: in Cherry Hills Village the obstacle is not an architectural review board, it is the CITY. Sport courts need an Accessory and Recreational Structure permit; R-1 recreational structures sit behind a 75-foot front setback; the Village charges $0.10 per square foot as a sport-court service expansion fee; and the moment a project adds more than 2,500 square feet of impervious surface it triggers a Phase III Drainage Report at $390 of review time, with a Stormwater Construction Permit on top if the site touches a waterway or floodplain. An installer who says 'we pull the CHV recreational-structure permit and handle the Phase III drainage report' beats every competitor leading on price. Third beat, and only third: the drought. Under Denver Water Stage 1 a 1.5-acre bluegrass estate is capped at two watering days a week and banned outright from Oct. 1, 2026. Nothing on this page should read like Greenwood Village's HOA angle, Columbine Valley's low-maintenance-retiree angle, or Sheridan's affordability angle.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE CITY IS THE GATEKEEPER HERE, NOT AN HOA - and this is the single most useful, most checkable competitive edge on the page. Sports courts (how a large backyard green or sport surface reads to the Village) require an Accessory and Recreational Structure permit. Unenclosed recreational-structure setbacks: R-1 75 ft front / 25 ft rear / 25 ft sides; R-2 and the 1.25-acre R-3A tier the same; R-3 50/25/25; R-4 25/15/15; R-5 25 / 7.5 / 7.5. If the structure is enclosed by walls or a fence on more than two sides it is RECLASSIFIED as an accessory structure and starts consuming the enclosed-footprint and structure-count caps (R-1: 3 structures, 1,100 sq ft max footprint; R-5: 2 structures, 500 sq ft) - pool safety fencing excepted. Fees: $340 for 2 hours of accessory/recreational review, $170/hr additional building review, $390 for a Phase III Drainage Report review, $390 for SWMP/GESC review, $195/hr additional civil engineering review, $300 stormwater construction permit, building permit 1% of valuation above $2,000, plus Arapahoe County use tax at 1/8 of 1% of valuation. And a Service Expansion Fee of $0.10 PER SQUARE FOOT for sport courts. Planning must approve before Building or Civil Engineering review, with 10 business days per review cycle. Construction hours: Mon-Fri 7 a.m.-6 p.m., Sat 8 a.m.-4 p.m., no exterior construction Sundays or federal holidays. Adopted codes: 2021 I-codes, 2020 National Green Building Standards, 2023 NEC. Statewide, SB23-178 bars HOAs from prohibiting nonvegetative turf grass in backyards while allowing aesthetic guidelines - relevant inside Buell Mansion and Glenmoor. Zoning is Municipal Code Chapter 16; stormwater is Chapter 19.
facts.water_and_rules: The most fragmented water map in this batch, and a genuinely distinctive page hook. The City states: 'Cherry Hills Village has a Total Service Agreement with Denver Water for the majority of residences.' But the City's own published Water and Sewer District list names more than a dozen micro-utilities inside 6.3 square miles: Charlou Park Water District, Cherry Hills Farm Metro District, Cherry Hills North Metro District, Cherry Hills Village Sanitation District, Cherrymoor Water District, Cherryvale Sanitation District, Country Homes Metro District, Devonshire Heights Water and Sanitation District, East Cherry Hills Water District (routed to the City), Hillcrest Water and Sanitation District, Holly Mutual Water District, Mansfield Heights Water and Sanitation District, South Englewood Sanitation District #1, South University Place Water District, Southgate Water and Sanitation District, Southwest Cherry Hills Water District (routed to Denver Water), plus Englewood Utilities. Cherrymoor South and South Clarkson are dissolved and now handled by the City. RESTRICTIONS (checked 2026-09-07): the City has posted Denver Water's Stage 1 Drought Declaration dated March 25, 2026. Stage 1 runs March 25, 2026 through April 30, 2027 - two assigned days per week (even addresses Sunday/Thursday, odd Wednesday/Saturday), no watering 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; and from Oct. 1, 2026 all lawn watering and all spray irrigation are prohibited, hand-watering of grass included, with penalties to $2,000 plus flow restrictors or disconnection. On a 1.5-acre bluegrass estate that is a five-figure annual irrigation problem and a guaranteed brown lawn. REBATES: Denver Water's ColoradoScaping and the Resource Central lawn replacement / Garden In A Box programs fund water-wise LIVE plantings; no Colorado or Denver Water rebate found that covers artificial turf. Verify by phone before making a rebate claim on the page.
facts.soil_and_yard: Same Front Range expansive-clay setting - CGS: smectitic clays swelling up to 20% by volume, pressures over 30,000 psf, 3% swell already damaging, damage showing as heaved slabs, cracked foundations and buckled flatwork. The locally named Englewood soil series is 35-60% clay, smectitic with slickensides, slow permeability, 0-10% slopes. The Village's own permit packet makes the drainage risk explicit and billable: a soils investigation report is required where referenced in the structural plans; a PHASE III DRAINAGE REPORT is triggered by adding more than 2,500 sq ft of impervious surface area; a Stormwater Management Plan or Grading, Erosion and Sediment Control plan plus a Stormwater Construction Permit is required if disturbing one acre or more OR working adjacent to a waterway, watercourse or floodplain. The Village sits on Little Dry Creek and the High Line Canal and maintains 26 miles of bridle trails and 74 acres of parks and open space, so floodplain and watercourse adjacency is a live condition on many estate lots. Slopes are gentle to rolling with hilltop view lots in R-1.
facts.housing_stock: 2,381 units and effectively 100% detached: 2,334 detached single-family, 38 attached, 9 mobile homes, ZERO units in any multifamily building of any size. Tenure 2,155 owner / 66 renter households - 97% owner-occupied, the highest in this batch. Median home value tops the ACS scale at $2,000,001+. Age: 466 units built 1960-69, 414 built 1970-79, 366 built 1980-89, 344 built 1990-99, 274 built 2000-09, 242 built 1950-59, 140 before 1950, 135 since 2010. So the fabric is 1950s-1980s ranch and traditional estate houses with a continuous scrape-and-rebuild layer on top. LOT SIZE IS THE DEFINING FACT and it is set by zone district: R-1 minimum 2.5 acres, R-2 1.25 acres, R-3 1 acre, R-3A tiered at 2.5 / 1.25 / 1 / 0.5 acre, R-4 0.5 acre, R-5 16,000 sq ft. Named enclaves include Old Cherry Hills (the 111-year-old subdivision renamed from 'Swastika Acres' in 2019), Cherry Hills Farm, Cherry Hills North, Cherry Hills Park, Cherryridge, Cherrymoor, Chaumont in Cherry Hills, Mansfield Heights, Devonshire Heights, Charlou Park, the gated Buell Mansion, and gated Glenmoor of Cherry Hills. Backyards commonly run half an acre to two-plus acres - by far the largest turf canvases in this batch. HOA prevalence is comparatively LOW for the price point: most of the Village is governed by city zoning and by micro water/sanitation districts rather than by a master association, with Buell Mansion and Glenmoor the notable gated exceptions.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 6,354 (ACS 2020-24); 6,442 at the 2020 census. Median household income is top-coded at $250,001+; per capita income $171,382 - five times Sheridan's. Median age 45.3, with 29.3% under 18 and 20.0% aged 65+; 82% married-couple families; 87.8% White, 4.1% Hispanic, 3.6% Asian. Historic and current residents have included John Elway, Peyton Manning and Condoleezza Rice. This is precisely the 'upper echelon / Cherry Creek type' the owner named on the call - and it is the one town in this batch where a $40,000-plus single job is routine.
facts.golf: CHERRY HILLS COUNTRY CLUB - founded 1922, William Flynn design, renovated by Tom Doak in 2008, with a championship 18, a 9-hole par-3 course, eight tennis courts and a lap pool. It has hosted three U.S. Opens (1938, 1960, 1978), two PGA Championships (1941, 1985), the 2005 U.S. Women's Open, the 1993 U.S. Senior Open, U.S. Amateurs in 1990, 2012 and 2023, the 1976 U.S. Senior Amateur and the 2014 BMW Championship. GLENMOOR COUNTRY CLUB, the gated golf community inside the Village ('Glenmoor of Cherry Hills' is a named residential enclave). Columbine Country Club is a short drive southwest in Columbine Valley.
facts.commercial_targets: Kent Denver School - 200 acres, 770 students, 70-plus state championships, campus bordered by the High Line Canal: the marquee synthetic-field prospect in the Village. St. Mary's Academy. Cherry Hills Village Elementary (Cherry Creek School District 5); parts of the city fall in Englewood Schools. Cherry Hills Country Club and Glenmoor Country Club - practice greens, tee lines, short-game areas, clubhouse and pool-surround landscape, and 27 holes between them. The City's 74 acres of parks and open space and 26 miles of bridle trails (John Meade Park / Alan Hutto Memorial Commons is the flagship civic project). Buell Mansion and Glenmoor gated-community common areas and entries. The dozen-plus water and sanitation districts' facility yards. Equestrian estates in R-1 needing dust-free paddock aprons, wash-rack surfaces and barn-alley matting - a product line unique to this town and the Greenwood Village Rural Homestead area.
facts.landmarks: Cherry Hills Country Club and its U.S. Open history. Glenmoor Country Club. Kent Denver School, 4000 E Quincy Ave at Colorado Boulevard - a 200-acre campus centered on two lakes and bordered by the High Line Canal, 770 students in grades 6-12, 68 classrooms in six building complexes, more than 70 state athletic championships. St. Mary's Academy. The High Line Canal Trail and 26 miles of city bridle trails. John Meade Park and the Alan Hutto Memorial Commons; Three Pond Park; Blackmer Common; Woodie Hollow Park; Dahlia Hollow Park. Village Center and City Hall at 2450 E Quincy Ave. Old Cherry Hills, the 111-year-old subdivision renamed from Swastika Acres in 2019. The Buell Mansion gates. The Village was incorporated July 19, 1945 and is named for a grove of cherry trees near the original town site.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE MONEY, BECAUSE HERE THE MONEY IS PUBLISHED: 'The Village bills your water by the square foot of lawn you own. Turf is budgeted at 18 gallons per square foot per season. Go 40% over your budget and you pay $31.50 per thousand gallons instead of $6.75 — and Tier 3 and Tier 4 both went up on January 1, 2026.' No other page in this batch can put a 4.7x price multiplier and a district-published per-square-foot allocation on the screen. And the district itself supplies the closing line: 'Reduce the amount of turf on your property.' Frame the whole page around a single non-renewable fact — the Village's water 'comes entirely from non-renewable groundwater in the Denver Basin aquifers beneath our community,' pumped from 13 wells with no river and no reservoir behind it — which reframes turf conversion from a lifestyle choice into estate stewardship. Then take the second angle that only Castle Pines Village supports: THE PRIVATE PUTTING GREEN. This is 1,900 households at a median $1.45M with a median age of 53.9, 39.2% working from home, wrapped around two Jack Nicklaus courses and the 2024 BMW Championship venue. A tour-spec backyard green on a wooded Dawson Arkose lot where bluegrass never grew under the ponderosas anyway is exactly the $10-12/sq ft job the owner is chasing. Third, quietly technical: this is a certified Firewise community with a fire-hardening programme already running — talk product fire rating and noncombustible perimeter, and mention that the DRC meets 8 a.m. on the third Wednesday, so the calendar sets the start date. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Roxborough's constraint is a prohibition, Stonegate's is a written rear-yard-only covenant, Meridian's is state commercial law, Sterling Ranch's is a builder-era approved-vendor list. Castle Pines Village is the only one where the argument is a published price schedule and a finite aquifer — and the only one where the product is a Nicklaus-neighbourhood putting green rather than a lawn replacement.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Castle Pines Homes Association Design Review Committee. Written DRC approval is required for exterior modifications — explicitly including 'room additions, outdoor kitchens, lighting, hot tubs, play sets, SPORTS COURTS, and more' — and for landscape modifications including 'trees, water features, boulders, SOD, or hardscape items such as patios, deck fire pits, or retaining walls.' The DRC meets at 8:00 a.m. on the THIRD WEDNESDAY OF EACH MONTH (drc@thevillagecastlepines.com, 303-814-1345), which means the calendar, not the crew, sets the project start date — a scheduling fact worth publishing. HOA dues vary by home type and cover security, common-area maintenance, trash/recycling, snow removal, neighbourhood landscaping and amenity access. Five staffed gates and 40 full-time Emergency Services officers on 24/7/365 with an EMT always on shift — access coordination for crews and materials deliveries is a real operational detail. HONEST GAP: the public DRC page does NOT specifically address artificial or synthetic turf, xeriscape, or defensible-space landscaping rules; the governing documents sit behind the resident portal. The page should not assert a specific artificial-turf covenant here without confirming it with the DRC administrator. Also: SB24-005 restricts new artificial turf on common interest community property (athletic fields of play exempt) — directly relevant to the Canyon Club and Summit Club playing fields.
facts.water_and_rules: Castle Pines Village Metropolitan District (cpvmetroco.gov, 5880 Country Club Drive, Castle Rock CO 80108, 303-688-8330). THE CRITICAL FACT: 'Our water supply comes entirely from NON-RENEWABLE GROUNDWATER in the Denver Basin aquifers beneath our community.' Thirteen wells, ~5 million gallons/day treatment capacity being expanded to 7 MGD, two storage tanks and a new 2MG tank in progress. No river, no reservoir, no renewable source — the district is actively 'evaluating several potential renewable water projects.' CURRENT STATUS (checked 2026-09-07): NO mandatory watering restrictions — the district states 'The Village has not reached the point [of] mandatory restrictions.' Instead it controls demand with a BUDGET-BASED RATE SYSTEM, which is far more useful to sell against than a schedule. Each property gets a customised Total Water Budget derived from the SQUARE FOOTAGE OF TURF, BEDDING AND NATIVE GRASS on the lot: TURF IS BUDGETED AT 18 GALLONS PER SQUARE FOOT PER SEASON, bedding at 6 gallons/sq ft, and native grass receives ZERO allocation. Tiers (per thousand gallons): Tier 1 within budget $6.75; Tier 2 (100-120% of budget) $10.50; Tier 3 (120-140%) $16.50; Tier 4 (over 140%) $31.50 — a 4.7x penalty at the top. Tier 3 and Tier 4 rates were INCREASED effective January 1, 2026. Tiered pricing applies April-October; November-March everything bills at Tier 1; unused budget rolls over month to month during peak season. Base rates: $33.40 water + $28.20 sewer + $4.75 storm monthly on a 3/4-inch meter, plus an $89/month Capital Improvement Fee per lot. Over 60% of residents already run WaterSense smart controllers; a 2022 Irrigation Efficiency Program cut district-wide use 20-30%. THE DISTRICT ITSELF TELLS RESIDENTS TO 'Reduce the amount of turf on your property.' TURF REBATE: none — no rebate program at CPVMD, and the state CWCB program closed to applications March 2025 and funded living water-wise landscape only. HONEST OPEN QUESTION: the district does not publish whether converting live turf to ARTIFICIAL turf gets the area re-classified out of the 18-gal/sq ft turf allocation. That is a one-call verification and it is the most valuable single answer on this page.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 6,000-6,500 ft along the Front Range — the highest of the five. The Village sits on Dawson Arkose in a ponderosa pine and gambel oak forest, which weathers to coarse sandy/gravelly decomposed-granite soils on the ridges (good drainage, easy compaction, excellent for a turf base) with clay-rich pockets and expansive bentonite/montmorillonite layers in the swales — the Colorado Geological Survey confirms expansive clay underlies most Front Range development and specifically cites irrigation water entering soil beside foundations as a landscaping-caused damage mechanism. Practical site conditions: heavily sloped, treed lots; long steep driveways; erosion and needle-cast; deep shade under mature ponderosa where bluegrass will never establish (a decisive artificial-turf argument on this specific terrain); and wildfire exposure — the Village is a certified FIREWISE community, having done 'enhanced landscaping to incorporate more fire-resistant plant varieties, the removal of dead or overgrown vegetation and tree limbs, and maintenance aimed at establishing safer spacing around homes.' Residents can request a Firewise certification letter for insurance purposes, which makes turf-product fire ratings and a noncombustible perimeter a legitimate technical conversation here and almost nowhere else in the batch.
facts.housing_stock: Approximately 1,900 homes across 2,800 acres — roughly 1.5 acres of land per home, the lowest density in the batch by a wide margin. 1,733 housing units at the 2020 census with an 8.0% vacancy rate (second-home and lock-and-leave ownership). Development began around 1981 alongside Castle Pines Golf Club and continued in phases through the 2000s, so the stock ranges from early-80s and 90s custom mountain-contemporary and Tudor/Mediterranean estates through 2000s and newer luxury builds. Lots are large, wooded, sloped and irregular — carved into ponderosa pine and gambel oak, with homes sited among trees rather than on graded pads. Usable back-yard turf is often SMALL relative to lot size (the rest is forest, rock outcrop and slope), which is precisely why a defined 800-2,500 sq ft manicured turf area plus a private putting green is the natural product. Median property value $1.45M in 2024, up 15.3% year over year. 100% HOA: every home is in the Castle Pines Homes Association (est. 1981) and served by the Castle Pines Village Metropolitan District (est. 1973).
facts.who_lives_there: ~4,327-4,436 residents. Median household income $250,001 — this is the Census top-code, meaning true median income is at or above a quarter-million dollars; the largest single household-income bracket is $200k+. HOMEOWNERSHIP 100%. Median age 53.9 — twenty-two years older than Meridian. 82.1% married-couple households. 39.2% work from home (highest in the batch) and only 56.6% drive alone. Employed residents 2,152, up 17% year over year, concentrated in Professional/Scientific/Technical Services. Poverty 4.06%; health coverage 98.6%. THIS IS THE 'UPPER ECHELON / CHERRY CREEK TYPE' BUYER THE OWNER ASKED FOR — empty-nester and semi-retired executive money, at home all day looking at the yard, with a golf membership 400 yards away. If $10-12/sq ft works anywhere in this batch, it works here first.
facts.golf: Castle Pines Golf Club — founded by Jack A. Vickers, designed by JACK NICKLAUS, opened 1981; hosted The International on the PGA Tour every year from 1986 through 2006, and hosted the 2024 BMW CHAMPIONSHIP (won by Keegan Bradley at 276, -12). The Country Club at Castle Pines — the community's second Jack Nicklaus course. The Village physically surrounds both. Nearby: The Ridge at Castle Pines North, Sanctuary (private, Sedalia), Colorado Golf Club and Pradera in Parker. No other place in this batch is wrapped around two Nicklaus courses and a major championship venue.
facts.commercial_targets: Castle Pines Golf Club and the Country Club at Castle Pines (practice greens, short-game areas, tee lines, clubhouse surrounds — screen against SB24-005's athletic-fields-of-play exemption). Canyon Club playing field and its 5 tennis / 4 pickleball / basketball / sand volleyball complex. Summit Club playing field and pool deck. Village Lake Fitness Center (indoor training turf, yoga/functional-fitness flooring). The two pocket parks and playgrounds. Wildcat Corner community room grounds and The Village Shoppes. Schools serving the Village: American Academy Castle Pines (charter), Buffalo Ridge Elementary, Timber Trail Elementary, Rocky Heights Middle School, Rock Canyon High School. Also: the Homes Association's own neighbourhood landscaping contracts (dues explicitly cover neighbourhood landscaping) — that is a recurring institutional buyer sitting inside the gates.
facts.landmarks: Castle Pines Golf Club (Nicklaus, 1981; The International 1986-2006; 2024 BMW Championship). The Country Club at Castle Pines. The five staffed entry gates. The Canyon Club swim and court complex — 5 tennis courts, 4 pickleball courts, a basketball court, sand volleyball court, pavilion and playing field. The Summit Club — zero-entry pool, picnic pavilion and playing field. The Village Lake Fitness Center (cardio, lap pool, yoga studio, free weights). Wildcat Corner community room and The Village Shoppes. 13 miles of paved, groomed and natural trails plus two pocket parks. Daniels Park to the west. I-25 at Happy Canyon Road.

name: Englewood

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE SMALL, SHADED, ALLEY-BACKED CITY LOT — the exact opposite of every other page in this batch. Englewood was essentially finished being built by 1960: 6.65 square miles of 1920s–50s bungalows and brick ranches on roughly 5,000–7,000 sq ft grid lots with detached rear garages off alleys, mature trees casting deep shade, and back yards small enough that a whole job is 400–800 sq ft. That reframes the offer completely — not 'replace your lawn' but 'make the one small yard you have work all year round': dog-proof turf on a compacted, root-bound, north-facing patch where bluegrass has already given up, and a compact backyard putting green that actually fits. Two supporting hooks belong to Englewood alone. FIRST, half the city rents (49.2% homeownership) — there is a real landlord and small-multifamily market here that no turf competitor is addressing, sold on zero mowing, zero irrigation cost and no turnover re-landscaping between tenants. SECOND, Englewood is NOT on Denver Water: it has owned its own supply since buying 2,500 acres in Platte Canyon and building McLellan Reservoir in 1948, so the Denver Water rules and the 1 October spray-irrigation ban that everyone in the south metro assumes apply here do not automatically do so — being the installer who can explain that correctly is instant credibility. Then use the postal-boundary quirk deliberately: 'Englewood, CO' addresses reach into Cherry Hills Village and Greenwood Village, where Cherry Hills Country Club, Glenmoor, Kent Denver, St. Mary's Academy and the Denver Tech Center sit — the estate-lot, $10–12/sq ft work hiding behind a modest-income ZIP. That combination, tiny old rented lots plus a millionaire postal shadow, exists nowhere else in the batch.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Colorado SB24-005 from 1 January 2026: no new nonfunctional turf or ARTIFICIAL TURF on commercial, institutional, industrial or HOA common-interest property, or in street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors; artificial turf on athletic fields of play is exempt; single-family residential yards are NOT covered. Given Englewood's dense commercial strip along South Broadway and its large hospital district, that is a real and immediate constraint on commercial sales here — pitch functional and athletic surfaces only. Colorado HB19-1050 protects xeriscape in HOA common and limited common elements but does not mention artificial turf. HONESTY FLAG: I could NOT retrieve Englewood's municipal code (403 from both Municode and Code Publishing), so any Englewood-specific ground-cover, front-yard living-material, or artificial turf provision must be confirmed with the city before it appears on the page. Given the age of the housing and the very small lots, also check alley access, setback, lot-coverage and drainage-onto-neighbouring-property rules — those matter more in Englewood than anywhere else in this batch, and a 5,000 sq ft lot leaves no room for error.
facts.water_and_rules: Englewood's genuine distinction and the page's credibility hook: IT IS ONE OF VERY FEW METRO CITIES THAT OWNS ITS OWN WATER SUPPLY rather than buying from Denver Water. In 1948 the city bought 2,500 acres in Platte Canyon and created McLellan Reservoir, which made Englewood water-independent and, in time, a wholesale water provider to the broader south metro. Wastewater goes to South Platte Water Renewal Partners, jointly owned with Littleton and serving 19 other connecting communities. IMPORTANT HONESTY FLAG: I could NOT load Englewood's utilities page (HTTP 403) and therefore could NOT confirm Englewood's 2026 drought stage, its watering schedule, or whether it offers any turf or landscape rebate. Do not state one. Verify directly with Englewood Utilities before publishing. The honest and genuinely useful framing meanwhile: Englewood is NOT on Denver Water, so Denver Water's Stage 1 rules and its 1 October 2026 spray-irrigation ban do not automatically apply to an Englewood address — which is exactly the thing residents get wrong, and being the installer who can answer it correctly is instant local authority.
facts.soil_and_yard: Englewood sits in the South Platte River valley, which gives it a slightly milder cold semi-arid climate than the rest of the metro and, near the river and Little Dry Creek, deeper alluvial and terrace soils. Away from the river it is the Front Range clay story again — and there is an unusually good checkable detail here: the USDA maintains a soil series literally named ENGLEWOOD — a fine, smectitic clay loam grading to heavy clay loam or clay, 35–60% clay, well to moderately well drained with SLOW permeability, formed in alluvium weathered from adjacent sedimentary bedrock on alluvial fans and valley side slopes, slopes 0–10%, with high shrink-swell potential. BE ACCURATE ON THE PAGE: the series type location is in Douglas County and it is mapped across eastern Colorado and Wyoming, so it is not exclusive to the city — but the name is a legitimate, verifiable hook and no competitor will have found it. Combine with the Colorado Geological Survey's swelling-soil guidance (pressures to 30,000 psf; annual losses exceeding tornadoes, floods, earthquakes and hurricanes combined) and the practical picture for an Englewood job is: flat or gently sloping small lots, slow-percolating clay, mature trees with aggressive surface roots, and shaded north-side yards where bluegrass has already failed. The technical challenge is drainage and base depth on a 5,000 sq ft lot with a rear alley and a neighbour three feet away — not grade.
facts.housing_stock: The oldest and smallest-lot housing in the batch, and the only town here that is majority renter. Settlement dates to 1858 gold on Little Dry Creek and Thomas Skerritt's Orchard Place (1860); incorporated 9 May 1903. The decisive fact is that MOST OF THE CITY WAS BUILT UP BY 1960 — so the stock is dominated by 1920s–40s bungalows and 1950s brick ranches and minimal-traditional cottages on tight, flat, alley-served grid lots, typically around 5,000–7,000 sq ft with genuinely small back yards, plus a heavy layer of 1960s–70s apartment and duplex product. 17,045 housing units in 2020 across just 6.65 sq mi, 6.4% vacancy. HOMEOWNERSHIP IS ONLY 49.2% — half the city rents — with a median property value of $572,900. HOA prevalence in the old core is very low; newer condo/townhome and CityCenter-adjacent product carries associations. Two physical facts shape every job: many lots have detached rear garages off alleys, so the back yard is a small enclosed rectangle; and a real share of properties are landlord-owned, which changes the sale from lifestyle to maintenance economics.
facts.who_lives_there: 34,129 residents (33,659 in the 2020 census); median household income $86,800 (up 5.83% year on year); median age 37.4; poverty 7.7%; 21,242 employed. Predominantly non-Hispanic white (~23,200); 95.5% US citizens, 8.25% foreign-born; average commute 22.6 minutes, the shortest in the batch. Employment skews professional/scientific/technical (2,851), healthcare and social assistance (2,806) and retail (2,366). Younger, denser and more transient than Centennial or Littleton. BUT NOTE THE INCOME GRADIENT AT THE BORDER: the 'Englewood, CO' postal footprint historically reaches into Cherry Hills Village (median household income $190,805 in 2000; median house value about $1.19m in 2005; residents have included John Elway, Peyton Manning and Nikola Jokic) and Greenwood Village (median household income $116,147 in 2000; ZIPs 80110–80112, 80121, 80155; home to the Denver Tech Center, Fiddler's Green Amphitheatre, Empower Retirement and Charter Communications). VERIFY current USPS preferred-city defaults before leaning on this — Wikipedia's Greenwood Village entry disputes the 'Englewood address' framing — but the DTC and Cherry Hills addresses that read 'Englewood' are exactly the upper-echelon buyer the owner wants.
facts.golf: BROKEN TEE ENGLEWOOD GOLF COURSE — the city's own municipal course (brokenteegolf.com now redirects to englewoodco.gov/parks-recreation-library-golf/broken-tee-golf-course; the page returned 403 for me, so confirm the address, the par-3 course and the range details directly with the city before publishing). Far more commercially important is what sits just over the line: CHERRY HILLS COUNTRY CLUB in Cherry Hills Village — founded 1922, William Flynn design, restored by Tom Doak 2008–09, at 5,300 ft — host of three U.S. Opens (1938, 1960, 1978), two PGA Championships (1941, 1985), the 1993 U.S. Senior Open, the 2005 U.S. Women's Open, three U.S. Amateurs (1990, 2012, 2023) and the 2014 BMW Championship, and the stage for Arnold Palmer driving the first green in the 1960 U.S. Open; it has a championship 18 plus a 9-hole par-3 course. GLENMOOR COUNTRY CLUB is also in Cherry Hills Village. That adjacency — not Englewood's own housing — is the premium putting-green market.
facts.commercial_targets: CRAIG HOSPITAL — a nationally known spinal-cord and traumatic brain injury rehabilitation hospital, and an unusually strong fit for accessible, wheelchair-firm, all-weather synthetic surfaces in therapy courtyards and outdoor rehab space; a marquee reference if won. SWEDISH MEDICAL CENTER. ENGLEWOOD PUBLIC SCHOOLS — Englewood High School, Colorado's Finest High School of Choice, two middle schools and four elementary schools; plus All Souls School (K-8). Pirates Cove water park and Belleview Park. Broken Tee Golf Course practice areas. The Museum of Outdoor Arts. Just over the line in Cherry Hills Village with Englewood-adjacent addresses: ST. MARY'S ACADEMY and KENT DENVER SCHOOL, plus Cherry Hills Country Club and Glenmoor Country Club. Dog daycares, groomers and veterinary practices along South Broadway — functional use and therefore unaffected by SB24-005. CRITICAL CAVEAT for the whole list: under SB24-005 ornamental synthetic landscape at commercial and institutional sites is now prohibited, so every commercial pitch here must be framed as play areas, athletic surfaces or functional therapy/pet surfaces.
facts.landmarks: CityCenter Englewood — city hall, the public library, the MUSEUM OF OUTDOOR ARTS, city departments, courts and an RTD light rail station — built on the site of CINDERELLA CITY, which opened in 1968 as the largest mall west of the Mississippi and was demolished about thirty years later for transit-oriented redevelopment; SWEDISH MEDICAL CENTER and CRAIG HOSPITAL, a top-ten rehabilitation hospital for spinal cord and traumatic brain injury, together forming the city's economic backbone; Pirates Cove water park (opened 2004); Belleview Park, the largest city park, with its reservoir; the South Platte River trails; Broken Tee Golf Course; the South Broadway antique and retail corridor; Little Dry Creek, where gold was found in 1858; the Thomas Skerritt / Orchard Place heritage.
