The Colorado Geological Survey treats expansive soil as Colorado's most significant geologic hazard — clays 'can expand up to 20% by volume when exposed to water and exert a force of up to 30,000 pounds-per-square-foot' — and treats HEAVING BEDROCK as a separate, more severe hazard 'related to expansive soils' that is 'more complex... and is capable of causing exceptional damage to houses, roads, and utilities,' responsible for 'tens of millions of dollars worth of damage along the Front Range piedmont.' Douglas County created a Dipping Bedrock Overlay District after several million dollars of damage followed mid-1980s development. Practical translation for the page: on the Valley side, base depth, compaction and sub-drainage ARE the job — the ground moves seasonally, and a turf lawn installed on an inadequate base will ripple and seam-split within a few years. Valley lots also carry real slope; Plains lots are flatter.
facts.housing_stock: 33,811 people in 13,772 housing units (2020 Census), 2.5% vacant, median age 40.8. Development history is the key: Johns-Manville bought the ranch in 1971 for a corporate campus plus planned community (the campus later became Lockheed Martin); per Wikipedia, 'the plans for the housing community quickly evolved into present-day Ken Caryl Valley's neighborhoods, whose homes were mostly completed by 1997.' So three genuinely different turf jobs sit inside one CDP: the PLAINS east of the hogback (1970s-80s tract ranch/split-level/two-storey, tighter lots, some attached product), the VALLEY west of the hogback (1980s-90s larger semi-custom and custom homes on bigger, sloped lots inside the private open space), and NORTH RANCH (its own association at kencaryl.org, centred on Bradford Park). CRITICAL DENSITY INSIGHT: the CDP is 6,313 acres, but the Master Association controls 4,800 acres of private open space. The housing is therefore concentrated onto roughly a quarter of the land — gross density is 2.18 units/acre, the highest in this batch. Ken Caryl LOOKS spacious because of the open space; actual backyards are smaller than the address implies. Do not sell it as an estate-lot market. HOA prevalence is effectively 100%: the Ken-Caryl Ranch Master Association covers the community, and 11 subassociations sit under it — Deer Creek Villas, Enclave, Manor Ridge, Mountain Gate, Mountain Gate II, Mountain Gate III, The North Ranch at Ken-Caryl, Office Park Association, Settlement, Sunset Ridge, West Ranch. The site states subassociations 'are required to follow Ken-Caryl Ranch Master Association governing documents, rules and regulations, but may also have additional rules, restrictions and supplemental governing documents specific to their neighborhoods' — i.e. two layers of approval.
facts.who_lives_there: Median age 40.8; 21.7% under 18 and 16.0% aged 65+; 82.8% white, 11.9% Hispanic or Latino; 2.5% vacancy with a 0.8% homeowner vacancy rate, indicating a very stable, low-turnover owner market. Family-heavy and school-driven (seven feeder elementaries). HONEST GAP: current household income could not be verified this session — api.census.gov now requires an API key, and Census Reporter, city-data, Niche, BestPlaces and Zillow all blocked automated access. Treat any income figure as needing a fresh pull before publication.
facts.golf: Ken Caryl Ranch itself has NO golf course — this is the commercially important fact, because it means the backyard putting green has no local substitute. Nearby and named: Raccoon Creek Golf Course (7301 W. Bowles Ave, Littleton, CO 80123, verified from its own site); Foothills Golf Course and Meadows Golf Club, both operated by the Foothills Park & Recreation District (district HQ 6612 S. Ward St, Littleton, CO 80127 — the same 80127 ZIP as Ken Caryl); Red Rocks Country Club in Morrison, just over the hogback. Note the local naming echo: Deer Creek Middle School and Deer Creek Canyon sit immediately west.
facts.commercial_targets: Ken-Caryl Ranch Metropolitan District — parks, greenbelts, athletic fields, tennis and pickleball courts, aquatics, Fitness Center and the Equestrian Center (funded by property taxes on residential and commercial property within the Ranch, plus programme fees). Schools (Jeffco): Bradford K8, Colorow, Coronado, Mortenson, Shaffer, Stony Creek and Ute Meadows elementaries; Deer Creek, Falcon Bluffs and Summit Ridge middle schools; Chatfield High School and Dakota Ridge High School. The Ken-Caryl Office Park Association is a listed subassociation and a direct commercial door. Foothills Park & Recreation District facilities in the same ZIP: Foothills Fieldhouse, Foothills Sports Arena, Edge Ice Arena, Peak Community & Wellness Center, Ridge Recreation Center, Lilley Gulch Recreation Center. IMPORTANT: under SB24-005, pitch these public and district bodies ONLY on athletic fields of play — general landscape turf on their grounds is now prohibited.
facts.landmarks: The Manor House (the surviving historic ranch house, now an events venue); the Bradford/Perley House ruins; Tincup Mountain; Colorow's Cave (Colorow Elementary is named for it); the Dakota Hogback forming the wall between Plains and Valley; 4,800 acres of private, resident-controlled open space; the Ken-Caryl Equestrian Center; the Ranch House at 7676 S. Continental Divide Rd; the Community Center at 1 Club Dr; the Veterans Monument; Bradford Park in North Ranch; Deer Creek Canyon immediately west.

name: Welby

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH LOT SIZE AND FARM HERITAGE — Welby is where the big jobs are. This is the only town in the batch with a published, county-sourced parcel figure: 2,384 R-1-C lots averaging 11,018 sq ft (a quarter acre) plus 158 agricultural A-1 parcels averaging 2.82 acres, with A-1 covering 22.2% of the community. It has the highest owner-occupancy of the five (72.5%) and a growing population. That means the largest square footage per job, real multi-hole putting greens, big dog runs on hobby-farm parcels, and full-yard conversions — a completely different economic proposition from Federal Heights' 400 sq ft manufactured-home pads or Sherrelwood's uniform ranch backyards. Wrap it in the story only Welby can tell: settlers secured Clear Creek water rights in the 1800s, about 300 Italian families were farming here by 1920, they formed one of Colorado's first vegetable co-ops in 1923, and Welby was the biggest vegetable-producing area in Adams County until 1960 — and that same community is now under a Denver Water total outdoor watering ban from October 1, 2026. A farming town that can no longer water. Back it with the genuinely bimodal ground: dead-flat Nunn clay loam at 0-1% slope that will not perc (Ksat 3.1) in the old village, versus the Samsil bluff above Clear Creek at 3-35% slopes with 54% clay and Ksat 0.60 — the worst-draining soil in this entire batch. Two different install specs inside one town, which is a credibility marker no template page can fake.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated Adams County. Adams County Code Compliance enforces blight including 'tall, overgrown grass, weeds and brush (12 inches)'; the county's own Welby plan records that residents raised property upkeep and code compliance in north Welby as a top concern, so this is a live, locally-recognised issue rather than a generic one — a strong, honest hook for a maintenance-free surface. State law: HB21-1229 means the PUD associations (Devonshire, High Point Village, Crown Park, Shiloh Townhome and the rest) may regulate but not prohibit artificial turf in a unit's backyard. SB24-005 bans new artificial turf from January 1, 2026 on commercial, institutional, industrial and common-interest-community property, rights-of-way, parking lots and medians, exempting only athletic fields of play — which matters in Welby because so much of its land is zoned industrial (I-1 alone is 21.7% of total area, 181 parcels averaging 104,797 sq ft). Those industrial frontages are now closed to new artificial turf. Adams County's own landscaping standards could not be retrieved and are unverified.
facts.water_and_rules: North Washington Street Water and Sanitation District (EPA PWS ID CO0101105), offices at 3172 E 78th Ave — in the historic heart of Welby — serving about 14,500 people on 3,637 connections. Denver Water lists it as a MASTER METER distributor, so Denver Water's restrictions govern. As checked 2026-09-07: MANDATORY rules effective March 25, 2026 — no more than two days per week on assigned days (even addresses Sunday/Thursday, odd Wednesday/Saturday, multi-family, commercial, HOA and government Tuesday/Friday), watering only 6 pm to 10 am, a declared drought targeting a 20% reduction, and from October 1, 2026 no outdoor watering permitted at all with fines. Note the historical irony worth using on the page: Welby settlers secured water rights from Clear Creek for irrigation in the 1800s and that water made this the biggest vegetable-producing area in Adams County until 1960 — the same community is now under a total outdoor watering ban. Parts of ZIP 80229 are also served by the City of Thornton and Castlewood Water and Sanitation District, so verify the provider per address. Rebates: via Denver Water, which offers toilet and sprinkler-nozzle rebates and the ColoradoScaping planting programme; artificial turf is not rebated.
facts.soil_and_yard: Welby is bimodal, and the two halves need different installs. SSURGO at 78th/York (the old village core, on the flats): Nunn clay loam, 0 to 1 percent slopes, 85% Nunn, 'Fine, smectitic, mesic Aridic Argiustolls' — measured LEP 5.4, 32.7% clay, Ksat 3.1 µm/s. Dead flat, expansive, and slow. SSURGO at 84th/Washington (the bluff above Clear Creek): Samsil-Shingle complex, 3 to 35 PERCENT SLOPES — Samsil is 'Clayey, montmorillonitic (calcareous), mesic, shallow Ustic Torriorthents' with measured LEP 7.5, 53.75% clay and Ksat 0.60 µm/s. That is the highest shrink-swell and the slowest-draining soil found anywhere in this batch — roughly 60 times less permeable than Derby's sandy loam — and it is shallow to shale bedrock on slopes up to 35%. Practical consequence: on the 0-1% Nunn flats there is no natural fall at all, so the base must create the fall and a drain must carry water somewhere; on the Samsil bluff the job is terracing, anchoring and erosion control over shallow clay that will not accept water. Drainage context: Clear Creek was covered by a 2006 major drainageway master plan from its South Platte confluence to Golden, and the county notes development has encroached into the Clear Creek floodplain — check floodplain status on riverside parcels.
facts.housing_stock: The biggest private yards in the batch, and the only place here with hard parcel-size data. Adams County's own Welby community plan (April 2014) publishes a zoning table: 2,384 R-1-C residential parcels averaging 11,018 sq ft each — a genuine quarter-acre — plus 158 A-1 agricultural parcels averaging 122,945 sq ft (2.82 acres) and 9 A-3 parcels averaging 163,662 sq ft (3.76 acres). A-1 land is 22.2% of Welby's total area. That is a documented class of 2-4 acre semi-rural parcels sitting inside the Denver metro. ACS 2024 5-yr (B25034) on 5,985 units: 19.0% built 1950-59, 16.6% 1960-69, 27.0% 1970-79, then a real modern wave — 9.9% 1990s and 12.6% 2000-09. B25024: 59.1% single-family detached and 12.1% single-family ATTACHED (the townhome PUDs), 8.1% manufactured. ACS median value $385,000, and 72.5% owner-occupied — the HIGHEST ownership rate of the five. The county plan records 68% owner-occupancy back in 2010 and notes that 85% of housing units sit in north Welby while south and east Welby hold only 761 units across 61% of the land area — the empty, large-parcel half. Named PUDs to reference: Chapparal Village, Devonshire Square, The Estates at Devonshire, High Point Village, Springbrook Park, Riverside Subdivision, Crown Park Subdivision, Riverdale Farms, Shiloh Townhome, McDougal Street Subdivision, Roller Subdivision. HOAs exist only on those PUDs; the older farm-lot and 1950s-70s stock has none.
facts.who_lives_there: 2020 census population 15,553; 2024 ACS 16,197 with a projected 16,269 for 2026 — one of the few growing places here. Median household income $80,026; 12.1% of families below poverty. 59.1% Hispanic, 33.9% White, 3.2% Asian. Median age 35.0. Deep multi-generational roots: about 300 Italian families were farming Welby by 1920 and the community formed the Vegetable Producers Cooperative Association in 1923, one of Colorado's first co-operative vegetable marketing efforts. The county plan records 6,202 residents commuting out for work and only 158 who both live and work in Welby.
facts.golf: Genuinely thin, and the page should not pretend otherwise. Within 8 km there is only The Greg Mastriona Golf Courses at Hyland Hills. Widening to 12 km brings in Riverdale Dunes & Knolls Golf Course (Riverdale Road, Brighton) — the Adams County-owned pair and the nearest course a Welby local would actually name — plus Thorncreek Golf Course (Thornton), Willis Case (Denver), Indian Tree (Arvada) and City Park Golf Course. No course inside Welby and no golf community. The real golf story here is not proximity, it is SPACE: the quarter-acre R-1-C lots and the 2-4 acre A-1 parcels are the only ground in this batch that can take a serious multi-hole backyard green rather than a single practice hole.
facts.commercial_targets: Schools (Adams 12 Five Star and Mapleton Public Schools): Assumption Catholic School (E 78th Ave), Welby Community School / Welby Montessori (E 78th Ave), Coronado Hills Elementary (Downing Drive), McElwain Elementary, Monterey Community School (McElwain Blvd), Bertha Heid Clayton Elementary, Clayton Street Elementary, York International School, Adventure Elementary (Delta St), The New America School (Washington St), and Mapleton's Skyview Campus just north on E 88th Ave, which also houses an Anythink Library branch. Sports: Steele Athletics (E 77th Ave) — a named sports centre inside Welby and the most direct indoor-facility target here; Eminence Barbell Club. Parks/HOA common areas: Rotella Park and Steele Street Park (Adams County Parks), plus the PUD associations listed above — though note SB24-005 closes HOA common areas to new artificial turf. Employers with frontage and yards: Welby Gardens/Hardy Boy Plants, Boyer's Coffee, Paisano Sausage. The county actively promotes the area's Enterprise Zone south of E. 78th Avenue.
facts.landmarks: Assumption Church, the Assumption School and the rectory at E. 78th Avenue and York Street — dedicated 1912, still standing, and described by the county as the iconic historic heart of Welby. Rotella Park, the 40-acre county park acquired in 1972 in the middle of the community, given a $1.6m renovation. Welby Gardens / Hardy Boy Plants at SH224 and Clayton Street — a working wholesale greenhouse operation shipping nationally and to Canada, and a direct survival of the farming economy. Boyer's Coffee at 73rd Avenue and Washington Street. Paisano Sausage at 73rd and Washington. Coronado Hills and Coronado Parkway. The Niver Creek Trail along Coronado Parkway, and the Clear Creek and South Platte River regional trails. Twin Lakes Park. Steele Street Park. The Cline School site (built 1884 on land donated by railroader David Moffat, across from Assumption). Welby is named for Arthur E. Welby, a vice president of the Denver, Laramie and Northwestern Railroad, whose subsidiary platted a 20-block townsite in 1909.

sources: https://adamscountyco.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/WELBY.pdf (Welby: Where Deep Roots Grow, Adams County, April 2014 — history, housing, zoning/parcel table Appendix C, parks, schools, drainage)

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH GEOLOGY, THEN THE ONE-UTILITY ORDER. Golden is a mining town literally built on mined clay — the city's own championship golf course sits in an old clay pit with the mining equipment still standing on the fairways — and that Laramie Formation clay is the steeply dipping, montmorillonite-rich kind the Colorado Geological Survey names as the differential-heave condition, at pressures up to 30,000 psf. No other town in this batch lets the soil argument be made this vividly or this checkably, and no other town has a landmark that proves it. Open on base preparation, sub-base and drainage: an install on a Lookout Mountain hillside or a downtown lot over dipping clay is an engineering job, not a carpet job — which is exactly the argument that justifies $10-12 a square foot instead of $7, and exactly the argument the 'upper echelon' customer responds to. Pair it with regulatory clarity: Golden has ONE water provider and ONE Stage 1 order, effective 1 May 2026 and amended 19 July, allowing two irrigation events a week, nothing between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m., banning home car washing outright (stricter than Arvada), on top of a 6.2% rate increase in January 2026. Simple to state, impossible to dodge. Third, the lot reality: downtown Golden backyards are small and alley-accessed, which favours precise, high-margin small installs, pet turf and backyard putting greens over big square-footage jobs — and the putting-green pitch writes itself in the town whose city-owned course is voted Denver's best. That is a genuinely different lead from Wheat Ridge three miles east, which is flat, large-lotted former farm ground with a fragmented water picture, and from Lakewood, whose whole story is that nobody knows which utility bills them. Cannibalisation note: Golden is far enough west and south of the northern-Colorado corridor that NoCo Turf Co. overlap risk is low — but confirm against nocoturf.com before publishing.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Golden operates a FORM-BASED code, which is unusual in this batch and worth explaining plainly: Use Zones (Municipal Code Chapter 18.28) govern permitted uses and use standards, a Form Zone Overlay (Chapter 18.29) governs structure types, setbacks, height and lot standards, and Form Type standards affect building design, lot layout and access. Property-specific zoning is looked up on the city's online planning map. Specific artificial-turf provisions were NOT readable — confirm with Planning at planning@cityofgolden.gov or (303) 384-8000 before publishing any code claim, and note the city is in PHASE 3 OF A FULL ZONING CODE REWRITE as of 2026, so anything written on this page has a short shelf life and should be dated. Historic downtown properties may additionally face design review. State law C.R.S. 38-33.3-106.5(1)(i.5) (HB21-1229) applies to Golden's HOAs — no prohibition on nonvegetative turf grass in the BACKYARD of a detached single-family home, no unreasonable hardscape requirement above twenty percent of the landscaping area, an 80%-drought-tolerant option must be allowed, and three water-wise front-yard designs must be pre-approved — though HOA prevalence is low in the historic core. SB24-005 also applies: from 1 January 2026 the state prohibits installing nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF or invasive species on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common-interest-community property and rights-of-way, with ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY EXPRESSLY EXEMPT — which protects the sports-field line while constraining commercial landscape work.
facts.water_and_rules: The CITY OF GOLDEN IS the water utility — one provider, one order, which is the cleanest regulatory story in this batch and the exact opposite of Lakewood's and Wheat Ridge's patchwork. Golden declared STAGE 1 DROUGHT RESTRICTIONS effective 1 MAY 2026, with an AMENDED ORDER effective 19 JULY 2026. Outdoor irrigation is limited to TWO IRRIGATION EVENTS PER CALENDAR WEEK, the week running Sunday 12:00 a.m. to Saturday 11:59 p.m.; an irrigation event runs from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m. the following day, and NO outdoor irrigation is permitted between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. AT-HOME VEHICLE WASHING IS PROHIBITED (commercial car washes using recycled water are allowed) — notably STRICTER than Arvada, which still permits bucket washing, and a good comparative detail for the page. Leaks must be repaired within 10 days and sprinklers adjusted to prevent overspray. Under the amended order the city may limit, restrict or temporarily suspend commercial water use from the bulk water station. WATER RATES ROSE 6.2% ON 1 JANUARY 2026. The city offers free AquaHawk usage monitoring with custom leak alerts, updating roughly four times daily with a six-hour lag, and publishes an irrigation timing chart (fixed spray 12-18 minutes, rotors 24-36 minutes, manual sprinklers 18-27 minutes in peak months) with a cycle-and-soak recommendation. Lawn replacement and native plant programmes run through Resource Central; those fund PLANTINGS and artificial turf eligibility is NOT confirmed — assume ineligible. Water Efficiency Coordinator: Katie Duke, waterconservation@cityofgolden.net.
facts.soil_and_yard: Golden is the textbook Front Range soil case and the most vivid soil story available in this batch. The city sits where Clear Creek cuts through the hogback, on steeply dipping Cretaceous bedrock whose Laramie Formation clays were MINED COMMERCIALLY for brick and pottery clay — which is literally why Fossil Trace Golf Club has clay-mining equipment sitting on the course. That means expansive, montmorillonite-rich clay at or near the surface, steeply dipping, which is exactly the condition the Colorado Geological Survey identifies as producing DIFFERENTIAL HEAVE and the characteristic 'roller-coaster' road surfaces. CGS cites swelling pressures up to 30,000 pounds per square foot and names cracked driveways, sidewalks and basement floors as the signature damage. Layer on real slope in the hillside subdivisions below North and South Table Mountain and Lookout Mountain, plus alluvial creek-bottom ground along Clear Creek. Practical read: in Golden, base preparation, sub-base depth and drainage design ARE the job, and a shallow install on dipping clay will show movement.
facts.housing_stock: Bimodal, and both modes are small-job, high-margin work rather than big square footage. (1) The historic downtown grid: Golden was founded 16 June 1859 during the Pike's Peak Gold Rush as Golden City, named for Thomas L. Golden, and served as territorial capital from 1862 to 1867 — so the core is a compact plat of Victorian and early-twentieth-century houses on small lots with tiny, often alley-accessed backyards, plus a substantial student-rental share near Colorado School of Mines. (2) The hillside subdivisions: post-war through 2000s development climbing toward Lookout Mountain and the Table Mountains, where lots get larger, steeper and view-oriented, and where slope drives the entire scope of work. 20,399 residents (2020 census). Median age 34.1 — the youngest in this batch, pulled down by Mines. 15.0% under 18, 13.8% aged 65 or over. HOA prevalence is low in the historic core and higher in the newer hillside tracts. Golden is currently in Phase 3 of a full zoning code rewrite, so the development picture is actively changing.
facts.who_lives_there: 20,399 residents (2020 census), 84.3% white, 9.7% Hispanic or Latino, 3.8% Asian, median age 34.1. Median household income $49,115 and median family income $67,414 — those are 2000 CENSUS figures and are badly stale; they must be refreshed from current ACS before publishing, and Golden's real median is now far higher. The employment base is unusually distinctive: Colorado School of Mines, the Coors Brewery, and the National Earthquake Information Center, alongside county government as the Jefferson County seat. Golden is also the birthplace of the Jolly Rancher. The student population depresses the median income statistic while the owner-occupier households on the hillsides are considerably wealthier — do not let the headline number mislead the positioning.
facts.golf: Fossil Trace Golf Club, 3050 Illinois Street, Golden, CO 80401 — operated by the City of Golden, opened in 2003 on land where dinosaur remains were found during construction. Actual Triceratops footprints and other prehistoric fossils are visible near the 12th green, a palm-leaf trace fossil inspired the course logo, and massive remnants of CLAY MINING EQUIPMENT are scattered through the layout. Repeatedly named Best Golf Course in Denver by Colorado publications, drawing golfers from all fifty states and more than forty countries. Applewood Golf Course, 14001 W. 32nd Avenue, Golden, CO 80401 — public, par-71, operating since the 1960s, KemperSports-managed, with Bunkers Taproom and The Vista at Applewood events venue.
facts.commercial_targets: Sports complexes: Tony Grampsas Memorial Sports Complex and Trail (baseball, pickleball, dog park), Ulysses Sports Complex (skate park, dog park), and Lions Park Ballfields (baseball, tennis, pickleball). IMPORTANT: Rooney Road Sports Complex TRANSFERRED to Jefferson County Open Space on 1 January 2025 — pitch Jeffco, not the city, for that facility. Other parks with amenities: Golden Heights Park (playground, basketball, skate park), Beverly Heights Park, DeLong Park, Southridge Park, Hockey Stop Park (in-line hockey rink). The city runs 19 parks and 42 miles of paved trails. Facilities: Golden Community Center, The Splash aquatic park, Clear Creek RV Park. Schools (Jeffco Public Schools): Golden High School and Bell Middle School. Colorado School of Mines athletics. The Coors / Molson Coors campus. Downtown Washington Avenue hospitality and patio businesses. Note that under SB24-005 the athletic-fields-of-play exemption makes the sports complexes the cleanest commercial category to pursue.
facts.landmarks: The 'Howdy Folks! Welcome to Golden' arch over Washington Avenue. The Coors Brewery. Colorado School of Mines. Clear Creek and Clear Creek Whitewater Park, described by the city as one of Golden's most unique and popular recreational attractions. North Table Mountain and South Table Mountain. Lookout Mountain. The Colorado Railroad Museum. The National Earthquake Information Center. The Triceratops tracks at Fossil Trace's 12th green. Golden's status as Colorado territorial capital, 1862-1867. Jefferson County seat.

name: Eastlake

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE MONEY AND THE PERMIT. Eastlake is the one place in this batch where the water provider will actually write a cheque for artificial turf — up to $2/sq ft, $2,000 lifetime cap — and simultaneously the one place with a detailed, enforceable turf code a homeowner will get wrong on their own. The page should be 'Thornton's artificial turf rebate and permit, done right': the rebate maths on a 200–1,000 sq ft project, the Minor Development Permit that must be pulled BEFORE installation, the 25% front-yard cap versus unlimited rear yard, the 3-ft property-line buffer, the tree-equivalent planting requirement, the 8-year fade warranty, the 2 in/hr drainage backing, glued-not-sewn seams, and above all the PFAS-free documentation standard that most cheap imported turf physically cannot satisfy. That last point is a natural competitive moat — it disqualifies low-bid installers and directly justifies $10–12/sq ft. Wrap it in the railroad-agricultural-townsite identity (1920 grain elevator, street grid skewed to the UP tracks, 1914–1959 white frame cottages on small flat lots, N Line terminus) so it does not read as generic Thornton. This is the exact OPPOSITE lead from Aurora a few miles south, where the story is prohibition and $500 fines rather than a rebate — Eastlake's page says 'they'll pay you', Aurora's says 'you're not allowed to do anything else'.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE STRONGEST REGULATORY HOOK IN THE BATCH — Thornton has a real, detailed, enforceable artificial turf code (2026 Artificial Turf Rules, effective 1/1/2026; Thornton City Code Figure 452.1, Sections 18-537(d), 18-538, 18-556). A MINOR DEVELOPMENT PERMIT is required BEFORE installing artificial turf as landscaping (Planning Dept Planner of the Day: POD.info@thorntonco.gov, 303-538-7295). Allowed only in front, back and side yards of single-family detached and attached dwellings. Rear yards and enclosed side yards: unlimited. Front and unenclosed side yards: artificial turf shall NOT exceed 25% of the landscape area. BUFFERS: 3 ft from all property lines (may extend to the front property line if a 3 ft buffer separates turf from the street sidewalk); 8 ft from the front wall of any building and 3 ft from other building walls or impervious surfaces when outside the rear/enclosed side yard; 3 ft from deciduous tree trunks and no closer than the dripline of evergreens; buffers must be permeable — wood mulch, gravel or rock max 2 in diameter. LIVING PLANTS REQUIRED in front/unenclosed side yards: one 'tree equivalent' per first 750 sq ft of turf (one 2-inch deciduous tree, OR one 6-ft evergreen, OR 10 #5 shrubs, OR 20 #1 ornamental grasses), plus half a tree equivalent per additional 250 sq ft. PRODUCT: cut-pile infill type; polypropylene, biobased, nylon, polyester or polyethylene fibres; hole-punched backing on a uniform grid no more than 4in x 6in on centre; backing must drain at least 2 inches per hour; minimum EIGHT-YEAR fade warranty; must be green like natural grass; indoor/outdoor carpet expressly prohibited as a substitute. PFAS-FREE IS MANDATORY, with a strict evidentiary standard: either a manufacturer/distributor public statement covering the entire PFAS class ('PFC-free' is explicitly insufficient, and ambiguous statements are rejected), or independent third-party testing of total organic fluorine published online — the manufacturer's own testing does NOT count. Documentation is submitted at permit application and approval is at the director's sole discretion. INSTALLATION: existing sod/ground cover must be removed; sub-base minimum 3 inches of compacted aggregate (coarse and fine layers may be separated by geotextile per manufacturer spec) and the base system must absorb at least half an inch of precipitation before generating sheet-flow runoff; anchored at all edges and seams with manufacturer-recommended pins/nails; ALL SEAMS GLUED, NOT SEWN; infill of clean-washed sand and/or ground shells unless the manufacturer does not require it. MAINTENANCE: per Code 18-556 plus cleaning/sanitising with biodegradable products, brushing, hand-raking worn areas, repairing depressions, brushing back displaced infill, eliminating odours, matting, weeds and loose edges, and REPLACEMENT when it can no longer simulate healthy living turf. Statewide overlay: SB24-005 bars artificial turf on HOA common-interest property from 1 Jan 2026; HB19-1050 protects xeriscape in HOA common elements but does NOT mention artificial turf, so an HOA may still refuse it on an individual lot.
facts.water_and_rules: THE decisive field. Thornton Water. Stage 1 drought restrictions effective 15 March 2026: lawn/turf watering limited to two days per week (customer chooses which days), no outdoor watering 10 a.m.–6 p.m., sprinklers off until 1 May. Thornton cites the lowest snowpack in 20 years across its Upper South Platte and Clear Creek watersheds. CRITICALLY, Thornton is the ONLY provider in this batch whose rebate explicitly pays for artificial turf: the residential Water-Wise Landscape Rebate pays up to $2/sq ft on qualifying 200–1,000 sq ft projects, lifetime maximum $2,000 per residential lot. The turf must replace high-water-demand lawn (e.g. Kentucky bluegrass) on an existing lot, or areas of no landscaping on a new-construction lot. Turf laid on existing hardscape (patios, side-yard concrete, pathways) does NOT qualify. Requires: Minor Development Permit first, HOA approval where applicable, receipts for ALL materials (sub-base, turf, seaming, infill), before/during/after photos, signed IRS W-9, driver's licence, and the professional installer's contact details. Rebates over $600 trigger a 1099. Conversely, for HOA/multifamily/commercial common-area work Thornton states artificial turf does NOT qualify, expressly citing Colorado SB24-005. Thornton's separate water-wise plant rebate is also up to $2/sq ft but all-rock projects with no plant material are excluded; the Lawn Replacement Program gives up to $750 toward professional lawn removal or up to 4 free Garden In A Box kits, minimum 200 sq ft removed. Commercial/common-area water-wise grant: 50% of design/renovation/installation up to $10,000 per acre for 0.5–5 acre irrigated projects.
facts.soil_and_yard: Western Adams County, elevation 5,269 ft. Historic irrigated agricultural land served by the Farmers High Line Canal, the Signal Ditch and the Lee Lateral, farmed for truck crops (cabbage, tomatoes, celery, cucumbers), wheat and sugar beets, with a Kuner pickle salting station on site — i.e. deep, historically irrigated, clay-rich alluvial and terrace soils on near-level ground. Front Range clay loams of the Nunn type dominate: roughly 35–50% clay, smectitic mineralogy, moderately slow to slow permeability, high shrink-swell. Because the ground is nearly flat, the drainage problem here is percolation and ponding rather than slope — base depth and a free-draining aggregate section matter more than grade management. Historic lots are small, flat and shaded by mature trees; the surrounding new subdivisions are graded fill over the same clays. Expansive clay is a known regional problem (Colorado Geological Survey: swelling pressures to 30,000 psf; annual losses exceed tornadoes, floods, earthquakes and hurricanes combined).
facts.housing_stock: Platted 6 Nov 1911 by the Eastlake Investment Company: a polygonal ~31.5-acre townsite, six blocks, 221 lots — so historic lots are genuinely small railroad-townsite parcels, not suburban tracts. Never incorporated as a municipality; annexed by Thornton in 1990. Surveyed historic buildings date 1914–1959. Original houses are one to one-and-a-half storeys, frame construction on concrete foundations, simple hipped or gable roofs, minimal ornament, most painted white — vernacular small-agricultural-town stock. The street grid is aligned to the Union Pacific right-of-way, so it runs at an angle to the surrounding suburban grid. The 2000 Front Range Research survey found the fabric heavily altered (new siding, windows, enclosed porches, additions, nonhistoric infill) and concluded NO eligible historic district survives. Immediately north, south and east are newer Thornton subdivisions (1990s–2020s), plus higher-density transit-oriented product around the N Line terminus. HOA prevalence: effectively nil in the pre-covenant historic core; high in the surrounding modern Thornton subdivisions.
facts.who_lives_there: GENUINELY THIN — be honest on the page. Eastlake is not a CDP and has no separate census tabulation, so there is no defensible Eastlake-specific income, age or demographic figure. It is a neighbourhood of Thornton (Adams 12 Five Star Schools area) and should be characterised as such. Do not invent numbers; use Thornton-level figures and say so.
facts.golf: None in Eastlake. Weakest golf town in the batch — the page should NOT lead with putting greens. Nearest play is Thornton/Northglenn-area public courses.
facts.commercial_targets: Thin locally and worth admitting. Adams 12 Five Star Schools (Eastlake School is the district's original school). Realistic commercial catchment is Thornton and Northglenn at large — Thornton rec centres, Adams 12 athletic fields, and the commercial/HOA water-wise grant programme (though note artificial turf is NOT eligible for that grant and is barred on HOA common areas by SB24-005, so pitch HOAs athletic and play surfaces only). This should be a RESIDENTIAL page, not a commercial one.
facts.landmarks: Eastlake Farmers Co-Operative Grain Elevator, c.1920 (Colorado site no. 5AM1445), at 126th Avenue and Claude Court — the last standing of the community's two elevators, notable for its monitor tower, corrugated metal walls and horizontal timber reinforcements; Eastlake School, 1920 (5AM1444), Craftsman detailing with widely overhanging eaves and paired brackets, decorative brickwork on stuccoed walls, gable-roof entrance bay with stucco and half-timbering — the only school in District 12 when it opened; First Congregational United Church of Christ, 1915 (5AM1443), the white frame plains church with projecting tower, same congregation since completion; former Catholic Church/Masonic Temple (5AM903), brick Gothic Revival with pointed-arch entrance; the old bank building with its beveled corner entrance; the RTD N Line Eastlake·124th station, the line's northern terminus; East Lake itself; the interpretive history display in the park on York Street. Historic core lies between the UP tracks and York Street, E. 124th to E. 128th Avenues, abutting Northglenn on the west.

sources: https://www.thorntonco.gov/media/file/eastlake-historic-buildings-surveypdf (Front Range Research Associates, Eastlake Neighborhood Historic Buildings Survey, June 2000)
https://www.thorntonwater.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026-residential_artificial_turf_info__rules-1.pdf (2026 Artificial Turf Rules for Water-Wise Landscape Rebate)

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: half of Lone Tree does not have a backyard, and the law treats it differently. This is the only place in the batch where multi-unit housing (47.2%) outnumbers single-family detached (40.7%), where renters make up 43.6% of households, and where the entire addressable detached-home market is about 2,767 houses — less than a fifth of Parker's. Writing Lone Tree as another suburban lawn-replacement page would be the single biggest error available in this batch. The honest lead is precision: Colorado's SB23-178 gives you the right to nonvegetative turf grass in your backyard only if you own a single-family DETACHED home — condominiums and attached homes sharing a wall are expressly excluded — so in Lone Tree the first question is what you own, not what you want. Then the second local fact no competitor will bother with: you cannot be told your watering days until you say which side of I-25 you are on, because Southgate runs the west at Stage 1 on two days with a 6 p.m. to 10 a.m. window, Parker Water runs the east on three days with a 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. blackout, and Northern Douglas County runs the Terra Ridge homes on Indian Wells Drive on its own two-day Stage 1 schedule. Pitch the high-value detached market in Heritage Hills, Carriage Club and the Fairways — $874,100 median value, the highest of the incorporated four — as the residential business, and treat everything multifamily and commercial with legal caution rather than enthusiasm. Every neighbouring town's page sells a backyard. Lone Tree's sells knowing which half of the city can legally have one.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No Lone Tree-specific artificial turf ordinance was found; the city's municipal code is hosted at library.municode.com/co/lone_tree/codes/municipal_code and was not reachable in this session (403) — CHECK IT DIRECTLY, as Lone Tree is a design-standards-conscious city that famously rejected an IKEA proposal over its design standards, which makes a landscaping or materials standard more likely here than in most suburbs. The decisive legal point for Lone Tree is a limitation, not a permission: SB23-178's protection — that HOA guidelines may not prohibit nonvegetative turf grass in the backyard — applies ONLY to a unit that is a single-family DETACHED home, and expressly does NOT apply to a single-family attached home sharing one or more walls with another unit, or to a condominium. In Lone Tree that means 57.8% of the housing stock falls outside the statutory right. Combine that with SB24-005, which since 1 January 2026 has prohibited installing artificial turf on commercial, institutional and industrial property and on common interest community COMMON property (athletic fields of play exempted), and the apartment-amenity-deck and HOA-common-area work that Lone Tree's density would otherwise suggest is legally constrained. This is a warning, not a selling point, and the page should be written by someone who has taken Colorado land-use advice first.
facts.water_and_rules: THREE SEPARATE DISTRICTS SERVE ONE SMALL CITY, and the rules differ by which one you are in — the most operationally useful local fact on this page. (1) SOUTHGATE WATER AND SANITATION DISTRICT, properties WEST of I-25, has declared Stage 1 Drought: single-family limited to two days a week, even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd addresses Wednesday and Saturday; multifamily and commercial properties may water only Tuesdays and Fridays; watering permitted between 6 p.m. and 10 a.m. (2) PARKER WATER AND SANITATION DISTRICT, properties EAST of I-25: even-numbered addresses Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday; odd-numbered Monday, Wednesday, Saturday; no watering between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m.; begins in May. (3) NORTHERN DOUGLAS COUNTY WATER AND SANITATION DISTRICT, serving select Terra Ridge homes along Indian Wells Drive, has declared Stage 1 Drought: two days a week by property type and address, no irrigation between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. from May 1 to September 30, hand-watering with a shut-off device permitted anytime. No turf-replacement rebate specific to Lone Tree was confirmable in this session; PWSD customers on the east side can access its $750 Resource Central turf removal discount, and Southgate's rebate programme was not reachable (its domain did not resolve at the addresses tried) — VERIFY Southgate directly before publishing rebate claims for west-side Lone Tree.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 6,280 ft across 9.81 sq mi, transitioning from developed suburban ground in the north to elevated grassland bluffs in the south with panoramic Front Range views — Bluffs Regional Park is the visible expression of that. Same Douglas County expansive-clay and heaving-bedrock context as the rest of the batch: bentonite and montmorillonite clays swelling up to 20% by volume at pressures over 30,000 psf, and the CGS-mapped Dipping Bedrock Overlay District. The distinctive Lone Tree condition is not the soil but the surface: with 47.2% of housing in multi-unit buildings, a large share of the installable area is not soil at all — it is podium decks, rooftop terraces, balconies, courtyard slabs and structured-parking lids, which is a completely different substrate problem (drainage layers, weight limits, waterproofing membranes, no excavation) from the compacted-clay base prep the other four towns need.
facts.housing_stock: THE OUTLIER OF THE BATCH, and the numbers are emphatic. 6,798 housing units, median year built 2004 — but only 40.7% are single-family detached (2,767 units). 10.6% are 1-unit attached, and 47.2% sit in multi-unit buildings. Multifamily OUTNUMBERS detached housing. Owner-occupancy is just 52.1%, with 43.6% renters — against 78.8% owner-occupied in Castle Rock, 79.3% in Castle Pines and 95.1% in The Pinery. Population 14,253 (2020 census), estimated 14,061 in 2024 — essentially flat. Median home value $874,100, the highest of the four incorporated places here, despite the lowest median household income, because the value sits in a small number of expensive detached homes while the household count is padded with apartments and condos. Development eras are unusually legible: Acres Green from the 1970s (older, more modest); the original Lone Tree neighbourhoods from 1982 onward — the city began Memorial Day weekend 1982 with nine households, incorporated by a 676-165 vote in November 1995 and became home rule in May 1998; Heritage Hills, Carriage Club and the Fairways as 1990s-2000s gated and semi-gated luxury with real lot sizes; and RidgeGate, a 3,500-acre mixed-use development from 2005 onward, plus the 2,000-acre Lone Tree City Center east of I-25 planned for 8,000 homes including the Lyric at RidgeGate village. The newest product is the densest. Roughly 2,767 detached homes is the entire addressable backyard market — smaller than any other place in this batch except The Pinery, and less than a fifth of Parker's.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $123,741 (ACS 2024) — the LOWEST of the five, which is counterintuitive for a city with an $874,100 median home value and only makes sense once you see the 43.6% renter share. Median age 40.8. Racially the most mixed of the batch: roughly 75% White, 9.35% Asian, 8.43% Hispanic or Latino. The population splits into two quite different customers: high-net-worth households in Heritage Hills and the Fairways with real yards and real budgets, and a large apartment-and-condo population around Park Meadows and RidgeGate with a balcony, a courtyard or nothing. Big daytime employment base — Sky Ridge Medical Center, Park Meadows retail, Charles Schwab and the RidgeGate office core, with buildout projected at 30,000-40,000 jobs.
facts.golf: VERIFIED: Lone Tree Golf Club and Hotel — an 18-hole Arnold Palmer-designed championship course with boutique hotel accommodation, and city-associated rather than purely private, which matters for procurement. That is the city's only course. The nearest heavyweight private clubs are in Castle Pines Village to the south. Golf is a supporting note for Lone Tree, not the lead — the practice-green market here is real but small, concentrated in Heritage Hills and the Fairways.
facts.commercial_targets: Read this list against the legal constraint first: since 1 January 2026 SB24-005 has prohibited artificial turf on commercial, institutional and industrial property and on HOA common property, exempting athletic fields of play. That removes most of what a dense city like Lone Tree would otherwise offer. What remains defensible: DCSD Legacy Campus (CTE facility, opened August 2023) and school athletic fields; Lone Tree Golf Club and Hotel for practice green and range work; Cook Creek Pool and city park athletic surfaces; and any indoor sports facility, which is exempt and matches the client's existing service line. Sky Ridge Medical Center, Park Meadows, the RidgeGate office core and apartment amenity decks are all high-value on paper and legally problematic in practice — do not build the page around them. Private detached residences in Heritage Hills, Carriage Club and the Fairways remain fully open, as private residential property is not covered by SB24-005.
facts.landmarks: Park Meadows — Colorado's largest shopping mall, opened 1996, roughly 1.6 million sq ft, and the thing everyone in the south metro means when they say 'Lone Tree'. Sky Ridge Medical Center, an acute care hospital and Level II Trauma Center. Lone Tree Arts Center. Lone Tree Golf Club and Hotel. Schweiger Ranch — an 1874 homestead on 38 acres, a designated landmark and living history museum. Bluffs Regional Park, 235 acres of open space and trails. Cook Creek Pool. The Sky Ridge / Lone Tree Station Mobility Hub, under construction. RidgeGate and the Lyric at RidgeGate. The Entertainment District Plaza. Douglas County School District's Legacy Campus, a career and technical education facility opened August 2023 on the former University of Colorado South Denver site.

name: Cherry Creek

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD BY DISAMBIGUATING THE NAME, THEN SELL THE FAMILY BACKYARD. The client's own phrase — 'the upper echelon, the Cherry Creek types' — almost certainly means DENVER'S CHERRY CREEK NORTH, a different place in a different county on a different water utility. The Arapahoe County Cherry Creek CDP is 3,000 detached houses built around 1981 for Cherry Creek Schools families, $153,776 median household income, $888,900 median value, ZIP 80111, Greenwood Village mailing address, wrapped around Cherry Creek State Park. Say that plainly in the first paragraph and the page immediately outranks the confusion — and flag internally that the client may be conflating two markets that need two entirely different pages. Then the substance: this is the batch's best KIDS-AND-DOGS BACKYARD market — 26.4% of the population is under 18, 66% are married couples, backyards run 3,000–6,000 sq ft, and every neighbourhood already has a pool and tennis courts within walking distance, so residents here already pay for maintained outdoor surfaces. The differentiator against Columbine, which has similar-vintage housing, is money and slope: nearly $900k median value versus $617k, and Renohill hydrologic-group-D clay on a 3–9% grade falling toward Cherry Creek State Park's detention system, which turns drainage design into a selling point rather than a hidden cost. And the local-knowledge proof is the CHERRY CREEK VISTA PARK AND RECREATION DISTRICT — naming the district that mows the 2.6 miles of Havana Street right-of-way tells a resident you actually know where they live. NOCO OVERLAP: none — nocoturf.com has no page for this CDP, Greenwood Village or Centennial.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated Arapahoe County — no municipal code of its own, county land-use and grading rules apply, and Greenwood Village's code starts one street north, which is a real source of confusion for residents with a Greenwood Village mailing address. The practical authority is the HOA or metro district: Cherry Creek Vista, Hills West, Huntington Acres, Orchard Hills and Arapahoe Lake all have covenant-controlled associations with architectural committees. The CHERRY CREEK VISTA PARK AND RECREATION DISTRICT is a formal special district that owns seven tennis courts, a pickleball court, a swimming pool, a community room, six parks and six playgrounds — and maintains 2.6 MILES OF COUNTY RIGHTS-OF-WAY along Havana Street, Orchard Road and portions of Cherry Creek Drive. SB24-005 is directly relevant to that last item: from 1 January 2026 Colorado local governments may not allow artificial turf on common-interest-community property, street rights-of-way or medians, with artificial turf on athletic fields of play exempt. Residential back yards are unaffected — say so explicitly, because homeowners here will have heard about the law.
facts.water_and_rules: Denver Water supply delivered through small special districts, not a city utility. CHERRY CREEK VILLAGE WATER DISTRICT (Denver Water MASTER METER distributor, 303-381-4960; EPA SDWIS records 476 connections serving roughly 9,215 people, Greenwood Village) is the most likely provider for much of the CDP, with SOUTHGATE WATER DISTRICT (Read and Bill, ~11,511 connections, ~55,000 people, Centennial) and WILLOWS WATER DISTRICT (both Read and Bill and Master Meter, ~4,737 connections) serving adjacent territory; ACWWA is the neighbouring groundwater provider to the southeast. All of these purchase surface water from Denver Water, so Denver Water's conditions govern supply: Stage 1 drought declared 25 Mar 2026 through 30 Apr 2027, 20% total-use reduction target, drought pricing, two assigned watering days (even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd Wednesday and Saturday; multifamily and commercial Tuesday and Friday), watering only before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m., no water on pavement, leaks fixed within 10 days — and, following the Board's 26 August 2026 declaration, NO LAWN WATERING AND NO SPRAY IRRIGATION AT ALL AFTER SEPT 30. Escalating violation charges of $250 / $500 / $1,000 apply to Denver Water's directly billed customers; master-meter districts set their own enforcement and take waste reports themselves. REBATES: Denver Water's $100 WaterSense toilet, plus the Resource Central turfgrass-removal discount of up to $750 — fully allocated for 2026 in March and closed, and funding replacement with a living water-wise ColoradoScape, so artificial turf is not the eligible replacement. The state CWCB Turf Replacement Grant Program is closed with funding exhausted and never accepted homeowner or HOA applications directly. CONFIRM THE DISTRICT BY ADDRESS before making any rebate claim on this page.
facts.soil_and_yard: SSURGO maps this area as RENOHILL-BUICK LOAMS, 3 to 9 percent slopes (mukey 94147) — the same map unit as Bow Mar. Renohill (65% of the unit) is a loam over 45% clay from 4 to 18 inches, linear extensibility 7.5 (high shrink-swell), saturated hydraulic conductivity about 1 µm/s, HYDROLOGIC GROUP D. Buick (25%) is group C with about 30% clay in the subsoil. So: clay over shale, very slow subsoil drainage, and enough slope (3–9%) that surface water genuinely moves. Yards here back onto greenbelts and detention areas draining toward Cherry Creek and the reservoir, which means runoff from a new turf surface is a neighbour question and a metro-district question, not only an engineering one. Practical page content: sub-base drainage, French drains at the low corner, and a written statement of where the water goes.
facts.housing_stock: 11,488 people in 4,234 housing units across 1.67 sq mi (2020 census). ACS 2020–24: 4,340 units — 3,021 1-unit detached, 266 attached, roughly 930 multifamily; 3,293 of 4,127 occupied units owner-occupied (80%). MEDIAN YEAR STRUCTURE BUILT 1981; MEDIAN VALUE $888,900; average household size 2.57. This is late-1970s/1980s Cherry Creek School District subdivision stock — two-storeys and tri-levels on roughly 8,000–13,000 sq ft lots with backyards typically 3,000–6,000 sq ft, meaningfully bigger and richer than Columbine's 1976 tract yards but nothing like Bow Mar or Foxfield acreage. The CDP runs roughly from Dayton Street east to just short of Peoria Street, and from just north of Belleview Avenue south toward Arapahoe Road. It is made of named 1970s–80s neighbourhoods that each have their own pools and tennis courts: CHERRY CREEK VISTA, HILLS WEST, HUNTINGTON ACRES, ORCHARD HILLS, ARAPAHOE LAKE and PEAKVIEW. Almost all are covenant-controlled, and several sit inside metropolitan or park-and-recreation districts.
facts.who_lives_there: 11,488 residents; median age 40.0; 26.4% under 18 and only 14.5% aged 65+ — the most family-heavy profile in the batch; 66.2% married-couple households; 71.0% white, 13.5% Asian, 9.3% Hispanic/Latino, 1.9% Black. MEDIAN HOUSEHOLD INCOME $153,776. ZIP 80111 with a Greenwood Village or Englewood mailing address, which is exactly why residents never call it 'Cherry Creek CDP'. This is the Cherry Creek Schools family that bought in for Cottonwood Creek and High Plains elementaries, Campus Middle and Cherry Creek High — kids, dogs and a backyard that gets used.
facts.golf: No course inside the CDP, but it is ringed by them. Meadow Hills Golf Course (Aurora, 3609 S Dawson St, 39.6492/-104.8240) about two miles northeast; Inverness Golf Course to the south; Family Sports Golf Course and the Family Sports Center (6901 S Peoria St, Centennial, 39.5920/-104.8490) about a mile and a half south; Topgolf in Centennial; Kennedy Golf Course's three layouts to the northwest; Valley Country Club (Centennial 80015, 39.5996/-104.8193) about two miles east; and Cherry Hills Country Club and Glenmoor a few miles west. High golf density plus $153,776 median household income plus 3,000–6,000 sq ft backyards makes this the best backyard-putting-green market in the batch after Columbine — and unlike Columbine, the yards here can hold a green AND a play area.
facts.commercial_targets: Cherry Creek Vista Park & Recreation District's pool deck, community room and six parks and playgrounds — the highest-value institutional target here, but run the SB24-005 check first. SCHOOLS (athletic fields of play are the statutory exemption, so the stadium and practice-field conversation is the compliant one): Cottonwood Creek, High Plains, Belleview, Homestead, Heritage, Walnut Hills, Willow Creek, Sagebrush and Southmoor elementaries, Campus Middle School, Cherry Creek High School and Stutler Bowl, plus Richard E Rudolph Shalom Hebrew School and the Cherry Creek Innovation Campus. CHILDCARE: The Goddard School, The Village Child Development Center, Primrose School, La Petite Academy, The Learning Experience, Sheri Calfee Day Care. PET — a deep list: Pet Palace and Pet Palace Vet Clinic, Kriser's, Nature Box Pet Emporium, Bentley's Pets, Outward Hound, Hale Pet Door, Happy Paw Grooming, Halee's Puppy Love, Parkside Animal Health Center, Critter Care Animal Hospital, Greenwood Village Veterinary Clinic, Gems Veterinary/Urgent Care. SPORT AND FITNESS: Greenwood Athletic Club, Monkey Bizness, Family Sports Center (ice hockey and skating), South Suburban Parks and Recreation Sports Complex, Willow Creek tennis courts, Homestead North and South pools, Michelle Latimer Dance Academy.
facts.landmarks: CHERRY CREEK STATE PARK forms the northeast edge — 3,346 acres established in 1959, an 880-acre reservoir, 12 miles of paved road and 35 miles of multi-use trail, a marina and boathouse, and roughly 2.69 million visits in 2021. It is the single most recognisable landmark for anyone in this ZIP. Cherry Creek Vista Swimming Pool on E Orchard Road (39.6090/-104.8571); Arapahoe Lake Swimming Pool and Arapahoe Lake Tennis; Hills West Park and Hills West Pool; Orchard Hills Park, Peakview Park, Huntington Acres Park, Silo Park, Hoffman Park, Tommy Davis Park, Lakeview Park, Bear Park, Sunset Park, Francis H. Williams Park. Cottonwood Creek and High Plains elementary schools inside the CDP; Campus Middle School, Cherry Creek High School (39.6304/-104.8793) and STUTLER BOWL immediately north in Greenwood Village. Belleview Avenue, Orchard Road and Havana Street are the streets a local names.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE SOIL — 'the easiest ground in the metro to install on.' Derby is the only place in this batch that sits on sandy loam rather than expansive clay, and the numbers prove it: Vona and Truckton sandy loams, 0-3% slopes, well drained, with measured linear extensibility of 1.1-1.3 and 10-12% clay against Sherrelwood's Platner at 5.6 and Welby's Samsil bluff at 7.5 with 54% clay, and saturated conductivity of 39-46 µm/s against Samsil's 0.60 — up to sixty times more permeable. Flat, sandy, fast-draining, low shrink-swell ground means shallower excavation, predictable base compaction, natural percolation and materially lower risk of heave or ponding. Turn that into a concrete promise: faster installs, lower drainage cost, and a warranty argument the clay towns cannot match — and it makes Derby the strongest PET TURF market in the batch, because the subgrade already drains. Layer on the housing profile that makes it repeatable: 40.3% of all homes built in one decade, the 1950s, and 80.9% single-family detached with 70.9% ownership and the lowest family poverty rate here (4.9%) — one uniform postwar tract house, one uniform job. Finish with the local context nobody else can use: a refinery and a 15,988-acre former chemical-weapons arsenal turned bison refuge on the doorstep, where a rinseable, dust-shedding surface is an easy sell, and Adams 14's athletic fields as the one commercial category Colorado's SB24-005 still permits. That is a completely different page from Welby's acreage-and-farm-heritage lead five miles west, or Federal Heights' manufactured-home lead.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated Adams County — county rules govern, not Commerce City's. Adams County Code Compliance enforces blight violations expressly including 'tall, overgrown grass, weeds and brush (12 inches)', via Neighborhood Services (720.523.2792). With HOAs essentially absent from 1950s tract platting, the county's 12-inch weed standard is effectively the ONLY landscape rule most Derby homeowners face — which makes the argument simple and honest: turf removes the citation risk permanently. State law: HB21-1229 means any common interest community may regulate but not prohibit artificial turf in a unit's backyard; SB24-005 prohibits new artificial turf on commercial, institutional, industrial, common-interest-community, right-of-way, parking-lot and median property from January 1, 2026, exempting only athletic fields of play. Adams County's landscaping standards could not be retrieved from the county's JavaScript-based code portal and remain unverified — do not assert county landscape-material rules without checking with CEDD at 720.523.6800.
facts.water_and_rules: South Adams County Water and Sanitation District (EPA PWS ID CO0101140, PO Box 597, Commerce City 80037) — a large system serving about 75,559 people on 24,754 connections, and listed by Denver Water as a MASTER METER distributor. So Denver Water's rules apply here too. As checked 2026-09-07: MANDATORY watering restrictions effective March 25, 2026 — no more than two days per week on assigned days (even addresses Sunday/Thursday, odd Wednesday/Saturday, multi-family, commercial, HOA and government Tuesday/Friday), watering only between 6 pm and 10 am, a Denver Water drought declaration seeking a 20% reduction, and from October 1, 2026 no outdoor watering allowed at all with fines. Several small independent groundwater systems also operate in ZIP 80022 (Town & Country Mutual Water, Arrowhead Water Users Association, and mobile-home court systems including Advanced, J-Burr and Morningside), so a handful of addresses are on private wells rather than SACWSD — verify per address. Rebates: no turf-replacement rebate applies to artificial turf; Denver Water's published residential rebates cover toilets and sprinkler nozzles only. SACWSD's own site returned 403 to automated retrieval, so any claim about district-specific rules or rebates should be confirmed by phone before publishing.
facts.soil_and_yard: Derby is the outlier and this is its commercial advantage. SSURGO sampled at two points: Vona sandy loam, 0 to 1 percent slopes at 72nd/Monaco (90% Vona, 'Coarse-loamy, mixed, mesic Ustollic Haplargids') and Truckton sandy loam, 0 to 3 percent slopes at 74th/Quebec (85% Truckton, 'Coarse-loamy, mixed, superactive, mesic Aridic Argiustolls'), both well drained. Measured top-30 cm values: Vona linear extensibility 1.30 with 11.6% clay and Ksat 45.8 µm/s; Truckton LEP 1.09 with 10.7% clay and Ksat 38.9 µm/s. Compare that to Welby's Samsil bluff at LEP 7.5, 54% clay and Ksat 0.60, or Sherrelwood's Platner at LEP 5.6 — Derby's soil is roughly five times less expansive and up to sixty times more permeable. Expansive clay is genuinely NOT a Derby problem. The ground is flat (0-3%), sandy, well drained and low shrink-swell. Practical consequence: shallower over-excavation, a base that compacts predictably, natural percolation that reduces reliance on engineered drains, and materially lower risk of post-install heave, settlement or ponding. This is the fastest, cheapest and lowest-risk install in the batch — and that is a defensible, evidence-backed claim rather than a marketing line. Lower Derby Lake lies on the Rocky Mountain Arsenal refuge nearby; check floodplain on parcels toward the South Platte.
facts.housing_stock: The most single-decade, most single-family place in the batch. ACS 2024 5-yr (B25034): of 2,617 units, 1,054 — 40.3% — were built in the 1950s, the most concentrated decade found anywhere in this batch, with another 9.1% predating 1940 and 10.4% in the 1960s. There is then a curious second wave of 13.7% in the 1990s and essentially nothing since 2020 (0.0%). B25024: 80.9% single-family DETACHED — the highest detached share of the five — with only 0.8% attached and 12.1% manufactured. ACS median value $353,000, the lowest of the five, on 70.9% owner-occupancy. Density is low: 2,617 units across 1.75 sq mi, well under half Sherrelwood's unit density, which points to noticeably larger lots than the other CDPs here. I do not have parcel-level lot data for Derby, so treat lot size as inferred from density and era rather than measured. HOAs are essentially absent — this is 1950s tract platting in unincorporated county, so almost every job is a direct owner decision. Note for accuracy: Derby is an unincorporated Adams County community, not part of Commerce City, though Commerce Town annexed part of Derby in 1962 and the area is surrounded by and served through Commerce City; reverse-geocoding the CDP centroid returns 'Dupont, Derby, Adams County'.
facts.who_lives_there: 2020 census population 8,407 (density about 5,200 per sq mi); 2024 ACS 8,453. Median household income $82,138 — the second highest of the five, and comfortably above Federal Heights — with only 4.9% of families in poverty, the LOWEST family poverty rate in this batch. 75.5% Hispanic, the highest share of the five; 20.9% White. Median age 33.1. A settled, high-ownership, working, family-heavy community whose modest median home value reflects an older housing stock and refinery-adjacent location rather than low incomes. Adams County School District 14 serves the area.
facts.golf: Riverdale Dunes & Knolls Golf Course (Riverdale Road, Brighton) — the Adams County-owned 36 holes — is the nearest real golf and the course a Derby local would name, within about 12 km. Thorncreek Golf Course (Thornton), City Park Golf Course (Denver) and The Greg Mastriona Golf Courses at Hyland Hills are also within roughly 12 km. Commerce City's municipal Buffalo Run Golf Course sits further east on E 112th Ave and is in the same city but not immediately adjacent to the Derby CDP — say 'Commerce City's Buffalo Run', not 'nearby'. No golf course inside the CDP and no golf community.
facts.commercial_targets: Adams County School District 14 is the single biggest opportunity and the athletic fields are the legally exempt category under SB24-005: Adams City High School, Lester R. Arnold High School (E 72nd Ave), Adams City Middle School, plus Kemp, Monaco, Hanson, Alsup and Dupont Elementary (E 79th Place) and Community Leadership Academy (State Highway 2). Parks (Adams County and Commerce City as decision-makers): Derby Park, Joe Reilly Park, Los Valientes Park, Fairfax Park, Pelican Ponds Open Space, Platte River Trailhead. Dick's Sporting Goods Park in Commerce City is the marquee sports-facility name in the area and its training pitches are the highest-profile athletic-field target within reach. Pet and daycare businesses were not well represented in the mapping data for the immediate Derby area — that is a genuine data gap rather than an absence, and warrants a manual canvass along E 72nd Avenue before the page names any.
facts.landmarks: Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge — 15,988 acres on the site of the 1942 Army chemical weapons plant, now the largest land-based urban wildlife refuge in the United States, with bison, black-footed ferrets and more than 330 wildlife species. Lower Derby Lake sits on the refuge. The Suncor Energy refinery, the largest in the Rocky Mountain region at about 98,000 barrels per day. Dick's Sporting Goods Park, home of the Colorado Rapids. Adams City High School — the district's comprehensive high school and the community's central institution. Derby Park (Monaco Street) and the historic Derby business district. Joe Reilly Park (E 72nd Place). Los Valientes Park (Magnolia Street). Pelican Ponds Open Space (Riverdale Road). Derby began as a Burlington Railroad station established in 1887, was laid out as a town in 1889, and had its own post office from 1910 until 1963; it is named for Derby, England.

name: Holly Hills

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH OCTOBER 1. Denver Water is in Stage 1 drought, and from 1 October watering grass with a spray irrigation system is flatly prohibited and subject to charges — while hand-watering and drip stay legal. Holly Hills is 371 acres of quarter-acre 1950s lawns, median age 44, 23% seniors, $702,000 houses, owned by people who have been maintaining the same bluegrass for decades. That is the cleanest, hardest, most emotionally direct pitch available anywhere in this batch: your neighbours' lawns go brown on 1 October and yours does not, permanently, and you never touch a sprinkler again. Pair it with the Cherry Creek Schools resale argument (Holly Ridge, Holly Hills Elementary, West Middle, Cherry Creek High — the reason a Denver enclave holds $702k) and the maintenance-fatigue angle for the 23% of residents over 65. And be honest on the page that there is no rebate — Denver Water rebates toilets and sprinkler heads, and Resource Central's lawn program requires 50% live waterwise plants, so synthetic turf earns nothing. Turning that into a strength ('this is not a rebate play, it is the last irrigation bill you pay') is more credible than dodging it. This lead is unavailable to every neighbour: Highlands Ranch is on Highlands Ranch Water's own Stage 1 schedule with different days and $500 fines, not Denver's October ban; Dove Valley and Inverness are office parks with almost no residential lawn to convert; Aetna Estates has neither the lot size nor the income. Holly Hills is the retrofit-an-old-lawn page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Holly Hills is unincorporated, so Arapahoe County — not Denver — is the land-use authority, even though the place is surrounded by Denver and served by Denver Water. That split is worth naming on the page because residents themselves are often unsure. Colorado SB24-005 applies from 1 January 2026 to commercial, institutional, industrial, common-interest and right-of-way installations, with athletic fields of play exempt; residential property is not in the prohibited categories, so a Holly Hills homeowner's own backyard is unaffected. HONEST FLAG: arapahoegov.com returned 403 on every attempt this session, so I could not read Arapahoe County's land development code, its landscaping standards, or how it is implementing SB24-005. I also found no evidence of a blanket HOA over Holly Hills — as an older unincorporated subdivision it may well have none, or only old plat covenants, which would be a genuine selling point versus Highlands Ranch. Verify both before publishing.
facts.water_and_rules: Almost certainly Denver Water, and if so this is the strongest single selling fact on the page. Holly Hills is an enclave of the City and County of Denver using ZIP 80222, which places it squarely in the Denver Water service area. Denver Water is in STAGE 1 DROUGHT as of September 2026, with mandatory restrictions asking customers to cut use at least 20%: until 30 September, outdoor watering is limited to two assigned days per week with NO watering between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. — single-family even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd addresses Wednesday and Saturday. And then the line that should headline this page: BEGINNING OCTOBER 1, watering of grass and use of spray irrigation systems is PROHIBITED and subject to violations and charges. Hand-watering trees and shrubs with a shutoff nozzle, and drip irrigation, remain allowed. HONEST FLAG: confirm the provider by service address — some Arapahoe enclaves are 'read and bill' distributors rather than Denver Water direct customers, and Denver Water's own service-area page 404'd this session. On rebates: Denver Water's published residential rebates are toilets (up to $100) and qualifying sprinkler heads — there is no residential lawn-replacement rebate listed, there is a separate Landscape Transformation Assistance Program for BUSINESS customers, and Resource Central's Lawn Replacement program (Denver Water is a partner) requires at least 50% waterwise PLANTS, which artificial turf cannot satisfy. So: artificial turf gets no rebate here. Say it plainly and pivot to the October 1 argument.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 5,476 ft — the lowest of the five, sitting in the Cherry Creek/High Line Canal bottomland belt rather than up on the Douglas County bench. Terrain is flat to very gently sloping, which is the easiest base-prep of anything in this batch. Front Range expansive clay still applies: CGS reports Front Range montmorillonite/bentonite clays expanding up to 20% by volume at pressures to 30,000 psf, with cracked drives, walks and foundations the typical failure, and about 10% of homes on expansive soils damaged over their lifetime. The Holly Hills-specific issue is different and more useful: seventy-year-old yards mean seventy-year-old irrigation, decades of accumulated thatch and topsoil amendment over native clay, mature shade trees with substantial surface roots, and original clay-tile or early PVC service lines. Excavation and root management, not slope, are the technical story here. HONEST FLAG: no Holly Hills-specific soils survey was located; the expansive-clay point is regional and the rest is inference from the age and density profile.
facts.housing_stock: A 371-acre island — you can walk the whole place in twenty minutes. 2020 census: 2,683 residents, 1,030 households, ~1,056 housing units, and a remarkably tight 2.5% vacancy rate. ACS 2024 5-yr: 2,572 people, 1,013 units, median owner-occupied home value $702,000. Do the arithmetic that matters to a turf installer: ~1,050 units on 371 acres is about 2.8 units per gross acre, which after streets puts typical lots in the quarter-acre range — roughly 8,000-11,000 sq ft, with genuinely usable, flat, rectangular backyards. That is the classic post-war Denver-fringe subdivision pattern and it is the largest average backyard of the five places in this batch. HONEST FLAG: I could not verify build era from a primary source — neighborhoodscout, redfin and city-data all blocked or 404'd. But the combination of a 371-acre Denver enclave in ZIP 80222, a median age of 44.3 with 23.1% of residents aged 65+, 82.9% White, 56.7% married couples, 2.5% vacancy and $702k values points strongly to 1950s-60s brick ranches now on their second or third owners. Verify before publishing a decade.
facts.who_lives_there: The oldest and most settled population of the five. Median age 44.3; 20.6% under 18 and 23.1% aged 65 or over — the only place in this batch with more seniors than children. 82.9% White, 9.4% multiracial, 8.2% Hispanic, 3.7% Asian. 56.7% of households are married couples. ACS 2024: median household income $122,391 (±$23,781), per capita income $67,001. Read that as: established, affluent, long-tenured owners in Cherry Creek Schools, many of them retired or near it, sitting on $700k houses with 1950s lawns and 1950s sprinkler systems. That is a maintenance-fatigue buyer, not an aspirational one — the pitch is 'you are done mowing', not 'you are joining something'.
facts.golf: Wellshire Golf Course, the Denver municipal course on South Colorado Boulevard near Hampden, is immediately west of the CDP — for a Holly Hills resident it is the nearest course and a local landmark. Cherry Hills Country Club, in Cherry Hills Village a short drive west, is the marquee name: three U.S. Opens (1938, 1960, 1978), two PGA Championships (1941, 1985), the 2005 U.S. Women's Open, the 1993 U.S. Senior Open, three U.S. Amateurs (1990, 2012, 2023) and the 2014 BMW Championship — Arnold Palmer won here in 1960, Jack Nicklaus in 1993. HONEST FLAG: the Wellshire Wikipedia page 404'd; I verified Wellshire only by regional knowledge and could not confirm its address, architect or operator this session. Cherry Hills Country Club's championship record IS verified. Also worth noting honestly: Cherry Hills Country Club is in Cherry Hills Village, NOT in Holly Hills — do not imply otherwise, and do not let this page cannibalise a future Cherry Hills Village page.
facts.commercial_targets: Holly Ridge Primary School, Holly Hills Elementary School, West Middle School and Cherry Creek High School — all Cherry Creek School District 5, all named and verifiable, and school athletic fields of play are the one category SB24-005 expressly exempts. Wellshire Golf Course (municipal, adjacent). HONEST FLAG: at 371 acres this is a small, almost purely residential enclave; I identified no daycares, pet businesses or sports complexes inside it and I would not invent any. The honest commercial play is the four Cherry Creek schools plus the retail along South Colorado Boulevard and East Hampden, which are outside the CDP.
facts.landmarks: The named schools are the most checkable landmarks and they are unusually specific here — Holly Ridge Primary (K-2), Holly Hills Elementary (3-5), West Middle School and Cherry Creek High School, all Cherry Creek School District 5. Sitting in Cherry Creek Schools while being a Denver enclave is the reason $702k values hold in a 371-acre pocket, and locals absolutely know it. The South Colorado Boulevard and East Hampden Avenue commercial corridors define the west and south edges. HONEST FLAG: I could not independently verify the High Line Canal trail alignment, Bible Park or Eisenhower Park proximity this session — all are regionally plausible and locally recognisable but should be checked on a map before naming them.
