https://www.denverwater.org/residential/rebates-and-conservation-tips/residential-rebates — toilet and sprinkler-head rebates only; Landscape Transformation Assistance is business-only (checked 2026-09-07)
https://resourcecentral.org/lawn/ — Denver Water is a partner; 50% waterwise plants required (checked 2026-09-07)

name: Bow Mar

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE DESIGN REVIEW BOARD AND THE DRAINAGE PLAN. Bow Mar is the only place in this batch where a turf install is a permitted, board-reviewed municipal project rather than a weekend landscaping job — and the winning page is written for a homeowner who already knows that and wants a contractor who has actually read the guidelines: sport courts and putting greens must sit inside the building envelope, cannot be lit, and any grade change over four cubic yards goes to the DRB, with BMOI written approval stacked on top. Then bind that to the second Bow Mar-only fact — the lakes. Renohill clay at hydrologic group D on a 3–9% slope falling toward Bowles Lake makes every square foot a stormwater question, and the Town explicitly disclaims responsibility for drainage impacts on neighbours. That is a completely different page from Columbine two miles west, where 9,800 tract houses need no permit at all and the whole sale is price and speed. SECONDARY SEO PLAY: rank 'Bow Mar South' separately — it is a distinct unincorporated Arapahoe County neighbourhood immediately south of the town line (OSM: 39.6132/-105.0508, 'Bow Mar South, Littleton, Arapahoe County') with none of these rules and a different water district; people conflate the two constantly. NOCO OVERLAP (checked 2026-09-07): nocoturf.com's sitemap has exactly 17 /areas/ pages — Fort Collins, Greeley, Loveland, Windsor, Timnath, Wellington, Berthoud, Johnstown, Mead, Firestone, Frederick, Dacono, Erie, Broomfield, Brighton, Thornton, Dacono. NO page for Bow Mar or any town in this batch, so town-level cannibalisation for this batch is zero. Brand-level overlap IS real though: NoCo's homepage title tag is 'Noco Turf CO. | Artificial Turf in Denver' and its meta description says 'artificial turf installation in Denver & surrounding areas' — the two brands will compete on generic Denver head terms even where the town pages do not collide.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: TWO overlapping layers, and this is the most regulated small yard-market in the batch. (1) TOWN OF BOW MAR DESIGN REVIEW BOARD, created by Ordinance 323 (2018). Its 24 June 2019 guidelines require DRB approval for landscaping in three circumstances: with a new residence or major remodel; when the work may affect neighbours' views (heavy hedges, multiple trees); and when it substantially alters existing landscaping. Section XII requires DRB approval for ANY change in grade — including landscape berms — disturbing more than 4 CUBIC YARDS of soil. Sport courts and tennis courts 'must be located within the Building Envelope unless a variance from the Town of Bow Mar is obtained' and 'shall not be lighted'; tennis courts are 'in general discouraged.' All patios and decks, even at-grade, must sit inside the building envelope and require DRB approval. Town Code Sec. 16-14 limits landscaping and shrubbery that would 'obstruct unreasonably the view of the lake, mountains or city lights from any other lot.' (2) BOW MAR OWNERS INC. covenants — the Amended and Restated Declaration requires prior WRITTEN approval before any building, fence, wall or other structure, and even shrubs and trees, are installed. Also note the Town itself buys landscape services: 2026 resolutions approve agreements with Lifescape, Designscapes Colorado, Signature Landscape and a Weed Wrangler agreement.
facts.water_and_rules: Bow Mar Water and Sanitation District serves 296 residences (EPA SDWIS: 290 connections, ~899 people, purchased surface water). It is a Denver Water MASTER METER distributor — Denver Water sells wholesale through a master meter and the district bills residents on its own rate schedule, so waste reports go to the district, not Denver Water. Denver Water's supply conditions still govern: Stage 1 drought declared 25 Mar 2026 through 30 Apr 2027 with a 20% total-use reduction target and drought pricing; mandatory two assigned watering days (even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd Wednesday and Saturday, commercial/multifamily Tuesday and Friday), only before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m.; no watering in rain or high wind; no water on pavement; sprinkler leaks repaired within 10 days. On 26 Aug 2026 the Board of Water Commissioners declared an end to the lawn watering season, PROHIBITING lawn watering and all spray irrigation after Sept 30 (hand-watering and drip for trees and plants still allowed). REBATES: Denver Water's residential rebates are a $100 WaterSense toilet plus a Resource Central turfgrass-removal discount of up to $750 — the 2026 discounts were fully allocated in March 2026 and applications are closed. That program funds replacement of bluegrass with a living water-wise 'ColoradoScape'; artificial turf is not the eligible replacement (confirm with Resource Central before advertising). The state CWCB Turf Replacement Grant Program stopped accepting applications in March 2025 and its funding is exhausted; single-family homeowners and HOAs were never directly eligible anyway. UNVERIFIED LOCAL WRINKLE worth a phone call: BMOI owns Bowles Lake and the town's 96 acres of water — whether any lake or ditch water is available for irrigation is a Bow Mar-only question no public page answers.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO maps the town as Renohill-Buick loams, 3 to 9 percent slopes (mukey 94147). Renohill is 65% of the unit: a loam surface over a subsoil of 45% clay from 4 to 18 inches, linear extensibility 7.5 (high shrink-swell), saturated hydraulic conductivity about 1 µm/s — hydrologic group D, the worst infiltration class there is. Buick (25%) is group C. So: high shrink-swell clay over shale, near-impermeable subsoil, and a genuine 3–9% fall running toward the lakes. Base depth, sub-base drainage and positive fall away from structures decide every job here, and the Town agrees — the DRB requires a stamped Engineer's Drainage Plan on certain applications and expressly 'makes no representation of approval for changes to drainage and subsequent impact on adjacent properties resulting from a change of grade.'
facts.housing_stock: ~300 single-family homes on one-acre lots inside a 520-acre town that includes 96 acres of water. ACS 2020–24: 375 housing units, ALL of them 1-unit detached; 364 of 369 occupied units owner-occupied (98.6%); only 5 rentals in the entire town. Median year structure built 1963. Median home value is top-coded at $2,000,001, meaning the true median exceeds $2M. The first house went up in 1947 (Lloyd and Eleanor King, of King Soopers); many originals were low-slung Frank Lloyd Wright-influenced prairie style, and there has been heavy scrape-and-rebuild since. The turf job here is a full acre — typically 8,000–20,000+ sq ft of usable yard behind the house, mature trees, and protected sightlines to the lake and mountains. There is no conventional suburban HOA; instead two layers of control: the Town's own Design Review Board and Bow Mar Owners Inc. (BMOI) covenants.
facts.who_lives_there: 853 people at the 2020 census (587 in Arapahoe County, 266 in Jefferson). ACS 2020–24 median household income $241,583 — the highest in this batch by a wide margin. Average household size 2.84; median age was 44 at the 2000 census; 82% married-couple households. Multi-generational lake families — BMOI runs a marina, yacht club, racquet club, beach and the Bow MarS Sharks swim team. Arapahoe-side kids go to Littleton Public Schools, Jefferson-side to Jeffco Public Schools. ZIP 80123, mailing address 'Littleton'.
facts.golf: No course inside the town — Bow Mar's recreation is water, not golf. Pinehurst Country Club (private, W Quincy Ave near Sheridan Blvd) is the closest club, roughly a mile north. Columbine Country Club (private, Columbine Valley, 39.5973/-105.0344), with an 18-hole course, a par-3 course and pool, is about two miles southeast. The Foothills Golf Course complex (Championship, Executive and Par-3, 3901 S Carr St, Denver 80235, 39.6460/-105.0960) is roughly 2.5 miles northwest. Broken Tee Englewood and Littleton Golf Course are within four miles. The golf sell here is the private backyard practice green for a club member, not course adjacency.
facts.commercial_targets: Be honest — a ~300-home town with essentially no commercial base. The genuine institutional targets are BMOI's own common areas: the beach and picnic area, the racquet club courts and the marina lawn, plus Town rights-of-way (the Town already contracts Lifescape, Designscapes Colorado and Signature Landscape). BUT read SB24-005 first: from 1 Jan 2026 Colorado local governments may not allow artificial turf on common-interest-community property or street rights-of-way. Real commercial prospects sit outside the line: Pinehurst Country Club, Columbine Country Club, the Foothills Golf Course complex, and the Littleton Public Schools (Arapahoe side) and Jeffco Public Schools (Jefferson side) campuses nearby.
facts.landmarks: Bowles Lake, the private lake inside the town (39.6185/-105.0511, OSM-confirmed as 'Bow Mar, Arapahoe County'), and Marston Lake / Marston Reservoir with Denver Water's Marston Treatment Plant immediately northwest (39.6285/-105.0666) — the two lakes the town is named for, after pioneer farmers Joseph Bowles and John Marston. BMOI's beach, picnic area, marina, yacht club and racquet club. The Bow MarS Sharks swim team, the pond hockey tournament and the beach concerts. Wolff and Quincy Park, Sunset Park, Mary's Meadow, Cimarron Trail Park. Sheridan Boulevard on the eastern edge, where the Town has been debating a traffic gate and the closure of W Tufts Ave (2026 resolutions).

sources: https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/ (SSURGO mukey 94147, Renohill-Buick loams 3-9% slopes, queried 2026-09-07)
https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/ (Bowles Lake 39.6185/-105.0511; Marston Lake 39.6285/-105.0666; Bow Mar South 39.6132/-105.0508)

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH 'WHICH WATER DISTRICT ARE YOU?' Centennial is the only place in this batch with no city water utility at all — service is carved up among independent special districts, so watering days, drought stage and rebate eligibility change street by street, and the district with the confusingly similar name (Centennial Water & Sanitation) isn't even in Centennial, it's Highlands Ranch. A page that opens by helping a homeowner identify their own provider and what it actually means for them is genuinely useful, unmistakably local, and impossible for a template competitor to fake. Then pivot to the money, because Centennial earns it: the highest household income ($131,928) and the highest owner-occupancy (80.6%) of the five — this is where $10–12/sq ft lives. Structure the offer around the I-25 split, which is a real physical divide and not a marketing device: WEST of I-25, 1960s–70s Southglenn/Cherry Knolls/Walnut Hills ranches on big lots with 50-year-old trees where bluegrass simply will not grow in dry shade; EAST of I-25, HOA-governed 1990s–2000s homes on graded, sloping lots needing architectural-review-ready submittals and real drainage engineering. Close with Family Sports Center's existing synthetic dome as local proof that this town already buys the product. That is a completely different lead from Littleton next door (historic-town identity, one single water provider) and from Englewood (small rented bungalow lots).
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Colorado SB24-005 applies from 1 January 2026: as a local government Centennial must prohibit installation of new nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF and invasive species on commercial, institutional and industrial property, on common interest community (HOA) property, and in street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors — with artificial turf on athletic fields of play exempt. Given how HOA-heavy Centennial east of I-25 is, that removes ornamental common-area synthetic lawn from the menu entirely and pushes the commercial pitch toward play areas and athletic surfaces. Colorado HB19-1050 protects xeriscape/drought-tolerant landscaping in HOA common and limited common elements but says NOTHING about artificial turf, so individual Centennial HOAs may still restrict or refuse it — expect an architectural-review submittal on essentially every east-side job, and make 'we prepare your ARC package' part of the offer. I could NOT retrieve Centennial's own land development code (Municode returned 403); confirm any city-specific artificial turf, ground-cover or landscape-area provision with Centennial Community Development on 303-325-8000 before asserting one on the page.
facts.water_and_rules: THIS is Centennial's genuine oddity and it deserves its own section on the page. CENTENNIAL HAS NO CITY WATER UTILITY. Service is split among a patchwork of independent special districts. Confirmed from a primary source: Arapahoe County Water and Wastewater Authority (ACWWA), which is itself headquartered in Centennial (303-790-4830). Commonly also cited — VERIFY EACH BEFORE PUBLISHING, as I could not confirm the full roster: Southgate Water District, Willows Water District, Cherry Creek Valley Water & Sanitation, Inverness Water & Sanitation, and Denver Water via distributor contracts in the western neighbourhoods. Two houses on opposite sides of the same arterial can have different providers, different assigned watering days and different rebate eligibility. A trap worth flagging on the page: 'Centennial Water & Sanitation District' is HIGHLANDS RANCH, not the City of Centennial. Where Denver Water serves, the customer is under Denver Water's STAGE 1 DROUGHT, declared 25 March 2026 and running through 30 April 2027, asking a 20% total reduction: two assigned days per week by address, no watering 10 a.m.–6 p.m. through 30 September, and — the big one — FROM 1 OCTOBER 2026 watering of grass and use of spray irrigation systems is PROHIBITED OUTRIGHT, with only hand-watering of trees and shrubs using a shutoff nozzle permitted. The independent districts set their own schedules; neighbouring ECCV reports winter 2026 produced the lowest snowpack on record for its basin. Do not publish a 'find your provider' table until every district and its 2026 rules are individually verified.
facts.soil_and_yard: Centennial's terrain is a real differentiator — the city has 'many hills, gullies and ravines,' threaded by the High Line Canal and the Dry Creek drainage, with Dry Creek Dam and DeKoevend Park as visible expressions of it. Many lots have genuine grade and genuine stormwater, unlike flat north Aurora. Soils are Front Range smectitic clay loams (Nunn and relatives: roughly 35–50% clay, slow permeability, high shrink-swell) over Denver Formation and Pierre Shale — the Colorado Geological Survey's core Denver-metro swelling-soil setting, where wetting cracks driveways, sidewalks and basement floors and swelling pressures reach up to 30,000 psf. West-side lots are large, flat to gently sloping and heavily shaded by 50-year-old trees, so bluegrass genuinely fails in dry shade under mature maples and ash — a strong, honest synthetic-turf argument. East-side lots have engineered grading, walk-out basements and drainage swales that must be respected in the base section rather than filled over.
facts.housing_stock: A post-war suburban assemblage that only became a city in 2001 — incorporated 7 February 2001 from unincorporated Arapahoe County including the former Castlewood and Southglenn CDPs, approved by 77% of voters and the largest incorporation in US history at the time with over 100,000 residents; home rule adopted 2008. I-25 splits the city roughly in half and is the real dividing line for housing type, HOA strength and yard size. WEST OF I-25: Southglenn — a master-planned community by Jordon Perlmutter that already held 22,899 people by 1970 — plus Cherry Knolls, Foxridge, Walnut Hills and Willow Creek: 1960s–70s brick ranches, tri-levels and split-levels on generous flat-to-rolling lots (commonly 8,000–12,000 sq ft), heavy mature shade trees, and weak or nonexistent HOAs in the older tracts. EAST OF I-25: Piney Creek, Smoky Hill, Dove Valley and Saddle Rock-adjacent areas — 1980s–2000s two-storey production homes on tighter engineered lots with active HOAs and real covenant control. Population 108,418 (2020), ~108,853 (2024), across 29.867 sq mi at 5,722 ft. OWNER-OCCUPANCY IS 80.6% — the highest in the batch — and median property value is $658,100.
facts.who_lives_there: The money town of this batch and the closest match to the owner's 'upper echelon' target. Median household income $131,928 — the highest of the five by a wide margin. Median age 42 (37.2 by another measure). Poverty just 3.29%; 96.2% insured. Roughly 75% non-Hispanic white, 9.6% Hispanic/Latino, 6.3% Asian, 3.3% Black; 9.79% foreign-born. Employment skews professional/scientific/technical, healthcare and education; 57,884 employed; average commute 25.9 minutes. Established, high-income, long-tenure homeowners with mature yards and the means to pay $10–12/sq ft.
facts.golf: Good, and conveniently inside the city limits. SOUTH SUBURBAN GOLF COURSE, 7900 S Colorado Blvd, Centennial 80122 — an 18-hole regulation course with an adjacent 9-hole par-3, a driving range, and a 3,000 sq ft practice area with putting surface, chipping zone and practice bunker. FAMILY SPORTS GOLF COURSE, 6901 S. Peoria St, Centennial 80112 — a 9-hole executive course with a heated, lighted driving range plus an 18-hole outdoor miniature golf course, located just east of the Denver Tech Center and next door to Centennial Airport. Adjacent: Lone Tree Golf Club & Hotel (Arnold Palmer-designed 18, just south in Lone Tree, also South Suburban-run); Valley Country Club and Cherry Creek Country Club nearby (verify addresses); and the Cherry Hills Country Club / Glenmoor cluster a short drive north-west. The South Suburban practice complex and the mini-golf course are checkable, on-the-doorstep proof points for putting-green and synthetic-surface work.
facts.commercial_targets: FAMILY SPORTS CENTER, 6901 S. Peoria St, Centennial 80112 — a two-sheet ice arena PLUS an 88 x 44 yard SYNTHETIC TURF indoor sports dome, heated lighted driving range, 9-hole executive course, 18-hole outdoor mini-golf, 30-ft climbing wall, laser tag, bumper cars and the Avalanche Grill. This single address is the best indoor-sports-turf reference in the batch and a live replacement/renewal prospect — the dome turf has a finite life. South Suburban Golf Course's 3,000 sq ft practice complex and par-3 course, 7900 S Colorado Blvd. Cherry Creek School District (Arapahoe-side schools) and Littleton Public Schools in the western neighbourhoods; St. Thomas More Parish School; Centennial Christian Academy; Gateway Seminary. The Streets at SouthGlenn common areas — play/functional use only under SB24-005. Centennial Airport's fixed-base operators and corporate hangars: image-driven, high-budget clients with entrance landscaping and hangar-side amenity space. Dove Valley and Denver Tech Center corporate campuses. Dog daycares, boarding kennels and veterinary practices along Arapahoe Road and S Parker Road — functional use, unaffected by the turf ban.
facts.landmarks: The Streets at SouthGlenn; the second-largest IKEA in the United States, opened 2011 (Colorado's first IKEA, site selected 2008); CENTENNIAL AIRPORT — 1,400 acres straddling Arapahoe and Douglas counties, three asphalt runways with the longest at 10,000 ft, averaging 874 daily operations, one of the busiest general aviation airports in the country, with a 24/7 FAA tower and continuous US Customs; the Denver Tech Center edge and Dove Valley; DeKoevend Park; Dry Creek Dam; the High Line Canal Trail; headquarters of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association and of Gamma Phi Beta; Gateway Seminary.

name: Aurora

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE BAN AND THE FINE. Aurora is the only town in this batch where you cannot legally lay a new sod lawn right now — new Kentucky bluegrass and fescue plantings are prohibited under Stage 1, a city permit is required to install any turf at all, watering is down to two assigned days a week with a hard 10-to-6 blackout, and a fourth violation costs $500. The page's opening line is not 'save water, it's nice'; it is 'artificial turf is your only legal route to a green lawn in Aurora this year.' That is a genuinely different lead from Eastlake a few miles north, where Thornton will PAY $2/sq ft for the same product. Then split the page geographically, because Aurora is really three cities: the 1970s–80s tract yards west of Chambers with dying bluegrass, 40-year-old sprinklers and cracked clay-heaved flatwork (volume work, pet turf, small back yards); and 2005-onward south-east Aurora with big graded lots, metro-district governance and golf-course frontage at Saddle Rock and Blackstone, which is where the $10–12/sq ft putting-green work lives. Add a plainly written SB24-005 warning aimed at HOA boards and property managers — telling them what they may NOT do positions the page as the authority rather than a sales sheet, and steers them toward the athletic-field exemption where the client can still sell.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Colorado SB24-005 (signed 15 March 2024, effective 7 Aug 2024) requires local governments, FROM 1 JANUARY 2026, to prohibit installation, planting or placement of nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF and invasive plant species on commercial, institutional or industrial property, on common interest community (HOA) property, and in street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors. Artificial turf on ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY is expressly exempt. Single-family residential yards are NOT covered. Practical translation for Aurora, which is thick with HOAs and metro districts: ornamental synthetic lawn in an HOA common area, a median or a shopping-centre island is now off the table, while residential back yards and genuine athletic fields remain the market. Separately, Colorado HB19-1050 prevents HOAs from banning drought-tolerant/xeriscape landscaping in common and limited common elements, but it does NOT mention artificial turf — so an Aurora HOA can still refuse synthetic grass on an individual lot. Say this plainly; homeowners routinely assume the opposite. Aurora's own Lawn & Irrigation Permit regime is the other live constraint — confirm with Aurora Water whether it captures synthetic installations.
facts.water_and_rules: THE headline for this page. Aurora Water — the state's third-largest provider, serving roughly 400,000 people. STAGE 1 WATER SHORTAGE declared April 2026 (City Council approved the measures 7 April 2026), in effect since early April. Outdoor irrigation limited to TWO DAYS PER WEEK and never between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. Even addresses water Sundays and Thursdays; odd addresses Wednesdays and Saturdays; multi-family, HOA and non-residential Tuesdays and Fridays. Hand-watering lawns follows the same schedule — only vegetable and flower gardens may be hand-watered in the 10-to-6 window. ENFORCEMENT HAS TEETH: warning, then $125, then $250, then $500 for the fourth and subsequent violations, with service interruption as a last resort. Reservoirs are about half full; Aurora is asking for a 20% total reduction and says returning to sustainable levels 'will likely require several winters.' THE DECISIVE FACT FOR THIS BUSINESS: NEW COOL-SEASON TURF INSTALLATION IS BANNED — new plantings of Kentucky bluegrass and fescue are prohibited under Stage 1. Aurora also requires a LAWN & IRRIGATION PERMIT for the installation or replacement of new turf (sod or seed) at any time of year, and for new or replaced sprinkler systems, with compost soil amendment required; anyone planning drought-resistant turf varieties must contact conservationinspections@auroragov.org before applying. Private pool filling and decorative water features are also banned. Aurora describes itself as high-desert and receives under 15 inches of precipitation a year. REBATES — BE CAREFUL: Aurora offers free water-wise landscape design to all customers plus commercial/HOA/large-property rebates, but I could NOT confirm a residential turf-replacement rebate that pays for artificial turf. Do not claim one. Verify with Aurora Water on 303.739.7195 before publishing any rebate figure.
facts.soil_and_yard: Aurora sits on the eastern-plains side of the metro over Denver Formation and Pierre Shale-derived clays. Expansive/swelling soil is the defining local hazard: montmorillonite and bentonite clays underlie much of the populated Front Range, swelling pressures reach up to 30,000 pounds per square foot, and the Colorado Geological Survey states annual losses from swelling soils regularly exceed those of tornadoes, floods, earthquakes and hurricanes combined. Typical mapped soils are Front Range clay loams of the Nunn type — roughly 35–50% clay, smectitic, moderately slow to slow permeability. On the ground that means cracked driveways, sidewalks, patios and basement floors, and flatwork that moves seasonally. The CGS's own mitigation advice — keep soil moisture consistent and avoid planting/irrigating right against foundations — is the honest engineering argument for turf here, because it removes the perimeter sprinkler spray that drives differential swell. Geographically: south-east Aurora is rolling with real fall on the Piney Creek and Senac Creek drainages and engineered lot grading; north and central Aurora is flatter with slow-percolating clay, so base depth and drainage design, not slope, is the challenge there.
facts.housing_stock: Three genuinely different eras that need three different turf jobs. (a) ORIGINAL AURORA / north-west, platted 1891 as Fletcher, incorporated 1903, renamed Aurora 1928: pre-war and immediate post-war bungalows and 1940s–50s ranches around East Colfax and the old Fitzsimons area, on modest flat alley-served lots, mostly no HOA. (b) THE 1970s–80s EXPLOSION — Aurora 'became the fastest-growing city in the United States during the late 1970s and early 1980s' — vast tracts of ranch and tri-level housing between Havana and Chambers, typically ~7,000–9,000 sq ft lots, mature trees, some HOAs, and 40-year-old sprinkler systems now failing. (c) SOUTH-EAST AURORA, 1995–present: Saddle Rock, Tallyn's Reach, Southshore, Blackstone, Beacon Point, Aurora Highlands — large two-storey production homes on engineered graded lots with strong metro-district/HOA governance, walk-out basements and young unshaded back yards that bake. Median property value $469,100 — the most affordable in the batch — with 62.4% homeownership. City covers 163.588 sq mi (54th largest in the US); elevation ranges 5,285 ft at Sand Creek to 6,229 ft at the Douglas County line.
facts.who_lives_there: 394,432 residents (2024 est.; 386,261 in the 2020 census; 410,053 by a 2025 estimate) — Colorado's third-most-populous city and roughly 50th in the US. Median household income $88,368; median age 35.3; poverty rate 11.9%. By far the most diverse town in the batch: non-Hispanic white 41.67% in 2020 (down from 59.19% in 2000), Hispanic/Latino 30.27%, Black 15.33%, Asian 6.34%, with substantial Ethiopian, Eritrean and Nepalese communities. Top employers: Buckley Space Force Base (~12,100), Anschutz Medical Campus (~6,360), Children's Hospital Colorado (~5,670). Income and yard type vary enormously west-to-east — treat north-west Aurora and Saddle Rock/Blackstone as separate markets.
facts.golf: Strong. Five city-run courses: Aurora Hills, Meadow Hills, Murphy Creek, Saddle Rock and Springhill (Springhill is the 18-hole executive layout) — verified on auroragov.org. Plus CommonGround Golf Course, the Colorado Golf Association's home course built on former Lowry Air Force Base / Mira Vista land. Adjacent private and semi-private clubs commonly cited include Heather Ridge Country Club, Valley Country Club and Blackstone Country Club (south-east Aurora, Douglas County corner) — VERIFY these three before publishing; I confirmed only the five municipal courses from a primary source. Golf-frontage housing at Saddle Rock and Blackstone is prime backyard putting-green territory.
facts.commercial_targets: Aurora Public Schools and Cherry Creek School District — Cherokee Trail, Eaglecrest, Grandview, Overland and Smoky Hill high schools all sit in Aurora (Cherry Creek's other schools are in Centennial and Greenwood Village). Aurora Sports Park, the metro's largest tournament field complex — confirm current field count before citing a number. The five municipal courses (Aurora Hills, Meadow Hills, Murphy Creek, Saddle Rock, Springhill) plus CommonGround for practice greens, tee-line surrounds and academy areas — CommonGround also runs the Solich Caddie & Leadership Academy (verify). Anschutz Medical Campus and Children's Hospital Colorado courtyards, play areas and therapy spaces. Buckley Space Force Base. The many south-east Aurora HOAs and metro districts — but pitch them ATHLETIC FIELDS AND PLAYGROUNDS, not ornamental lawn, because of SB24-005. Daycares, dog boarding, doggy daycare and veterinary practices along Havana Street, Parker Road and the E-470 corridor are functional-use and therefore unaffected by the ban.
facts.landmarks: Anschutz Medical Campus and Children's Hospital Colorado; Buckley Space Force Base; Stanley Marketplace; the Aurora History Museum and the Aurora Fox Arts Center; Southlands shopping centre; the Plains Conservation Center; Cherry Creek State Park; Aurora Reservoir and Quincy Reservoir; the 'Liberty' statue, among the 20 tallest statues in the United States; Del Mar Park; more than 100 parks and over 6,000 acres of open space; the former Lowry/Mira Vista land now under CommonGround Golf Course; the original 1891 Fletcher townsite along East Colfax.

sources: https://www.eccv.org/ (East Cherry Creek Valley W&SD, 6201 S Gun Club Rd, Aurora — serves SE Aurora)

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE MANUFACTURED-HOME YARD AND THE WATER-BILL DIVIDE. Nearly half of all housing in Federal Heights (46.8%) is a manufactured home and only one unit in five is a detached house — this is the one town in the batch where the typical job is a 200-600 sq ft pad yard, not a 2,000 sq ft backyard, and where the page must speak to a $56,597 median household income with small-job pricing, fast installs and a durability-over-luxury promise. Then land the fact no competitor is using: Federal Heights buys its water from Westminster (Standley Lake), not Denver Water, so as of 2026 it is under a VOLUNTARY Drought Watch — 3 days a week, no fines — while Sherrelwood, Berkley, Welby and Derby are under Denver Water's MANDATORY two-day rule and a complete outdoor watering ban with fines from October 1. The honest, locally-true line is that Federal Heights residents are on borrowed time rather than exempt: Clear Creek Basin snowpack is tracking near 2002, the driest year on record, and Westminster's own drought page is live. That is a completely different lead from Sherrelwood next door, whose page is about a uniform 1950s-70s ranch backyard, and from Derby, whose page is about easy sandy soil.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Two Colorado statutes govern, and they cut in opposite directions. (1) HB21-1229 (2021) names 'nonvegetative turf grass (also known as artificial turf)' among drought-tolerant landscaping that a common interest community may REGULATE BUT NOT PROHIBIT in a unit's BACKYARD — so an HOA cannot ban a backyard turf install. (2) SB24-005 (signed Aug 7, 2024; local-government effective date January 1, 2026) PROHIBITS installing artificial turf on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common interest community property, street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors — with artificial turf on athletic fields of play expressly exempted. It does NOT apply to single-family residential yards. For Federal Heights specifically that means: resident yards inside manufactured-home communities are fair game, but the park's own common areas are arguably commercial/common-interest property and are now closed to new artificial turf. Federal Heights' municipal code is hosted on Municode (nodeId 13967) and its Code Enforcement division is active — I could not retrieve a Federal Heights section specifically naming artificial or synthetic turf, so treat that as unverified and worth a call to 303-412-3526 before the page makes any claim about city rules.
facts.water_and_rules: THE differentiator for this page. Federal Heights is the ONLY one of these five NOT on Denver Water. Its 2026 Consumer Confidence Report (PWS ID CO0101055) states that in 2025 100% of supplied water was treated surface water purchased from the City of Westminster, sourced from Standley Lake; in prior years 1-3% came from an 800-ft city well in the Arapahoe aquifer. Westminster confirms it supplies 'the City of Federal Heights, Shaw Heights, and parts of unincorporated Adams and Jefferson County.' Current rule (checked 2026-09-07): Federal Heights declared a VOLUNTARY Drought Watch effective April 15, 2026 — limit watering to no more than 3 days per week, water before 10 am or after 6 pm, no penalties, no assigned days. The city cites Clear Creek Basin snowpack tracking near 2002 levels, the driest year on record. Contrast that with the other four places in this batch, which are on Denver Water and face MANDATORY 2-day-a-week watering plus a total outdoor watering ban with fines from October 1, 2026. Rebates: Westminster runs Garden In A Box, Slow the Flow, and a Lawn Replacement Program (all via Resource Central); nothing on Westminster's conservation pages states that artificial turf qualifies, and turf-replacement programs of this type are built around water-wise PLANTING, so treat artificial turf as NOT rebate-eligible unless Westminster confirms otherwise in writing (waterconservation@westminsterco.gov, 303-658-2500).
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO (Adams County Area, CO001) sampled at two points in the city: Platner loam, 0 to 3 percent slopes at 90th/Federal (85% Platner, 'Fine, smectitic, mesic Aridic Paleustolls'), and Renohill loam, 3 to 9 percent slopes at 96th/Pecos (85% Renohill, 'Fine, montmorillonitic'). Both are expansive-clay soils. Measured shrink-swell in the top 30 cm: Platner linear extensibility 5.6 with 33% clay and Ksat 8.4 µm/s; Renohill LEP 4.5, 34% clay. So: moderate-to-high shrink-swell, slow-to-moderate infiltration, gentle slopes (0-9%). Yes, expansive clay is a real local issue here. Practical consequence: on manufactured-home lots the subgrade is often disturbed fill placed around the pad rather than native Platner, so the base section — not the native soil — governs. Expect to over-excavate, use a compacted Class 6 base with a positive 1-2% fall away from the skirting, and never trap water against a manufactured home's frame or utility runs.
facts.housing_stock: The outlier of the batch and the reason its page cannot look like any neighbour's. ACS 2024 5-yr (B25024) counts 5,452 housing units of which 2,554 (46.8%) are MOBILE/MANUFACTURED HOMES and only 1,050 (19.3%) are single-family detached — the inverse of every other place here. Another 15.1% are 10-19 unit apartment buildings. The city's own demographics page independently reports 43.6% mobile home park spaces, 32.0% multi-family apartments, 19.9% single-family. Era: 22.9% built 1970-79, 18.2% 1990-99, 18.0% 1980-89, 17.9% 2000-09 — a 1970s-2000s city with almost no prewar stock (0.2% pre-1940). ACS median value of owner-occupied units is $95,300 — startlingly low, and that is the manufactured-housing effect dragging the median, NOT what a site-built house sells for; use with care. 59.3% owner-occupied, average household 3.85 persons (large households, small yards). Named manufactured-home communities inside city limits (OpenStreetMap): Denver Cascade, Kimberly Hills (2551 W 92nd Ave), Holiday Hills Village, Lamplighter, Redwood Estates, Friendly Village, Countryside Village. Several run their own EPA-registered water systems — Friendly Village of the Rockies (2100 W 100th Ave, 524 connections), Woodland Hills MHC (1500 W Thornton Pkwy, 434), The Grove at Alta Ridge (1201 W Thornton Pkwy, 409), Suburban Estates and Pleasant View Estates (both 9230 Federal Blvd). Yard reality: a manufactured-home pad yard is typically a few hundred square feet, often side-yard strips and a small fenced patch — jobs of roughly 200-600 sq ft, not 2,000. Traditional HOAs are rare; the functional equivalent is the park owner's community rules, and the park operator (not the resident) controls common areas.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 14,382 (2020 census); 14,125 in 2024 ACS. Median household income $56,597 — the lowest in this batch by about $19,000 and roughly 41% below Colorado's ~$95,470. City reports median FAMILY income $49,291, poverty 21.2%, and 75.2% of residents low-to-moderate income. 64.8% Hispanic, 28.2% White non-Hispanic. Median age 32.8. Nearly half of households speak Spanish at home (47.6%). This is the value/durability buyer, not the owner's 'Cherry Creek upper echelon' target — price the page accordingly.
facts.golf: No course inside the 1.78 sq mi city, but it is ringed by them. Adventure Golf (miniature golf, Sheridan Blvd, Westminster) sits beside Water World and is operated by the same Hyland Hills Park & Recreation District — the single most realistic named mini-golf/putting-surface commercial target in the batch. The Greg Mastriona Golf Courses at Hyland Hills (Westminster), including its separate North Par 3 course, is within 8 km, as are Thorncreek Golf Course (Thornton), Indian Tree Golf Club (Arvada) and Greenway Park Golf Course (Broomfield). No golf-course residential community in or adjacent to the city.
facts.commercial_targets: Schools: Federal Heights Elementary (W 96th Ave), Metz Elementary (Sherrelwood Dr), Iver C. Ranum Middle School (W 80th Ave), Rocky Mountain Elementary, Mesa Elementary, Hillcrest Elementary, Northglenn High School, Pinnacle Charter School, Crown Pointe Academy, Belleview Christian School, STEM Launch. Sports/recreation: Highland Hills Sports Complex, Hidden Hills Ice Arena (W 94th Ave), Federal Heights Skate Park, Carroll Butts Outdoor Roller Rink, Water World and Adventure Golf & Raceway (Hyland Hills Park & Rec District is a single decision-maker controlling all of these — the highest-value door to knock on in the city). Pet: PetSmart (Melody Dr, Northglenn), Petco (Sheridan Blvd, Westminster), Muttz, Puppies N Stuff (W 104th Ave, Northglenn). Manufactured-home park operators as landlords with common areas: Denver Cascade, Kimberly Hills, Holiday Hills Village, Lamplighter, Redwood Estates, Friendly Village, Countryside Village — note SB24-005 likely closes their common areas to new artificial turf from 2026, so sell to residents, not the park.
facts.landmarks: Water World, 8801 N Pecos St — one of the largest water parks in the United States, owned and operated by the Hyland Hills Park & Recreation District, with named attractions a local will recognise (Thunder Bay Wave Pool, Little Bear Pond, Minnow Creek). Adventure Golf & Raceway next door on Sheridan Blvd. Highland Hills Sports Complex. Hidden Hills Ice Arena (W 94th Ave). Federal Heights Skate Park. City parks: Ruston Park (9901 Zuni St), Carstens Park (2518 W 90th Ave), Messina Park, Carmenisch Park. City Hall at 2380 W 90th Ave. The city takes its name from Federal Boulevard and was incorporated May 19, 1940.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: twenty-year-old builder lawn, not drought. Parker is the one town in this batch where the water argument is weak — PWSD allows three days a week, declares no drought stage, and is materially more permissive than Castle Rock, Castle Pines, Pinery Water, Southgate or Northern Douglas County. Leading with scarcity there would ring false to a resident who waters three times a week without a second thought. What Parker actually has is 15,678 detached homes with a median build year of 2004, which means the largest concentration of failing original builder sod in the batch — bare dog-run corners, shade-dead patches under maturing landscape trees, and irrigation systems installed during the second Bush administration. Sell the repair, not the rescue: the strip of lawn behind the fence that has not grown grass in five years, the side yard the dog destroyed, the play area that turns to mud in April. Then run the second track that no neighbouring town can match on named targets — Parker Fieldhouse plus Ponderosa, Chaparral and Legend high schools plus the Salisbury Regional Park expansion make Parker the batch's best athletic-field and indoor-sports market, and athletic fields of play are the one commercial category Colorado law still allows after SB24-005. Castle Rock's page argues with an ordinance, Castle Pines' argues with money, The Pinery's argues with shade and Stage 3 restrictions. Parker's argues with worn-out grass at volume, and with fieldhouses.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: NO PARKER-SPECIFIC ARTIFICIAL TURF ORDINANCE FOUND. I could not reach Parker's municipal code (Municode returned 403) and the Town's own site surfaced no landscaping or synthetic turf rules; the relevant sections would be under Development and the Master Plans/Guiding Documents. This is a genuine gap — Parker should be checked against the municipal code directly, not asserted as unregulated. What does govern, and is the page's real legal content, is state law. SB23-178 bars HOA guidelines from prohibiting nonvegetative turf grass in the BACKYARD of a single-family detached home, requires at least three preapproved front-yard garden designs, requires an option that is at least 80% drought-tolerant plantings, and bars unreasonably requiring hardscape on more than 20% of the landscaping area — with attached homes sharing a wall and condominiums excluded. With 70% of Parker's stock detached and nearly all of it inside an HOA, that statute covers roughly 15,700 Parker households. And SB24-005 has, since 1 January 2026, prohibited artificial turf on commercial, institutional and industrial property and on common interest community common property — exempting athletic fields of play. So in Parker the HOA cannot stop a homeowner turfing their own backyard, but the HOA can no longer turf its own common areas.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: Parker Water and Sanitation District, 13939 Ancestry Drive, 303-841-4627 — and it is the MOST PERMISSIVE provider in this batch, which should change what the page argues. Three days a week, not two: even-numbered addresses Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday; odd-numbered addresses Monday, Wednesday, Saturday; multi-family, HOA and commercial Monday, Wednesday, Saturday. Watering prohibited between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. to limit evaporation. Water waste — runoff, overspray, leaks — is prohibited and reportable. New sod or seed requires a permit to be exempted from the standard guidelines. No formal drought stage is declared on the district's own pages, in contrast to Castle Rock (Stage 1), Southgate (Stage 1), Northern Douglas County (Stage 1) and Pinery Water (Stage 3). REBATES: $750 turf removal discounts delivered through Resource Central; EPA WaterSense smart irrigation devices, water-efficient nozzles, spray-to-drip conversions, high-efficiency toilets; $25 off Garden In A Box; no-cost sprinkler consultations with customised watering schedules. All first-come first-served until funding is exhausted; limited to current PWSD customers who own the property and are in good standing. ARTIFICIAL TURF ELIGIBILITY IS NOT STATED on PWSD's pages and I could not reach Resource Central (403) to confirm — but Resource Central's Lawn Replacement programme is a living-landscape conversion programme, so the working assumption is that artificial turf does not qualify. VERIFY BY PHONE before making any rebate claim on the page.
facts.soil_and_yard: Same Douglas County ground as the rest of the batch: expansive bentonite and montmorillonite clays that swell up to 20% by volume and exert over 30,000 psf, cracking flatwork and basement slabs, plus the heaving-bedrock hazard the Colorado Geological Survey maps specifically in Douglas County via its Dipping Bedrock Overlay District. Parker sits lower and flatter than Castle Rock or Castle Pines at 5,834 ft, with Cherry Creek running through town on its way north to Denver and the associated creek-corridor drainage. Rueter-Hess Reservoir sits west of town. Yards are mostly graded builder pads with modest slope, so the drainage problem here is less about grade and more about clay movement under flatwork and about where downspouts discharge relative to the foundation. Trees are young to middling — planted with the subdivision — so shade is a growing but not yet dominant problem, unlike The Pinery next door.
facts.housing_stock: 22,397 housing units, median year built 2004 — the batch's purest mid-2000s production-suburb profile. 70.0% single-family detached (15,678 units), 5.4% 1-unit attached, 19.8% multi-unit; 69.8% owner-occupied against 27.5% renter, notably more rental than Castle Rock or Castle Pines. Population 65,457 (ACS 2024). Median home value $646,300-$658,600. The growth story explains the stock: incorporated in 1981 with 285 residents, exploded through the mid-1990s and again mid-2000s as a Denver commuter town, hit roughly 48,000 by 2014. So the dominant product is 1995-2010 builder tract housing — Stroh Ranch, Clarke Farms, Canterberry Crossing, Cottonwood, Villages of Parker, Idyllwilde, Anthology, Reata Ridge — sitting on roughly 6,000-9,000 sq ft lots with usable rear yards in the 1,500-3,000 sq ft range, under near-universal HOA. LOT AND BACKYARD FIGURES ARE CHARACTERISED FROM DEVELOPMENT PATTERN, not from parcel data; ACS carries no lot-size variable. The operationally important fact is age, not size: a median build year of 2004 means the original builder sod is now over twenty years old, and twenty-year-old bluegrass in a shaded corner or a dog run is dead, not tired. Small historic Mainstreet core is the only pre-war fabric.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $130,936-$133,369 (ACS 2024) — comfortably affluent, second-lowest of the five here, well below Castle Pines and The Pinery. Elevation 5,834 ft across 22.455 sq mi. Commuter families with school-age children, three large public high schools and six public charter schools' worth of them. This is the batch's mass market: the most detached homes after Castle Rock, at a price point that supports a good job rather than an extravagant one. Realistically the $7-8/sq ft to low-$10s tier, not the 'upper echelon' tier the owner is chasing.
facts.golf: NOT VERIFIED IN THIS SESSION — treat as a research gap. The Wikipedia article on Parker names no golf courses, and the club sites I tried did not resolve. Believed relevant and worth confirming before publishing: The Club at Pradera (private, Jim Engh design, south Parker), Black Bear Golf Club (public), Colorado Golf Club (private, Coore & Crenshaw). The Pinery Country Club sits immediately south in The Pinery CDP. Do not publish course names or designers from this batch without a direct check — golf is not Parker's strongest hook anyway.
facts.commercial_targets: Parker Fieldhouse (303.805.6300) — an indoor sports facility and the strongest single target in Parker, sitting squarely inside the SB24-005 athletic-fields exemption and matching the client's existing indoor-sports-facility service line. Parker Recreation Center (303.841.4500). Salisbury Regional Park, actively under expansion, which means live procurement. Three large public high schools — Ponderosa, Chaparral and Legend (opened 2008) — plus multiple middle and elementary schools, six public charter schools, Ave Maria Catholic School and Lutheran High School Parker; school athletic fields are the protected commercial category. Camp Bow Wow Parker, 10325 S Progress Way, (720) 605-2364 — dog daycare and boarding, a direct pet-turf prospect. DO NOT pitch HOA common areas or commercial landscape turf: SB24-005 has banned both statewide since 1 January 2026, exempting only athletic fields of play. Note the district's own watering rules also treat multi-family, HOA and commercial as a single restricted class on Monday/Wednesday/Saturday.
facts.landmarks: Rueter-Hess Reservoir west of town, with recreation under development. Parker Arts, Culture and Events Center (PACE). Discovery Park, with public art sculptures and illuminated water fountains. O'Brien Park and its gazebo. Salisbury Regional Park, currently being expanded. Historic Mainstreet and the 1880s townsite. Ruth Memorial Methodist Episcopal Church, on the National Register of Historic Places. Parker Cemetery, established around 1884. The Tallman-Newlin Cabin. Cherry Creek through the middle of town. The Town holds roughly 250 acres of developed parkland and over 900 acres of open space.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH 'THE 600 SQUARE FOOT RULE' — Genesee is the one place in the metro where the HOA has already written the artificial turf specification, and a homeowner who hires an installer who has not read it will fail ARC review and pay twice. The page should quote the standard: 600 contiguous sq ft maximum, organic/curvilinear form, muted forest green only, minimally visible from adjoining lots, roads and Open Space, screening may be required, ARC submittal before work begins. Then demonstrate you know the adjacent rules nobody else quotes: no rubber infill within 5 ft of the deck because the Standards prohibit shredded rubber mulch there; retaining walls kept under 36 inches; existing drainage patterns preserved. Position the product as the compliant premium job — a 600 sq ft putting green or play lawn on a $1M mountain lot, which at $10-12/sq ft is exactly the price point the owner wants to reach. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Evergreen, eight miles away, has no single covenant to satisfy — it is a patchwork, so its page leads with wildfire and slope craft instead. Indian Hills is covenant-light cabin country. Edgewater's constraint is a water utility, not a homeowners association. Genesee is the compliance page: uniform covenants, one committee, one written spec, the highest incomes and the highest home values in the batch.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE GENESEE FOUNDATION ARC STANDARDS (2024) NAME SYNTHETIC TURF EXPLICITLY, AND THE SPEC IS EXACT — this is the most specific artificial-turf HOA rule found anywhere in this batch. Verbatim from Section E.3, 'Lawns, Native and Dryland Grasses, Synthetic Turf': (a) 'Although highly discouraged, synthetic turf will be considered for limited areas only.' (b) 'Must be part of a landscape design and located where it is minimally visible from adjoining Lots, roads, and Open Space.' (c) 'Installations will be limited to no more than 600 contiguous sq. ft. and must incorporate an organic/curvilinear form.' (d) 'Screening may be required to break up the view of the synthetic turf from adjacent Lots and Open Space.' (e) 'Must be in a muted, forest green color only.' Living lawns face the identical 600 sq ft contiguous cap. INFILL CONSTRAINT: the Firewise Landscaping section bans organic mulch within 5 ft of dwellings or structures, requires inorganic mulch there, and states that 'due to its highly hazardous combustion characteristics, shredded rubber mulch will not be approved in these areas' — a direct signal to spec silica sand or a non-rubber infill near structures and decks. Related rules: fenced areas capped at 600 sq ft; fences must not be detached or 'floating' and must start at an exterior wall or corner; dog runs must be sited for minimal visibility, and invisible dog fences are 'strongly encouraged' as an alternative and need no approval; no new plant material within Zone 1 (0-5 ft) of a dwelling or deck; new evergreens and conifers not allowed within 30 ft of a structure. ARC approval is required BEFORE work begins. Layer on statewide SB24-005, which reaches common interest community property — so Foundation common areas are legally constrained regardless of ARC willingness, with athletic fields of play exempt.
facts.water_and_rules: Genesee Water and Sanitation District. Genesee is NOT a Denver Water distributor — it does not appear on Denver Water's published distributor list, so Denver Water's Stage 1 order does not bind Genesee addresses. I could NOT retrieve the district's current 2026 restrictions in this session; verify directly with the district before publishing any restriction claim. What is confirmed: Genesee is in unincorporated Jefferson County, which was under STAGE 1 FIRE RESTRICTIONS at the time of this check (7 Sept 2026), per Jefferson County's own alert banner. TURF REBATE: Colorado's Turf Replacement Program (HB22-1151) funds replacement with 'water-wise landscaping' — statutorily 'a water- and plant-management practice that emphasizes using plants with lower water needs'. Artificial turf does not qualify. Genesee residents are not chasing a rebate anyway; they are chasing a compliant, good-looking, low-water yard.
facts.soil_and_yard: Foothills granitic and metamorphic bedrock at 7,500-7,700 ft — thin, gravelly, rocky soils over rock, on real slope. EXPANSIVE CLAY IS NOT THE GENESEE PROBLEM: the Colorado Geological Survey places swelling-soil hazards 'along the sides of mountain valleys and on the plains rather than in the mountains'. What replaces it is rock, grade and drainage, and the Foundation's own ARC Standards spell out the constraints better than any soil map: grading 'must be done with minimum disruption of the Lot'; grading and drainage alteration 'must not create a condition that could lead to soil erosion, accumulation of debris, water collection'; 'newly graded slopes must transition to meet existing slopes in a natural manner'; 'existing drainage patterns must be preserved and retained' and new drainage flows require review; retaining walls 'should be as low as possible, preferably 36" in height or less, and integrated into' the site; exposed cut-and-fill slopes are discouraged; and soil compaction must be corrected. Budget for rock, hand excavation, engineered sub-drainage and low integrated walls on virtually every Genesee job.
facts.housing_stock: CDP covers 6.663 sq mi / 4,264 acres at 7,733 ft elevation, 100% classified rural. 1,634 housing units, 6.2% vacancy. Structure mix: 1,349 one-unit detached, 161 one-unit attached (the townhome filings), 73 in 2-4 unit buildings, 65 in 5+, zero mobile homes. Owner-occupancy is 1,481 of 1,598 occupied units — 93%, the highest in this batch. MEDIAN YEAR STRUCTURE BUILT 1987, the newest of the five, and it reads exactly that way on the ground: 1970s-2000s custom mountain-contemporary — cedar, stone and glass, walkout lower levels stepped into the slope, decks on every elevation. The Genesee Foundation itself covers 885 homes across 2,000 acres with 1,200 acres of dedicated open space and 12 miles of maintained trails, organised into small neighbourhood filings, at 'over 7,500 feet'. Typical lots run roughly half an acre to an acre-plus of steep, treed ground; flat usable yard is scarce and expensive to create. HOA PREVALENCE IS EFFECTIVELY 100% inside the Foundation, and it is an active, well-resourced HOA with a working Architectural Review Committee — this is the single most important fact about doing business in Genesee.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 3,610 (2020 census) / 3,778 (ACS 2020-24). Median age 53.3-54.2, with 29.7% aged 65+. MEDIAN HOUSEHOLD INCOME $186,667 (±$25,501) and MEDIAN HOME VALUE $1,032,700 (±$80,063) — both the highest in this batch and squarely in the owner's 'upper echelon' target. Per capita income $107,628. 67.8% married-couple families; 89.7% White, 2.7% Asian, 4.3% Hispanic; 1,532-1,598 households at about 2.4 persons each. Empty-nester and near-retirement professionals who chose a million-dollar mountain house ten minutes from downtown Denver at I-70 exit 254. They will pay $10-12/sq ft; they will also expect drawings, an HOA submittal and a contractor who has read the covenants.
facts.golf: No golf course in Genesee itself. Nearest named: Hiwan Golf Club in Evergreen — per the Evergreen entry, the area's only country club, just east of Bergen Park — roughly 6 miles southwest; Evergreen Golf Course, operated by the Evergreen Park & Recreation District at Evergreen Lake; Fossil Trace Golf Club, 3050 Illinois St, Golden (City of Golden, opened July 2003), and Applewood Golf Course, 14001 W 32nd Ave, Golden (public, par 71, KemperSports, since the 1960s) down the hill. Genesee's real golf story is the private backyard putting green — and it is capped at 600 sq ft by covenant, which is the whole page (see ordinance field).
facts.commercial_targets: Genesee is realistically a RESIDENTIAL-ONLY market — 885 covenant-controlled homes at a million-plus, plus the wider CDP's 1,634 units. There is no retail strip, no school inside the CDP (Jeffco Public Schools serves it from outside), and no sports complex. The Genesee Foundation's own amenity sites and community playgrounds are the only plausible common-area work, and SB24-005's common-interest-community prohibition makes that a legally constrained pitch — do not lead with it. Treat Genesee as high-ticket residential: ARC-compliant 600 sq ft putting greens and small turf areas at the top of the price band.
facts.landmarks: Genesee Park (Denver Mountain Parks) and the BUFFALO HERD OVERLOOK — Denver Parks' bison herd visible straight off I-70, the single most recognisable landmark on the drive. Chief Hosa Lodge. Genesee Mountain. I-70 exit 254. Lookout Mountain and Beaver Brook nearby. The Genesee Foundation office at 24425 Currant Drive, Golden CO 80401 (303-526-0284). The community holds Firewise Community designation and has won awards 'for stewardship of native ecology and wildfire mitigation'. Golden post office, ZIP 80401. 1,200 acres of Foundation open space with 12 miles of maintained hiking trails.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE PUTTING GREEN, AND MEAN IT. Applewood is the only town in this batch with a real golf course inside its own boundary — a par-71 course at 32nd and Youngfield that has been there since the 1960s — plus a private club and a well-regarded municipal within minutes. It also has the flattest, most workable ground of the five (Clear Creek terrace, no hogback, no dipping bedrock), the second-lowest density at 1.15 units per acre, and the lowest approval friction, because the mid-century subdivisions largely predate HOAs and the area is unincorporated so there is no city design review. Big flat lot, no committee, golfer next door: this is where a genuinely premium backyard green gets built fastest and photographs best, and it is the most credible page in the batch for pushing $10-12 per square foot. Support it with the shade argument — seventy years of mature canopy means large patches where real grass has already lost, which is the single most persuasive before-and-after an Applewood homeowner can see. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Fairmount, one mile north, is a different water utility with a punitive drought surcharge and should lead with cost; West Pleasant View, immediately southwest and sharing the same 80401 ZIP, is a smaller-lot, younger, historically far less affluent market that needs an entry-level and pet-turf pitch; Ken Caryl leads with covenant compliance; Dakota Ridge with autonomy and difficult terrain. Applewood alone leads with leisure and craftsmanship, because it is the only one where the ground, the wallet and the golf all line up.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No municipal ordinance — Applewood is unincorporated Jefferson County, so there is no city landscaping code and no city design review, in contrast with Wheat Ridge and Lakewood immediately east and southeast. HOA prevalence is low because most subdivisions predate the covenant era; where a covenant does exist, Colorado HB21-1229 (signed 2 July 2021, Chapter 409, effective 7 September 2021) provides that artificial turf, as 'nonvegetative turf grass,' is among the drought-tolerant landscaping materials an HOA 'may regulate but not prohibit in the backyard area of a unit.' For commercial and institutional work, Colorado SB24-005 has since 1 January 2026 prohibited installing artificial turf on local government property, commercial, institutional and industrial property, and HOA common areas, with an explicit exemption for athletic fields of play. HONEST GAP: Jefferson County's building and permit pages could not be reached this session — verify whether any grading or drainage permit threshold applies to large residential installs before publishing a 'no permit required' claim.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: CONSOLIDATED MUTUAL WATER COMPANY (cmwc.net, 303-238-0451) — a customer-owned utility, 'Owned by Those We Serve Since 1926,' covering roughly 24 square miles and about 100,000 people through some 400 miles of pipeline across parts of Lakewood, Wheat Ridge and unincorporated portions of central Jefferson County, with Applewood specifically identified on its service area map. Current status: the company's own homepage states 'Due to Drought, Allowed Irrigation Ends Oct. 1, 2026,' citing moderate-to-severe drought conditions with below-normal snowpack and reservoir levels, and points customers to updated drought restrictions and a Drought Management Plan. Critically, this is a DIFFERENT provider and a DIFFERENT rule set from Fairmount's North Table Mountain district one mile north and from the Denver Water Stage 1 regime governing Ken Caryl and Dakota Ridge — do not copy watering-day language between these pages. REBATE ANSWER: no rebate applies to artificial turf. Denver Water's ColoradoScaping and Landscape Transformation programmes and the state turf-replacement programme all fund vegetative water-wise landscaping; synthetic turf is excluded.
facts.soil_and_yard: The easiest ground in this batch. Applewood sits on flat to gently sloping Clear Creek terrace deposits east of South Table Mountain — no hogback, no steeply dipping bedrock, no meaningful slope. General Front Range expansive clay still applies (the Colorado Geological Survey calls swelling soils Colorado's most significant geologic hazard, with clays expanding up to 20% by volume and exerting up to 30,000 psf), so base prep and drainage still matter, but the heaving-bedrock risk that defines Ken Caryl Valley and western Dakota Ridge is absent here. The real site conditions are different ones: seventy years of mature tree canopy means significant root plates to work around, heavy shade patches where natural grass has already failed (a strong turf argument), and old orchard and flood-irrigation-era soils that can be compacted and slow to drain. Large flat lots also mean large single-piece installs with fewer seams — genuinely better product on better ground.
facts.housing_stock: 7,833 people in 3,305 housing units, median age 42.8, 53.5% married-couple households, 1.2% homeowner vacancy. Area 4.486 sq mi (about 2,871 acres) for 3,305 units — a gross density of 1.15 units per acre, second-lowest in this batch and roughly half Ken Caryl's or Dakota Ridge's. Applewood is a low-density, large-lot, mature-tree enclave: predominantly 1950s through 1970s brick ranches, split-levels and mid-century two-storeys on flat, generous, orchard-succeeded lots ten miles west of downtown Denver. The name is literal — this was apple orchard ground before it was subdivided. Because most of the stock predates the covenant-community era, HOA prevalence is LOW compared with Ken Caryl; for most Applewood addresses the architectural committee is not the gatekeeper, which materially shortens the sales cycle. Bordered north by Fairmount, northeast by Wheat Ridge, southeast by Lakewood, southwest by West Pleasant View, with South Table Mountain on the west. Served by the Golden post office, ZIP 80401. Note the boundary history: West Pleasant View CDP was carved out of parts of Applewood in 2000, which is why the two read as one area on a map but diverge sharply on every demographic.
facts.who_lives_there: Median age 42.8, 53.5% married couples, 85.8% white and 8.2% Hispanic, with a 1.2% homeowner vacancy rate. This is a settled, high-equity, low-turnover owner market — people who bought a mid-century ranch on a big flat lot and stayed, whose original lawns and irrigation are now fifty to seventy years old. It is the closest thing in this batch to the 'upper echelon' buyer the owner is targeting, because the combination of large lot, long tenure, high equity and low HOA friction produces discretionary landscape spend. FOR CALIBRATION ONLY: the 2000 Census recorded Applewood's median household income at $66,210 versus West Pleasant View's $40,160 — a 65% gap between two adjacent CDPs sharing a ZIP code. Current figures could not be verified this session (Census API now requires a key; Census Reporter, city-data, Niche, BestPlaces and Zillow all blocked), so pull fresh ACS numbers before publishing any dollar figure.
facts.golf: THE BEST GOLF STORY IN THE BATCH, because the course is inside the CDP. APPLEWOOD GOLF COURSE, 14001 W. 32nd Ave, Golden, CO 80401 — a par-71 course 'at the foot of the Rockies' that has 'been wowing golfers since the 1960s,' open daily 6:00 a.m. to sunset, managed by KemperSports, and listed by Wikipedia as a facility associated with the Prospect Recreation & Park District. Adjacent: Rolling Hills Country Club, the private club in Golden immediately west; Fossil Trace Golf Club, 3050 Illinois St, Golden 80401, the City of Golden's 2003 course. So Applewood residents live minutes from a public course they already play, a private club, and a well-regarded municipal — a dense, verifiable golf identity that supports leading with putting greens.
facts.commercial_targets: PROSPECT RECREATION & PARK DISTRICT — a Title 32 special district with a 6.6 mill levy serving Applewood and Fairmount plus the Denver West Office Park, operating seven developed parks including APPLEWOOD PARK, Arapahoe, Crestview, Fairmount, Maple Grove and Tanglewood parks; PROSPECT ARENA and CRESTVIEW ARENA; the Arbor House and Kendrick Cottage rental facilities; the Applewood and Prospect Trails; the Serene Conservancy; plus youth and adult sports programmes. APPLEWOOD GOLF COURSE itself is a direct commercial prospect for practice greens, tee lines and clubhouse surrounds — and it is KemperSports-managed, meaning a national operator relationship if the job goes well. Schools (Jeffco): Maple Grove, Stober and Welchester elementaries; Everitt and Bell middle schools; Golden High School and Wheat Ridge High School. Under SB24-005 pitch the district and schools on athletic fields of play only.
facts.landmarks: South Table Mountain forming the western boundary; Applewood Golf Course at 32nd and Youngfield; the West 32nd Avenue corridor; Maple Grove Park and Maple Grove Reservoir; Clear Creek and the Clear Creek trail; Denver West and the Colorado Mills area just south; Golden minutes west; Applewood Village and the long-standing 32nd Avenue retail cluster. A local orients by 32nd Avenue, the golf course and South Table Mountain.

name: Four Square Mile

facts.strongest_angle: BE HONEST WITH THE CLIENT FIRST: this is NOT a $10–12/sq ft page. Median household income is $80,903 and 74% of households rent — the 'upper echelon' buyer is not here except inside the gates of Cherry Creek Country Club. Two defensible leads. FIRST AND BEST — THE NAME. 'Cherry Creek' appears in a dozen apartment names inside this CDP (Advenir at Cherry Creek North and South, Lugano Cherry Creek, Modena Cherry Creek, Sienna at Cherry Creek, Cherry Creek Meadows, The Parc at Cherry Creek, Addison at Cherry Creek, Advenir at Cherry Creek), and the area sits in the 80231/80247 'Cherry Creek' postal orbit while being NEITHER Denver's Cherry Creek North NOR the Arapahoe County Cherry Creek CDP eight miles south. A page that untangles which 'Cherry Creek' you actually live in — and which of four small water districts (Havana, Panorama Park, Cherry Creek Valley, Holly Hills) serves your street — will earn links and calls that a generic turf page never will. SECOND — THE SOIL IS THE OPPOSITE OF EVERYWHERE ELSE. Truckton loamy sand, hydrologic group A, 5% clay, Ksat 100 µm/s: this is the one part of the south metro where a turf base is genuinely straightforward, so the pitch can honestly be speed and price rather than engineering. Position for small owner-occupied yards, dog runs and pet-business flooring; route every multifamily and commercial enquiry through an SB24-005 compliance check rather than straight to a quote. NOCO OVERLAP: none — nocoturf.com has no page for this CDP or for Denver/Aurora at town level, though its homepage does target 'Artificial Turf in Denver' generically.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No municipal government of its own — unincorporated Arapahoe County land-use rules apply, and Denver's or Aurora's code governs the moment you cross the street, which makes jurisdiction genuinely confusing here. The controlling documents for most residents are CONDO AND APARTMENT HOA DECLARATIONS, which is where SB24-005 bites hardest in the entire batch: from 1 January 2026 Colorado local governments may not allow the installation, planting or placement of artificial turf on COMMON INTEREST COMMUNITY PROPERTY, on commercial, institutional or industrial property, or in street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians or transportation corridors. Artificial turf on athletic fields of play is the exemption. Four Square Mile is overwhelmingly CIC property, so do NOT build a page here that pitches apartment courtyards, condo dog runs and pool decks without first getting Arapahoe County's written read on how it applies. Residential single-family back yards are unaffected by the statute.
facts.water_and_rules: A patchwork — and telling residents which district they are actually in is the single most useful thing this page can do. Because the CDP is unincorporated Arapahoe County ringed by Denver on three sides and Aurora on the fourth, service comes from several small Denver Water distributors rather than one utility: HAVANA WATER AND SERVICE DISTRICT (Total Service, 303-779-4525, ~2,377 connections), PANORAMA PARK WATER ASSOCIATION (Total Service, 720-571-9095 — note the 'Elm at Panorama' and 'Sage at Panorama' complexes sit here), CHERRY CREEK VALLEY WATER AND SANITATION DISTRICT (Master Meter, 303-755-4474, ~2,317 connections serving roughly 22,000 people — a ratio that reflects master-metered apartment complexes), with Holly Hills W&SD and Lochmoor W&SD adjacent. All purchase surface water and all are on Denver Water supply, so Denver Water's 2026 Stage 1 drought applies: declared 25 Mar 2026 – 30 Apr 2027, 20% reduction target, drought pricing, two assigned watering days — and note MULTIFAMILY AND COMMERCIAL CUSTOMERS WATER TUESDAY AND FRIDAY, which is most of this CDP — only before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m., and after the Board's 26 Aug 2026 declaration no lawn watering or spray irrigation at all after Sept 30. Rebates: the $100 WaterSense toilet and the Resource Central turfgrass-removal discount of up to $750, closed for 2026 since March, and requiring replacement with living water-wise ColoradoScape rather than synthetic turf. Master-meter customers report waste to their own district, not Denver Water. VERIFY BY ADDRESS — residents here routinely assume they are direct Denver Water customers and are not.
facts.soil_and_yard: The one genuinely EASY site in the batch, and a real differentiator. SSURGO maps the area as TRUCKTON LOAMY SAND, 3 to 5 percent slopes (mukey 3390165). The Truckton component (80%) is 5% CLAY in the surface horizon with a linear extensibility of just 0.4 and saturated hydraulic conductivity of 100 µm/s — HYDROLOGIC GROUP A, the best infiltration class. Minor components are sandier still: Vona (group A), Valent (excessively drained, Ksat 300, LEP 0.0–0.1) and Blakeland (somewhat excessively drained). Compare with Foxfield's 47.5% clay and Bow Mar's group-D Renohill: Four Square Mile DRAINS, does not heave, and needs far less drainage engineering. The offsetting risks are the 3–5% slope (grade control matters) and the fact that loose sand still needs proper compaction — a sandy sub-base that is not proof-rolled will rut under traffic.
facts.housing_stock: HONEST HEADLINE: this is an apartment district, not a yard market. 22,872 people in 10,834 housing units (ACS 2020–24), of which only 1,489 are 1-unit DETACHED. The rest: 1,297 single-family attached, 190 duplex, 632 in 3–4 unit buildings, 1,159 in 5–9, 2,666 in 10–19, 1,703 in 20–49 and 1,666 in buildings of 50+. Just 2,672 of 10,138 occupied units are OWNER-OCCUPIED (26%); 7,466 are rented. Median year structure built 1990; median value $474,200; average household size 2.27. OpenStreetMap's building data for the CDP is a wall of complex names — Alta Springs, Timberline, Deerfield, Hunters Run, Griffis Highline, TAVA Waters, Legend Oaks, Advenir at Cherry Creek North and South, Lugano Cherry Creek, Modena Cherry Creek, Candlewyck, Raintree, Dayton Green, Windsong, Club Valencia, Five Star Residences of Dayton Place, Eastern Star Masonic Retirement Campus. The detached houses that do exist are 1960s–70s brick ranches on small lots in pockets like Hampden Heights and Tamarac Park, with backyards typically 1,500–3,000 sq ft.
facts.who_lives_there: The most diverse place in the batch by a wide margin: 48.9% white, 23.5% Black or African American, 19.5% Hispanic or Latino, 6.2% Asian. Median age 32.5 — the youngest here. MEDIAN HOUSEHOLD INCOME $80,903, roughly a third of Bow Mar's and 40% of Foxfield's. Only 30.1% married-couple households. Cherry Creek School District: Eastridge Elementary, Prairie Middle, Overland High (12400 E Jewell Ave, 39.6809/-104.8434, just east in Aurora). ZIPs 80231 and 80247. This is a renter-majority, moderate-income, high-turnover population — the client's 'upper echelon' customer is not here, with one exception noted under golf.
facts.golf: CHERRY CREEK COUNTRY CLUB (private, S Yosemite St, Denver 80231, 39.6690/-104.8778) sits inside the CDP's western edge — a gated residential golf community whose homes are the only genuine luxury turf prospects in Four Square Mile; OSM also records its pool ('CCCC Pool') and a chipping green. Beyond that: Kennedy Golf Course (Denver municipal — 18-hole, 9-hole regulation and 9-hole par-3) about two miles south, and Meadow Hills Golf Course (Aurora, 3609 S Dawson St, 39.6492/-104.8240) about two miles southeast.
facts.commercial_targets: Plenty of doors — but read the SB24-005 caveat before knocking on any of them. PET AND VET is the strongest vertical: Bel-Rea Institute of Animal Technology (a veterinary-technician college), Aquatic Dogs, Banfield Pet Hospital, VCA Southeast Area Animal Hospital, Aspen Commons Animal Hospital, Deerfield Dog Park, Bark Park. SCHOOLS AND CHILDCARE: Challenge School, Place Bridge Academy, Rocky Mountain Prep, Denver Campus for Jewish Education, International Learning Center, Three Bears Learning Center, Dancin' Dreams. FITNESS: Colorado Weightlifting, Front Range Weightlifting Club, Fitness Zone. Country Fair Gardens garden centre. And roughly 8,000 apartment and condo units under professional management — the largest concentration of multifamily common area in the batch and the most exposed to the new statute. Overland High School is two blocks east in Aurora (athletic fields of play are the statutory exemption).
facts.landmarks: The name itself is the hook — 'the four square miles bounded by Quebec Street, Mississippi Avenue, Havana Street and Yale Avenue', surrounded by Denver on the north, west and south and by Aurora on the east (Census GEOID 0827950, 2.70 sq mi, bbox 39.6639–39.6985 N / -104.9110 to -104.8709 W). Cherry Creek Country Club and its S Yosemite Street gates. Bible Park, Cook Park and Cook Park Pool, Babi Yar Park, Garland South Greenbelt Park, Frances Wisebart Jacobs Park, Long's Pine Grove Park, Tsistsistas-Hinono'ei Park, Havana and Cornell Park, with the High Line Canal running through. Denver Campus for Jewish Education and the Challenge School. Bel-Rea Institute of Animal Technology. The Eastern Star Masonic Retirement Campus. TAVA Waters on the old Breakers Resort lake.

facts.strongest_angle: BE HONEST WITH THE CLIENT FIRST: East Pleasant View cannot support a standalone town page on residential demand — 333 residents and roughly 190 homes, with ACS data too noisy to quote. Its value is as a geographically precise landing page for the GOLDEN / APPLEWOOD / DENVER WEST SEAM, and it should be written and optimised for how people there actually describe themselves ('Applewood', 'Pleasant View', 'west Lakewood', 'by Colorado Mills') rather than for a CDP name almost no resident uses. If the page is built, LEAD WITH THE MID-CENTURY RANCH BACK YARD: a median-1961 house on roughly a quarter acre with a real, flat, rectangular back yard — the exact opposite of Edgewater's cramped bungalow lots four miles east — sitting in a corridor where outdoor irrigation stops on 1 October 2026 and where expansive clay punishes any installer who skips base preparation. Then use the golf: Applewood and Fossil Trace are three and four miles away and give this page the most natural putting-green story of the five. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Genesee is a self-identifying, covenant-controlled, million-dollar brand where the CDP name is an asset; East Pleasant View is the reverse — the name is nearly worthless, so the page must earn its traffic on corridor landmarks and the ranch-house yard. It is also the only town in this batch that is simultaneously clay-soil territory AND golf-adjacent AND facing a dated irrigation cutoff.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated Jefferson County — county zoning applies and there is no municipal landscaping ordinance. Unincorporated Jeffco was under STAGE 1 FIRE RESTRICTIONS at the time of this check (7 Sept 2026). No HOA was identified for the CDP. The material rule is statewide: SB24-005 prohibits installing nonfunctional turf and ARTIFICIAL TURF on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common interest community property, and street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors, with a local-government trigger date of 1 January 2026 and artificial turf on ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY expressly exempted. That constraint lands hard here because East Pleasant View's whole commercial value proposition is the surrounding retail and office corridor — precisely the property class the statute reaches. Single-family residential yards are not addressed.
facts.water_and_rules: NOT FULLY RESOLVED IN THIS SESSION, AND IT MATTERS — get this right before publishing. Wikipedia states the Pleasant View Metropolitan District serves the area, but the district's own site could not be located. CONSOLIDATED MUTUAL WATER COMPANY (12700 W 27th Ave, Lakewood, 303-238-0451) serves roughly 24 square miles of Lakewood, Wheat Ridge and unincorporated central Jefferson County — explicitly including Applewood — through 400 miles of pipeline to about 100,000 people, bounded by Clear Creek to the north and by 32nd Ave, Pierce St, Sheridan Blvd, W Alameda Ave and W 6th Ave. East Pleasant View sits at or just inside that western edge. Consolidated Mutual is NOT a Denver Water distributor. As of this check it reports 'moderate-to-severe drought conditions' and states 'Allowed Irrigation Ends Oct. 1, 2026'.
