Whichever provider serves a given address, the operative fact for the corridor is identical and dated: outdoor irrigation stops on 1 October 2026. TURF REBATE: the state Turf Replacement Program (HB22-1151) funds 'water-wise landscaping' — statutorily 'a water- and plant-management practice that emphasizes using plants with lower water needs'. Artificial turf does not qualify.
facts.soil_and_yard: Plains/valley position at the foot of the hogbacks — EXPANSIVE CLAY COUNTRY, unlike the three foothills towns in this batch. The Colorado Geological Survey notes bentonite and montmorillonite clays 'underlie many populated areas of Colorado' with hazards concentrated 'along the sides of mountain valleys and on the plains rather than in the mountains', producing cracked foundations, driveways and basement floors, and it flags 'inappropriate landscaping' as a contributing factor. Clear Creek terrace gravels through parts of the Applewood/Pleasant View area give better drainage than the clay flats further east, so conditions vary lot to lot — a soils check is worth doing rather than assuming. Lots are flat to gently sloped. The technical story is identical to Edgewater's and opposite to Evergreen's: excavation depth, a properly compacted aggregate base, and positive drainage carried away from 1960s slab-and-crawlspace foundations.
facts.housing_stock: The smallest place in this batch by an order of magnitude: 71 acres / 0.111 sq mi at 5,837 ft — an unincorporated island of Jefferson County wedged into the Golden/Lakewood seam, roughly half a mile south of Colorado Mills (14500 W Colfax Ave) and just north of US 6. 188 housing units in the ACS: 165 one-unit detached, 23 one-unit attached, no 2-4 unit, no 5+ unit, no mobile homes. Tenure splits almost exactly evenly — 96 owner-occupied against 92 renter-occupied, unusual for a detached-house pocket and worth noting. MEDIAN YEAR STRUCTURE BUILT 1961: a small 1950s-60s ranch subdivision, slab and crawlspace, attached garages, mature street trees. Gross density is about 2.6 units per acre including streets, so lots run roughly a quarter acre — genuinely generous by inner-suburb standards and REAL BACK YARDS, in sharp contrast to Edgewater's 5.8 units per acre. No master HOA was identified. Historical origin: in 1908 'the Pleasant View Development and Investment Company was created by ranch property owners' who began subdividing the land for residential use.
facts.who_lives_there: THE DATA HERE IS GENUINELY UNRELIABLE AND THE CLIENT SHOULD BE TOLD SO RATHER THAN GIVEN PADDING. The 2020 decennial census counted 333 residents — down from 356 in 2010 and 369 in 2000, a steady two-decade decline. The ACS 5-year estimate, drawn from a sample far too small for this geography, reports 832 people in 188 households with median household income $106,920 ±$46,326, median home value $485,700 ±$134,871 and median age 26.2 ±14. Those margins are larger than any conclusion you could draw from them, and the ACS population is 2.5x the decennial count. USE THE DECENNIAL FIGURE (333 residents) and describe the ACS numbers as indicative only. The defensible reading: a couple of hundred people in a mid-century pocket, roughly half owners and half renters, middle-income by Jefferson County standards, and by a wide margin the least expensive housing of these five towns.
facts.golf: The best golf adjacency in this batch, and the strongest reason to write the page at all. APPLEWOOD GOLF COURSE, 14001 W 32nd Ave, Golden — public, par 71, KemperSports-managed, operating since the 1960s, with Bunkers Taproom and The Vista at Applewood event space, and CAGGY awards for Best Value and Best Course for Families, Women and Seniors — about 3 miles north. FOSSIL TRACE GOLF CLUB, 3050 Illinois St, Golden — City of Golden owned, opened July 2003, routed past dinosaur trace fossils near the 12th green, repeatedly named Best Golf Course in Denver — about 4 miles northwest. Rolling Hills Country Club (private, Golden) also sits in this corridor but its details could not be verified in this session; confirm before naming it. The Golden golf corridor is the credible local reference point for a putting-green page here.
facts.commercial_targets: The residential market is about 190 homes — far too small to carry a page on its own. The commercial surroundings are the entire point: Colorado Mills (14500 W Colfax Ave), the Denver West office park and its hotels, Applewood Golf Course and its Vista event space, and the Golden/Applewood retail corridor along 32nd Ave and Colfax. Red Rocks Community College sits on W 6th Ave nearby — verify the exact address before publishing, as I could not confirm it in this session. Jeffco Public Schools serves the area from surrounding attendance zones; I did not verify which specific schools, so name them only after checking the boundary map. CRITICAL CAVEAT: SB24-005 restricts artificial turf on exactly this commercial and institutional property class, so lead commercial conversations with athletic fields of play (exempt), practice greens and indoor installations rather than with landscape turf.
facts.landmarks: COLORADO MILLS, 14500 W Colfax Ave — 1,411,627 sq ft, the Denver metro's only indoor outlet centre, rebuilt as 'Colorado Mills 2.0' after the May 2017 hailstorm and reopened November 2017 with 180+ stores — roughly half a mile north of the CDP. The Denver West office campus and hotels. The US 6 / I-70 / West Colfax interchange complex at the Golden-Lakewood seam. Applewood immediately north, Golden west, Lakewood east. Golden post office, ZIP 80401; area codes 303/720/983; elevation 5,837 ft. Note that neighbouring West Pleasant View is a separate, much larger CDP (987 acres, 4,327 residents) — do not conflate them.

facts.strongest_angle: THE AFFORDABILITY AND CODE-COMPLIANCE PAGE - and it should be honest about being that. Per capita income is $34,101, one-fifth of Cherry Hills Village's, and 12% of the housing stock is mobile homes or non-conventional units on small, flat, floodplain-adjacent lots. Nobody in Sheridan is buying a $40,000 backyard, and pretending otherwise wastes the page. LEAD WITH THE SMALLEST DEFENSIBLE JOB IN THE CATALOGUE: a 300-600 sq ft dog run or a whole small backyard, at a fixed published price, that ends the Chapter 46 Article IX grass-and-weeds citation, kills the dust nuisance the same chapter also regulates, and never needs the two-day-a-week Denver Water allowance that disappears entirely on Oct. 1, 2026. SECOND BEAT: multifamily and mobile-home-park operators - more than 1,250 units in buildings of three-plus and 200 mobile homes in a 2.29-square-mile city, where property managers buy pet turf by the courtyard rather than by the yard. THIRD: Sheridan School District No. 2's five campuses and the Sheridan Recreation Center. This page is the deliberate mirror image of Cherry Hills Village - volume, speed and a fixed small-job price rather than bespoke greens - and it is the one town in this batch that should NOT be used to chase the $10-12/sq ft repositioning. Written properly, it is the lead-volume page that funds the estate work up the hill.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Sheridan Code of Ordinances Chapter 46, NUISANCES AND ENVIRONMENT, contains Article IX - GRASS AND WEEDS. The same chapter's Sec. 46-32(f) makes 'Dry or dead shrubs, dead trees, combustible refuse, waste, building materials/debris... or any material growing on a street, sidewalk or upon private property' a fire-hazard nuisance, and Sec. 46-32(a) and (j) prohibit escape into the open air of 'smoke, ashes, dust, dirt, grime...' that unreasonably interferes with property use. I could not retrieve the specific maximum grass or weed height from Article IX - verify the number with the city before quoting it. That pairing of a grass-and-weeds ordinance with a dust nuisance clause IS the local selling argument: a code-enforcement letter for tall weeds or a dust-blowing bare yard is a common, expensive nuisance in this housing stock, and synthetic turf ends both permanently. Other relevant chapters: 54 Planning and Development, 55 Subdivisions, 56 Zoning, 70 Stormwater. Statewide SB23-178 bars HOAs from prohibiting nonvegetative turf grass in backyards - relevant in Sheridan's newer attached-housing developments.
facts.water_and_rules: UNCONFIRMED AND FLAGGED. The City of Sheridan does not appear to run a water utility: its e-services portal bills STORMWATER only, its Code of Ordinances (updated July 15, 2026 through Ord. No. 7-2026) contains no water or utilities chapter in the table of contents, and Community Development refers residents to outside providers. Sheridan sits inside the Denver metro system between Denver, Englewood and Littleton, so supply almost certainly originates with Denver Water, possibly via an Englewood Utilities or district contract - VERIFY the exact provider by phone (City of Sheridan 303-762-2200) before publishing. RESTRICTIONS: Denver Water's Stage 1 drought runs March 25, 2026 through April 30, 2027 - two assigned days per week (even addresses Sunday/Thursday, odd Wednesday/Saturday, multifamily and commercial Tuesday/Friday), no watering 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and a total prohibition on lawn watering and all spray irrigation from Oct. 1, 2026, with penalties up to $2,000 plus flow restrictors or disconnection. REBATES: Denver Water / Resource Central lawn replacement and Garden In A Box target live water-wise plantings; no artificial turf rebate found anywhere in the Colorado or Denver Water programs.
facts.soil_and_yard: Sheridan sits on the South Platte River and Bear Creek bottomlands at 5,286 ft; 0.066 of its 2.29 square miles is open water. Expect alluvial river-terrace soils, shallow groundwater and floodplain across parts of the city alongside the regional expansive-clay problem (CGS: swelling up to 20% by volume, pressures over 30,000 psf, heaved slabs and buckled flatwork; the locally named Englewood series is 35-60% clay, smectitic, slow permeability). Lots are flat with minimal slope, which makes drainage design a positive-grade problem rather than a runoff problem - but the city has a dedicated Chapter 70 STORMWATER in its code and bills a separate stormwater fee, so added impervious area on a small lot is a real permitting consideration. On this housing stock, bare dirt and compacted, dog-worn back yards are the common starting condition rather than a healthy lawn.
facts.housing_stock: 2,486 units and by far the most mixed and most modest stock in this batch. Type: 1,236 detached single-family, 88 attached, 40 duplex, 224 in 3-4 unit buildings, 106 in 5-9, 187 in 10-19, 126 in 20-49, 172 in 50+, 200 MOBILE HOMES and 107 'boat, RV, van, etc.' - roughly 12% of all housing here is a mobile home or non-conventional unit, a share nothing else in this batch comes close to. Age: 616 units built 1970-79, 462 built 1960-69, 414 built 2000-09, 253 built 1950-59, 184 built 1980-89, 157 built 1940-49, 143 built 1939 or earlier, 150 built 2010-19, only 84 built 1990-99. Read that as three layers: a pre-war and 1950s-60s working-class bungalow and small-ranch core, a 1970s apartment layer, and a 2000s redevelopment layer tied to the River Point project. Tenure 1,367 owner / 949 renter households. Median home value $380,600 - roughly one-fifth of Cherry Hills Village. Lots are small city lots on 2.29 square miles total; backyards are typically a few thousand square feet, flat, often fenced, frequently bare dirt or weeds. HOA prevalence is low in the older core; the newer attached and multifamily product is metro-district or HOA-governed.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 6,005 (ACS 2020-24); 6,105 at the 2020 census. Median household income $60,608 and per capita income $34,101 - the lowest in this batch and about one-fifth of Cherry Hills Village's per capita figure. 2,539 residents (42%) are Hispanic or Latino; 2,910 White alone. Median age 35.8, the youngest of the five, with 21.3% under 18. Founded by John McBroom in 1859 as Petersburg, laid out and renamed by his brother Isaac after Gen. Philip H. Sheridan, incorporated April 14, 1890. This is a value market. It is explicitly NOT the 'upper echelon' segment the owner is chasing, and the page should be written accordingly.
facts.golf: No golf course inside the city. South Suburban Parks and Recreation - which serves Sheridan and operates the Sheridan Recreation Center - runs South Suburban Golf Course, Littleton Golf and Tennis Club, Family Sports Golf Course and Lone Tree Golf Club & Hotel nearby. Municipal courses immediately adjacent in Englewood (Broken Tee) and Denver (Overland Park) are commonly cited but were not verified in this pass - confirm before naming them on the page. Golf is not this town's angle.
facts.commercial_targets: Sheridan School District No. 2 - a compact five-site district with real field and playground needs: Sheridan High School, Fort Logan Northgate, Alice Terry Elementary, SOAR Academy and the Early Childhood Center, district office 4107 S Federal Blvd. The Sheridan Recreation Center plus South Suburban's Sports Dome, Family Sports Center and Family Sports Ice Arena nearby. River Point at Sheridan retail landlords - median and entry landscape, and pet-relief areas at the pet-oriented tenants. THE HIGHEST-VOLUME OPPORTUNITY: the 1,250-plus units in buildings of three or more, plus 200 mobile homes - apartment courtyards, dog runs and mobile-home-park common areas bought by property managers rather than homeowners. Carson Nature Center and South Platte Park a short distance upstream. Daycares and pet businesses serving a young, 42% Hispanic population with a median age of 35.8.
facts.landmarks: River Point at Sheridan, the city's big-box retail district on the South Platte, financed with a Public Improvement Fee and overseen by the Sheridan Redevelopment Agency (which still meets - a Sept. 28, 2026 meeting is on the city calendar). The Oxford-City of Sheridan RTD light rail station on the D Line, the city's main transit hub. US 85 (Santa Fe), US 285 (Hampden) and State Highway 88 (Federal). Sheridan High School and Fort Logan Northgate School, both named landmarks on the annual Sheridan Celebrates parade route (2026 theme: 'Cultures of Colorado'). The Sheridan Recreation Center, operated by South Suburban Parks and Recreation. The confluence of Bear Creek and the South Platte River, and the South Platte River Trail. Fort Logan National Cemetery lies immediately west across Sheridan Boulevard, in Denver - the district's Fort Logan Northgate school takes its name from it (verify the exact jurisdiction line before writing it as 'in Sheridan'). City Hall, 4101 S Federal Blvd.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE BILL, NOT THE LOOK. Fairmount is the only place in this batch where the homeowner is already being charged a per-gallon penalty to keep grass alive, and where there is explicitly no rebate to soften it — for a reason worth quoting on the page: 'Denver Water's rebates are only available to entities that buy treated water from Denver. NTM buys raw water.' Combine that with the density finding — 0.88 housing units per acre, the largest lots of these five towns — and the page writes itself as arithmetic. A big Fairmount lot on two permitted watering days a quarter is running straight into the $2.20 and $6.60 per thousand gallon tiers, on top of a $250 or $500 fine if a controller is set wrong. Open with a surcharge calculator or a worked example, name the exact tiers and the exact assigned days, and position turf as the only intervention that takes irrigated area to zero rather than merely reducing it. Then, and only then, talk about how it looks. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Applewood, one mile south, is served by Consolidated Mutual and has a completely different rule set and no surcharge — so the same pitch would be false there. Ken Caryl's page is about covenant compliance and Dakota Ridge's is about autonomy and terrain. Fairmount is the ROI page, and it is the one town here where a spreadsheet outperforms a photograph.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No municipal ordinance — Fairmount is unincorporated Jefferson County. The binding rules are the water district's, not a city's: NTM's two-day watering schedule, the 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. prohibition, and the tiered drought surcharge, backed by $250 and $500 penalties. Where a newer subdivision has an HOA, Colorado HB21-1229 (signed 2 July 2021, effective 7 September 2021) protects the homeowner: artificial turf is 'among the types of drought-tolerant landscaping materials that the HOA may regulate but not prohibit in the backyard area of a unit.' For institutional work, SB24-005 has since 1 January 2026 prohibited artificial turf on local government property, on commercial, institutional and industrial property, and in HOA common areas — except on athletic fields of play. Since the Prospect Recreation & Park District is a Title 32 special district, that exemption is the only route onto its grounds.
facts.water_and_rules: THIS IS THE PAGE'S ENTIRE REASON TO EXIST. Provider: NORTH TABLE MOUNTAIN WATER AND SANITATION DISTRICT (ntmwater.org, 303-279-2854, admin@ntmwater.org), serving more than 10,000 residents, businesses and industries for over 65 years — and its own site names 'the Fairmount Community' first in its service area, alongside portions of Arvada, Golden and Wheat Ridge and unincorporated areas. Effective 1 MAY 2026 a DROUGHT SURCHARGE is in force, billed per 1,000 gallons quarterly: 0-12,000 gallons free; 13,000-50,000 gallons $1.10 per 1,000; 51,000-90,000 gallons $2.20 per 1,000; OVER 90,000 GALLONS $6.60 PER 1,000. Lawn watering is 'ONLY allowed two days per week' — even-numbered residences Sunday and Thursday, odd-numbered Saturday and Wednesday, multi-family and commercial Tuesday and Friday — and 'is NOT allowed between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m.'; hand watering of trees and gardens is permitted anytime. Enforcement: first violation $0, second $250, third and subsequent $500. The rules run 'until both Denver Water and North Table Mountain determine that the drought has eased.' REBATE ANSWER, AND IT IS THE BEST LINE ON THE PAGE: there is no rebate at all, and the district explains why in its own words — 'Denver Water's rebates are only available to entities that buy treated water from Denver. NTM buys raw water.' So a Fairmount homeowner is paying a per-gallon penalty their Wheat Ridge neighbour is not, with no rebate to offset it. Artificial turf does not qualify for any rebate anywhere in this metro, which for once costs nothing here — there is nothing to lose.
facts.soil_and_yard: Below North Table Mountain's basalt cap the ground grades into clay and shale slopes and then onto the Clear Creek terrace. Front Range expansive clay applies throughout — the Colorado Geological Survey calls swelling soil Colorado's most significant geologic hazard, with clays expanding up to 20% by volume and exerting up to 30,000 pounds per square foot. Fairmount's specific complication is its agricultural water history: this is ditch country (the Church Ditch and Rocky Mountain Ditch corridors cross this part of Jefferson County), so many large lots were historically flood-irrigated, leaving heavy, compacted, poorly draining soils and, on some parcels, ditch easements and lateral crossings that constrain excavation. Slopes are gentle to moderate — far easier than Ken Caryl Valley, harder than Applewood. HONEST NOTE: the specific ditch alignments were not verified parcel-by-parcel this session; treat as a survey-at-site item rather than a published claim.
facts.housing_stock: 9,324 people in 3,548 housing units, 1.9% vacant with a homeowner vacancy rate of just 0.4% — the tightest in the batch. Population grew 23.3% from 7,559 in 2010, by far the fastest growth of these five places, so there is meaningful recent construction alongside older stock. Median age 44.5 and 20.4% aged 65 or older — the oldest population here. 67.9% married-couple households, the highest share in the batch. THE DECISIVE NUMBER: the CDP covers 6.281 sq mi (about 4,020 acres) for 3,548 units, a gross density of 0.88 units per acre — the LOWEST of these five places and roughly two and a half times more land per home than Ken Caryl or Dakota Ridge. Fairmount is the big-lot town. The character is a semi-rural, ditch-irrigated agricultural edge along the Highway 93 and Highway 58 corridor, with large older parcels and horse-property remnants, now infilling with newer subdivision product. Bordered north by Arvada, east by Wheat Ridge, south by Applewood, and west by Golden and undeveloped land on North Table Mountain. Served by the Golden post office, ZIP 80403; Fairmount has never had its own post office.
facts.who_lives_there: Median age 44.5, with 22.3% under 18 and 20.4% aged 65 or older — a barbell of established families and retirees. 87.6% white, 2.3% Asian, 7.7% two or more races. 67.9% married couples and a 0.4% homeowner vacancy rate signal long-tenure ownership on land people are not leaving. The 23.3% population jump since 2010 means a second, younger cohort has arrived into newer homes. Practically: retirees on large irrigated lots who are tired of mowing and paying for water, plus newer families with builder landscaping to finish. HONEST GAP: current income figures could not be verified this session (Census API key requirement; aggregator sites blocked).
facts.golf: Fairmount has no course inside its boundary. Adjacent and named: Fossil Trace Golf Club, 3050 Illinois St, Golden, CO 80401 — the City of Golden's course, opened July 2003, which describes itself as offering 'a mountain course feel in an urban setting'; Applewood Golf Course, 14001 W. 32nd Ave, Golden 80401, immediately south in the neighbouring CDP; Rolling Hills Country Club in Golden. Arvada's municipal courses (West Woods, Indian Tree, Lake Arbor) lie just north — NOT independently verified this session, so confirm before naming them in print. Golf is a secondary angle for Fairmount; water is the primary one.
facts.commercial_targets: PROSPECT RECREATION & PARK DISTRICT is the anchor institution — a Colorado Title 32 special district with a 6.6 mill levy serving northern Jefferson County, explicitly including Fairmount and Applewood plus the Denver West Office Park. Its assets: seven developed parks including FAIRMOUNT PARK, plus Applewood, Arapahoe, Crestview, Maple Grove and Tanglewood parks; PROSPECT ARENA and CRESTVIEW ARENA as athletic venues; the Arbor House (70-person) and Kendrick Cottage (36-person) indoor facilities; the Applewood and Prospect Trails; the Serene Conservancy; and youth and adult sports programmes. Fairmount Elementary (Jeffco). Under SB24-005 the arenas and athletic fields of play are the compliant targets, not park landscaping. The Highway 58/93 light-industrial and commercial corridor is a further door, but note that SB24-005 now closes NEW artificial turf on commercial and industrial property, so pitch existing-surface replacement and interior or athletic applications only.
facts.landmarks: North Table Mountain and North Table Mountain Park, forming the undeveloped western skyline; Highway 93 running north to Boulder and Highway 58 east to I-70; Fairmount Park; the Fairmount ditch-and-farm landscape along 58th Avenue; Golden and the Coors brewery complex immediately southwest; Arvada's edge to the north. Locals define Fairmount by being the last open, rural-feeling ground between Arvada, Wheat Ridge and Golden.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE PATCHWORK. Lakewood is the only city in this batch where the answer to 'what are my watering rules?' depends on which of at least three utilities bills you — Denver Water, Consolidated Mutual, or Green Mountain Water and Sanitation — and in 2026 all three are in drought on different calendars with different end dates, with Green Mountain customers additionally paying a Denver Water drought SURCHARGE passed straight through. Open the page with 'find out who bills you for water, because that decides your watering days and what your lawn costs you this year,' give the three schedules side by side, and then land the conversion point: artificial turf is exempt from every one of them, and from the 30 September spray-irrigation shutoff, and from drought pricing that runs to 30 April 2027. Nobody else in the metro can run that lead honestly — Golden has one utility and one order, Arvada has one utility and a published fine schedule. Secondary structure: three housing eras, three different jobs. The 1950s east-side bungalow is a shade-and-tree-root install; the 1970s-80s Green Mountain split-level is a slope-and-drainage install on expansive clay against the hogback; Solterra and Rooney Valley is the 'upper echelon' $10-12/sq ft install, where the closing argument is HB21-1229 — state law says the HOA cannot prohibit nonvegetative turf grass in your backyard — with the honest caveats that the protection stops at the backyard and does not cover attached homes. Cannibalisation watch: Lakewood is a central-metro town and a plausible NoCo Turf Co. overlap if that site has pushed south; check nocoturf.com for an existing Lakewood page before publishing, because two of the owner's own sites competing on 'artificial turf Lakewood' is the worst outcome here.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Lakewood administers zoning through its zone-district system and the Lakewood Atlas property lookup. Specific artificial-turf provisions in the Lakewood Zoning Ordinance were NOT verifiable — Municode blocks automated access — so confirm with Development Review (DR@LakewoodCO.gov, 303-987-7500) before publishing any municipal code claim. THE STRONG, CHECKABLE LEGAL FACT is state law: C.R.S. 38-33.3-106.5(1)(i.5), from HB21-1229 (2021). An HOA (a) may NOT prohibit the use of nonvegetative turf grass in the BACKYARD, (b) may not unreasonably require hardscape on more than twenty percent of the landscaping area, (c) must allow an at-least-80%-drought-tolerant plantings option, and (d) may not prohibit vegetable gardens in front, back or side yards; and each association must pre-approve at least three preplanned water-wise garden designs for front yards. Critical limits: the protection is BACKYARD-specific (front yards remain subject to design guidelines), and it applies ONLY to single-family DETACHED homes — not attached homes, townhomes or condos. Separately, SB24-005 prohibits installing nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF or invasive species on commercial, institutional or industrial property, common-interest-community property, and street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors, applying to local governments from 1 JANUARY 2026 — with artificial turf on ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY expressly EXEMPT. That combination is commercially decisive: residential detached backyards are legally protected, athletic fields are exempt, but HOA common areas and commercial landscape turf are now constrained.
facts.water_and_rules: THE defining Lakewood fact: there is no single city-wide water utility, and your neighbour three streets over may be on a different provider with different rules. Confirmed providers serving parts of Lakewood — Denver Water; Consolidated Mutual Water Company (headquartered in Lakewood at 12700 W. 27th Avenue, 303-238-0451); and Green Mountain Water and Sanitation District (13919 West Utah Ave, Lakewood), which buys its water from Denver Water. 2026 is a drought year across all of them. DENVER WATER declared a Stage 1 drought for 2026: mandatory two assigned days per week, watering only before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m.; even-numbered addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd-numbered Wednesday and Saturday, multifamily and commercial Tuesday and Friday; the Board of Water Commissioners proclaimed that lawn watering and all spray irrigation must cease after 30 SEPTEMBER 2026 (hand-watering and drip for trees and plants may continue); leaks must be fixed within 10 days; and DROUGHT PRICING on outdoor water use runs through 30 APRIL 2027. GREEN MOUNTAIN W&S is passing a Denver Water drought SURCHARGE through to its Lakewood customers and asking for a 20% reduction. CONSOLIDATED MUTUAL is under drought restrictions with allowed irrigation ending 1 October 2026, citing moderate-to-severe drought with snowpack and reservoirs significantly below normal. REBATES: Denver Water runs ColoradoScape, turfgrass removal, Garden In A Box and a Landscape Transformation Assistance Program — all aimed at drought-tolerant PLANTINGS. Denver Water does not state that artificial turf qualifies; treat it as INELIGIBLE until confirmed in writing, and never imply a rebate on an artificial turf install.
facts.soil_and_yard: Front Range Urban Corridor expansive clay — montmorillonite and bentonite — which the Colorado Geological Survey ranks among the state's most significant and widespread hazards, capable of 30,000 psf swelling pressure and known for cracking driveways, sidewalks and basement floors. Lakewood's west side runs up against the hogback and Green Mountain (6,854 ft), where slope and dipping bedrock add differential movement and where cross-slope on 1970s-80s lots is a real design constraint. The east side is flatter alluvial ground along Bear Creek and Weir Gulch. Practical read: east-side jobs are shade and tree-root problems, west-side jobs are slope, drainage and base-depth problems.
facts.housing_stock: Three distinct housing markets inside one city, and the page must treat them as three different quotes. (1) East side, toward Denver around Belmar and Alameda: 1950s-60s brick ranches and bungalows on modest lots under heavy mature shade — low-light turf spec and careful root-zone work around established trees. (2) Green Mountain and the central west: 1970s-80s split-levels and two-storeys with genuine cross-slope, where drainage and base depth drive the bid. (3) The far west edge in Rooney Valley: Solterra, started 2007 and grown to nearly six hundred properties in Tuscan, Andalusian and Provençal-inspired architecture — new-build luxury and the realistic $10-12/sq ft target. The city incorporated 24 June 1969 (briefly as Jefferson City) but the bulk of its housing predates incorporation by two decades. 155,984 residents across 44.6 sq mi — fifth most populous city in Colorado. HOA prevalence is low on the post-war east side and high in the Solterra/Rooney Valley new-build band.
facts.who_lives_there: 155,984 residents (2020 census). Median household income was $52,960 per the 2010 figure carried on Wikipedia — STALE, refresh from current ACS before publishing any income claim. The Denver Federal Center is the largest employer at roughly 8,000 people and holds the largest concentration of federal agencies outside Washington, D.C., which gives Lakewood an unusually large stable federal-professional household base. Three higher-education institutions: Red Rocks Community College, Colorado Christian University, and Rocky Mountain College of Art and Design. Cold semi-arid climate, 17.54 inches average annual precipitation.
facts.golf: Fox Hollow Golf Course and Homestead Golf Course, both operated by the City of Lakewood. CAUTION: do not link foxhollowgolf.com — that domain belongs to an unrelated course in Glasgow, Kentucky. Use the City of Lakewood's own golf pages. Bear Creek Lake Park sits adjacent to Fox Hollow. Private clubs in and near the city should be individually confirmed before naming.
facts.commercial_targets: Recreation centres: Carmody Recreation Center, Charles Whitlock Recreation Center, Green Mountain Recreation Center, Lakewood Link Recreation Center, Clements Community Center. Golf: Fox Hollow Golf Course, Homestead Golf Course (both city-run). Athletic fields: the city runs a 'Rent an Athletic Field' programme across its 115-park system — a direct route to field-conversion conversations, and the athletic-fields-of-play exemption in SB24-005 means this is the one commercial category still legally clear. Schools (Jeffco Public Schools): Lakewood High School, Green Mountain High School, Bear Creek High School. Higher education: Red Rocks Community College, Colorado Christian University, Rocky Mountain College of Art and Design. Belmar's retail and restaurant tenants and its plaza. Solterra's HOA and metro-district common areas — but note the SB24-005 constraint on common-interest-community property from 1 January 2026.
facts.landmarks: Belmar — the mixed-use downtown Lakewood district at 7337 W Alaska Drive, built on the former Villa Italia mall site, with a public plaza, The Rink at Belmar, farmers markets, summer concerts and the Hyatt House Denver Lakewood. Bear Creek Lake Park. Heritage Lakewood Belmar Park. Green Mountain, 6,854 ft. The Denver Federal Center. Red Rocks Community College. Two Creeks Park. Solterra in Rooney Valley. The city has 115 parks in total.

name: Berkley

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE SUBGRADE LOTTERY — 'in Berkley, the block decides the job.' No other town in this batch can honestly make this claim, and it is backed by hard data: seven soil samples across the CDP returned Truckton sandy loam, moderately wet loamy alluvium classed as somewhat poorly drained, 'Pits' from old Clear Creek gravel extraction, 'Dumps', and 'Urban land-Elyria-Weld complex' made ground. One street drains like a beach; the next is fill over a gravel pit with groundwater near the surface. That gives the page a genuinely technical, genuinely local lead — site assessment, variable excavation, geotextile over soft ground, drainage designed for water rising as well as falling — and it justifies premium pricing in the one town here that can pay it: highest median home value of the five ($468,100), highest median household income ($84,637), oldest median age, and a Tennyson Street/Regis University halo. Pair the engineering lead with backyard putting greens and Regis's athletic fields (the SB24-005 exemption), and note that Berkley's housing mix — 16.9% prewar, 20.2% manufactured, 12.6% townhome, 11.7% built since 2010 — means the page must show four different jobs, not one. Completely distinct from Sherrelwood's uniform ranch-lot volume story next door.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated Adams County — county rules, no city code. Adams County Code Compliance enforces blight including 'tall, overgrown grass, weeds and brush (12 inches)' via Neighborhood Services (720.523.2792). State law: HB21-1229 provides that a common interest community may regulate but not prohibit 'nonvegetative turf grass (also known as artificial turf)' in a unit's backyard — directly relevant here because Berkley has the batch's highest share of attached/townhome product and post-2010 infill, which is where HOAs actually exist. SB24-005 (local-government effective date January 1, 2026) prohibits new artificial turf on commercial, institutional, industrial, common interest community, right-of-way, parking-lot, median and transportation-corridor property, exempting only athletic fields of play — so an HOA's own common green cannot be turfed, while the homeowner's backyard inside it cannot be refused. That pairing is worth stating plainly on this page because Berkley is where both halves apply. Adams County's landscaping standards themselves could not be retrieved and remain unverified.
facts.water_and_rules: Denver Water, and unusually, in the most direct form available. Denver Water lists Berkeley Water and Sanitation District as a TOTAL SERVICE distributor, meaning 'Denver Water owns the water system and is responsible for its operation, maintenance and replacement' and bills individual customers directly — unlike the master-meter districts serving the other CDPs here. EPA SDWIS also records a Berkley Water & San District (CO0117358) and North Pecos Water and Sanitation District (CO0116553, 6900 Pecos St) in ZIP 80221, alongside Crestview (CO0101040) and several tiny systems (Holly Mutual Water Company, Eastwood Estates Water District, Valley Vista Estates) — so verify the provider per address rather than assuming. Either way the rules are Denver Water's, and as checked 2026-09-07 they are MANDATORY effective March 25, 2026: maximum two days per week on assigned days (even addresses Sunday/Thursday, odd addresses Wednesday/Saturday, multi-family, commercial, HOA and government Tuesday/Friday), watering only 6 pm to 10 am, a declared drought seeking a 20% cut, and from October 1, 2026 no outdoor watering at all with fines applied. Rebates: Denver Water's published residential rebates are toilets and sprinkler nozzles; its landscape programme (ColoradoScaping) is about water-wise planting. Artificial turf is not offered a rebate — do not imply one.
facts.soil_and_yard: This is Berkley's real story and it is unique in the batch. Seven SSURGO sample points inside and around the CDP returned five different answers: Truckton sandy loam, 3 to 5 percent slopes at 54th/Tennyson and 58th/Zuni (LEP 1.1, only 10.7% clay, Ksat 38.9 µm/s — fast, benign); 'Loamy alluvial land, moderately wet' at 60th/Lowell, classed Typic Haplaquolls and rated SOMEWHAT POORLY DRAINED at 0-1% slope, i.e. a high water table; 'Pits' at 62nd/Federal and 64th/Tennyson — former Clear Creek sand-and-gravel extraction; 'Dumps' at 56th/Sheridan; and 'Urban land-Elyria-Weld complex, 0 to 15 percent slopes' at 52nd/Lowell — made ground and disturbed urban fill. Translation: one block is clean sandy loam that drains beautifully; the next is uncontrolled fill over an old gravel pit; the next has groundwater near the surface. Expansive clay is NOT the headline problem here (unlike Sherrelwood, Federal Heights and Welby) — settlement, uncontrolled fill and a shallow water table are. Practical consequence: Berkley is the one town where a site-specific subgrade assessment genuinely earns its fee, and where a fixed per-square-foot quote sight-unseen is dangerous. Expect variable over-excavation depths, geotextile separation over soft or made ground, and on the wet alluvial pockets a drainage design that assumes water comes UP as well as down.
facts.housing_stock: The most temporally scattered and physically variable place in the batch. ACS 2024 5-yr (B25034): of 4,410 units, 8.9% predate 1940 and 8.0% are 1940s (16.9% prewar-to-wartime, by far the oldest core here), 12.5% are 1950s, then a second wave — 16.2% 1970s and 17.9% 1980s — and a genuine recent wave of 11.7% built since 2010, including 2.4% since 2020. Nothing dominates. B25024 is equally mixed: 52.7% single-family detached, 12.6% single-family ATTACHED (townhomes — the highest attached share in the batch), 20.2% MOBILE HOME (890 units), and 5.5% in buildings of 20+ units. ACS median value $468,100 — the HIGHEST of the five — and 67.3% owner-occupied. Land area 3.597 sq mi but much of it is Clear Creek corridor, gravel pits and industrial ground, so residential density is concentrated. Practical read: a Berkley street can be a 1920s bungalow, a 1980s townhome, a manufactured home and a 2021 infill build within one block, and each is a different turf job with a different budget. HOAs are rare on the old stock but likely on the attached/townhome and post-2010 infill product — check per address.
facts.who_lives_there: 2020 census population 12,536 (up 11.9% from 2010); 2024 ACS 10,789 with a projected decline. Median household income $84,637 — the HIGHEST of these five, and the closest thing in this batch to the owner's 'upper echelon' ambition. 54.1% Hispanic (the lowest Hispanic share here), 38.5% White. Median age 36.0 — the oldest median age of the five. 8.7% of families in poverty. Immediately north of Denver's gentrifying Berkeley neighbourhood and the Tennyson Street corridor, which is where the money and the design expectations bleed across the county line.
facts.golf: Willis Case Golf Course (Vrain Street, Denver) sits directly against the area and is the local course. City Park Golf Course (E 23rd Ave, Denver), Lakewood Country Club, The Greg Mastriona Golf Courses at Hyland Hills and its North Par 3, and Indian Tree Golf Club (Arvada) are all within about 8 km. Holey Moley (mini golf) is nearby. No golf-course residential community. The realistic golf revenue here is backyard putting greens for the higher-value, higher-income end of the CDP — this is the batch's best putting-green market on income and home-value grounds.
facts.commercial_targets: Highest-value target in the batch: Regis University's Soccer/Lacrosse Field, Baseball Field and Softball Field — athletic fields of play are the ONE commercial category SB24-005 expressly exempts, so collegiate and school fields are where commercial turf money legally remains. Schools: Guardian Angels Catholic School, Tennyson Knolls Elementary, Berkeley Gardens Elementary, Centennial Elementary (Raleigh St), Beach Court Elementary, J. Hodgkins Middle School, Westminster High School (Raleigh St), The Early College of Arvada, Colorado Outward Bound School (Sheridan Blvd). Childcare: Dottie's Daycare & Pre-School. Pet businesses, concentrated on the adjacent Denver side: Mouthfuls Pet Store (Tennyson St), Simpawtico (W 38th Ave), Pet Vet Supply (W 47th Ave), Denver Holistic Center Pets 4 PPL (Pecos St), Fish Den (W 44th Ave), Petco. Midtown Dog Park. Berkeley Park Tennis Courts. Clear Creek Valley Park pickleball courts (Adams County Parks as the decision-maker).
facts.landmarks: Regis University and its athletic fields sit immediately against the area. Clear Creek Valley Park — the Adams County regional park, with pickleball courts, volleyball and horseshoe pits. Tennyson Knolls Park and Tennyson Knolls Elementary. Berkeley Hills Park. Lewis Ralston Gold Site Park, marking the 1850 gold discovery on Ralston Creek. Little Dry Creek Lake. Westminster Station Park & Nature Playground. Guardian Angels Catholic School. Immediately south across the Denver line: Berkeley Park, Rocky Mountain Lake Park, Inspiration Point Park and the Tennyson Street shopping strip — the reference points locals actually use.

sources: https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Tabular/post.rest (SSURGO CO001, seven points across the CDP)

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE OCTOBER 1 IRRIGATION BAN — 'the smallest yards in the metro, under the strictest water rule in the metro.' Edgewater is a confirmed Denver Water master-meter distributor, so its residents are personally subject to Stage 1: two assigned days a week until 30 September, and from 1 October 2026 spray-irrigating grass is flatly prohibited with charges up to $2,000. Pair that legal hard stop with the physical fact that a typical Edgewater back yard is small enough that the entire job is one or two thousand square feet at a price an $76k-income, $637k-house owner can actually write a cheque for. Then layer the second Edgewater-specific hook: a renter-majority city of 1950s bungalows in active scrape-and-pop-top redevelopment, where young owners with dogs are rebuilding tiny yards from scratch anyway. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Golden next door leads with historic mining-town lots and Coors; Lakewood leads with 1970s ranch acreage; Genesee and Evergreen lead with covenants and wildfire. Edgewater is the only one of the five where a named utility has published a dated, enforceable, fineable prohibition on watering grass, and the only one where the median house predates 1960 and the median resident is 34. Do NOT lead with golf communities, estate lots or HOA compliance here — none of those describe Edgewater.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: NO Edgewater-specific artificial turf ordinance was found in this session (the city site and Municode both blocked automated retrieval — verify with the Community Development department before publishing). The binding rule in Edgewater is not a landscaping code, it is Denver Water's Stage 1 drought order. STATEWIDE AND IMPORTANT: Colorado SB24-005 prohibits the installation, planting or placement of nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF and invasive plant species on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common interest community (HOA) property, and street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors — trigger date 1 January 2026 for local governments, 1 January 2025 for state facilities. Artificial turf on ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY is expressly exempted. Single-family residential property is not addressed by the prohibition. This matters disproportionately in Edgewater because the city's growth stock is attached and multifamily — apartment courtyards and townhome HOA common areas are exactly the property class the statute reaches. Confirm scope with counsel before quoting a commercial job.
facts.water_and_rules: Denver Water — Edgewater is a named Denver Water MASTER METER distributor (confirmed on Denver Water's own distributor list, alongside Lakewood and Wheat Ridge). That makes Denver Water's drought order directly binding on Edgewater addresses, and it is severe: STAGE 1 DROUGHT declared 25 March 2026, in effect through 30 April 2027 or until further notice, with a 20% total-use reduction required. Through 30 September: single-family homes get two assigned days a week — even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd addresses Wednesday and Saturday; multifamily/commercial/irrigation accounts Tuesday and Friday; no watering between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. From 1 OCTOBER 2026, 'watering of grass or use of spray irrigation systems are prohibited' outright — only hand-held hoses with shutoff nozzles and drip for trees, shrubs and perennials remain legal. Violations carry charges up to $2,000, plus flow limiters or service disconnection for repeat offences. REBATES: Denver Water offers a WaterSense toilet rebate up to $100 and the ColoradoScaping / Landscape Transformation Assistance Program. ARTIFICIAL TURF DOES NOT QUALIFY — Colorado's statewide Turf Replacement Program (HB22-1151) defines the eligible replacement as 'water-wise landscaping', statutorily 'a water- and plant-management practice that emphasizes using plants with lower water needs', i.e. living plants. Say this plainly on the page: turf beats the restriction and saves the water, but it does not earn the rebate.
facts.soil_and_yard: Front Range plains/valley position — expansive-clay country. The Colorado Geological Survey states that bentonite and montmorillonite clays 'underlie many populated areas of Colorado' and that these hazards occur 'along the sides of mountain valleys and on the plains rather than in the mountains'; Edgewater is squarely inside that zone, unlike the three foothills towns in this batch. Documented local consequences include cracked foundations, driveways and basement floors, and CGS explicitly flags 'inappropriate landscaping' and unsuited maintenance practices as contributors. Practical translation: excavation depth, a properly compacted aggregate base and positive drainage away from the house are load-bearing on every job here — the same clay that heaves a driveway will telegraph through a thin turf base. Lots are flat to gently sloped toward Sloan's Lake; drainage is an alley-and-grid problem, not a hillside problem.
facts.housing_stock: The metro's densest small city: 0.695 sq mi / 445 acres, elevation 5,368 ft, holding 2,589 housing units (~5.8 units/acre gross). Median year structure built 1958 (ACS 2020-24). Structure mix: 1,282 one-unit detached, 83 one-unit attached, 255 in 2-4 unit buildings, 769 in 5+ unit buildings, zero mobile homes. Tenure is the headline — only 945 of 2,344 occupied units are owner-occupied; ~60% of Edgewater rents. On the ground: a tight streetcar-era grid of pre-1960 frame bungalows and minimal-traditional cottages on narrow alley-served lots, now being scraped, popped-top or replaced with modern infill duplexes, townhomes and apartments. Back yards on the detached stock are genuinely small — a few hundred to roughly two thousand sq ft — and new attached product is smaller still. HOA prevalence is LOW on the old single-family stock (no master-planned HOA anywhere in the city) but rising fast on new townhome/condo product, which almost always carries a small association. Practical read for a turf installer: whole-backyard jobs of 800-2,000 sq ft, high job count, low square footage per job. NOTE: the 25x125 ft original platting typical of streetcar suburbs is inferred from density, not verified from Edgewater's plat records — check before printing a lot dimension.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 5,005 (2020 census) / 4,932 (ACS 2020-24). Median age 34.3 — by far the youngest of these five and roughly 20 years younger than Genesee. Median household income $76,591 (±$7,890); per capita income $50,937; median home value $636,900 (±$23,337). 35.2% Hispanic/Latino, 63% White (2020 census); 23.8% of households have children under 18; poverty rate was 23.2% at the 2010 count. This is a young, urban, design-literate, dual-income buyer who just bought a 1950s bungalow at $600k+ — not the Cherry Creek estate client, but a high-volume, dog-owning, low-maintenance-seeking one. The renter majority also means a large landlord/small-multifamily owner segment.
facts.golf: No course inside the city's 445 acres, and Edgewater is not a golf-community market — this is a BACKYARD PUTTING GREEN page, not a golf-adjacency page. Nearest verified named courses: Fossil Trace Golf Club, 3050 Illinois St, Golden (City of Golden, opened July 2003, built through dinosaur trace fossils near the 12th green), ~8 mi west; Applewood Golf Course, 14001 W 32nd Ave, Golden (public, par 71, KemperSports-managed, operating since the 1960s), ~7 mi northwest. Willis Case Golf Course (Denver muni) and Lakewood Country Club sit closer but were not verified in this session — confirm before naming them. The honest pitch here is a 200-400 sq ft two- or three-hole green squeezed into a small yard.
facts.commercial_targets: Jefferson High School, Edgewater Elementary and Lumberg Elementary (Jeffco Public Schools) — but note these are institutional property under SB24-005; the athletic-field-of-play exemption is the legitimate opening, so pitch fields, not landscape beds. Edgewater Public Market's event space and tenant patios (commercial property — same caveat). The new multifamily buildings along Sheridan Blvd and W 20th/25th Ave represent the largest square footage in town (769 units in 5+ unit buildings) via dog runs and courtyards, again subject to the statute. Daycares, dog daycares and groomers along the Sheridan and W 25th Ave corridors should be named from a live Maps check before publishing — I could not verify individual businesses in this session and will not invent names.
facts.landmarks: Edgewater Public Market, 5505 W 20th Ave — 40+ food stalls, retail boutiques and wellness tenants (Barquentine Brewing, Shake Shack, Edgewater Books, American Axes), the city's social centre. Sloan's Lake immediately east across Sheridan Blvd — the city is literally named for its 'lakefront location at Sloan's Lake'. Edgewater Civic Center. Jefferson High School, Edgewater Elementary and Lumberg Elementary. West Metro Fire Rescue has covered the city since 2016. Elevation 5,368 ft; post office opened 1 March 1892; incorporated 5 November 1904; bordered by Denver east, Lakewood south and west, Wheat Ridge north.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE LOTS AND THE DIRT — NOT THE DROUGHT. Wheat Ridge is the one town in this batch where the yards are big, old, flat and largely un-HOA'd, and the reason is that they were market gardens and greenhouses before they were backyards. 'Carnation City' is not decoration here; it is the explanation for why a Wheat Ridge backyard is sixty feet deep when the same-era house in Arvada has twenty-five. Open the page on the 1940s-60s brick ranch on an oversized, irregular former farm lot, and then on the specific installation problems that ground creates and that a generic turf company will not have anticipated: buried irrigation ditch laterals, old greenhouse footings and glass in the excavation, a high water table near Clear Creek, and parcel shapes that make every job a custom cut. That is a soil story about ALLUVIUM AND BURIED FARM INFRASTRUCTURE, which is the exact opposite of Golden's story three miles west about steeply dipping mined clay — and it is what makes these two pages genuinely different rather than one template with the name swapped. Handle water second and honestly: unlike Golden and Arvada, Wheat Ridge has no single order, because Consolidated Mutual and Denver Water both operate inside the city on different calendars with different end dates. Then point the high-value work where it actually is: Applewood, straddling the western boundary, is the large-lot affluent pocket and the realistic home of the backyard putting green and the $10-12/sq ft install. One hard constraint to respect: Wheat Ridge's own landscaping code is the most likely municipal obstacle in this batch and has NOT been verified — get Chapter 26 Article V confirmed before the page makes any front-yard claim.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THIS IS THE ONE TO VERIFY BEFORE PUBLISHING. Wheat Ridge Chapter 26, Article V (Landscaping Regulations) could not be read — Municode returns 403 to automated access — and Wheat Ridge is exactly the kind of city that sets a minimum live-plant-material percentage and caps non-living ground cover, which would directly constrain front-yard artificial turf. Do not make ANY claim about Wheat Ridge's artificial turf rules until Community Development confirms it at 303-234-5900. State law C.R.S. 38-33.3-106.5(1)(i.5) (HB21-1229) applies — an HOA may not prohibit nonvegetative turf grass in the BACKYARD of a detached single-family home, may not unreasonably require hardscape on more than twenty percent of the landscaping area, must allow an 80%-drought-tolerant option, and must pre-approve three water-wise front-yard designs — but it is LESS relevant here than in any other town in this batch, precisely because Wheat Ridge has so few HOAs. The binding constraint in Wheat Ridge is the city code, not an association. Also note SB24-005: from 1 January 2026 the state prohibits installing nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF or invasive species on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common-interest-community property and rights-of-way, with athletic fields of play expressly exempt.
facts.water_and_rules: Fragmented, like Lakewood, and this is a trap worth naming on the page. Wheat Ridge has no single municipal water utility; addresses fall to different districts, with Consolidated Mutual Water Company and Denver Water both serving parts of the city. I could NOT obtain an authoritative, city-published list of every district serving Wheat Ridge — verify with the city at 303-234-5900 before publishing a list, and do not guess. What IS confirmed for 2026: CONSOLIDATED MUTUAL WATER COMPANY (12700 W. 27th Avenue, Lakewood, 303-238-0451) is under drought restrictions with allowed irrigation ending 1 OCTOBER 2026, citing moderate-to-severe drought with snowpack and reservoir levels significantly below normal, and publishing an updated October 2026 drought restrictions document. DENVER WATER is in a declared Stage 1 drought for 2026: two assigned days a week, watering only before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m., even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd Wednesday and Saturday, multifamily and commercial Tuesday and Friday; all lawn watering and spray irrigation ceases after 30 SEPTEMBER 2026; leaks fixed within 10 days; drought pricing on outdoor use through 30 APRIL 2027. No artificial-turf rebate found from either provider — Denver Water's turf programmes fund drought-tolerant plantings, not synthetic turf.
facts.soil_and_yard: Genuinely different from the rest of the batch, and the difference is the sales hook. Clear Creek runs through the city, and the old market-garden ground along and north of the creek is good alluvial soil — that is precisely why carnations, greenhouse crops and truck vegetables grew here rather than anywhere else on the Front Range. So Wheat Ridge's install problems are NOT primarily the swelling-clay heave that dominates Golden and Douglas County. They are: a relatively high water table near Clear Creek; a century of buried irrigation ditch laterals; old greenhouse footings, glass and farm debris turning up in excavation on redeveloping parcels; and irregular parcel geometry that makes almost every job a custom cut rather than a rectangle. Front Range expansive clay still applies on the higher ground away from the creek bottom. Terrain is flat to gently sloping — the easiest grading in this batch.
facts.housing_stock: Predominantly 1940s-1960s brick ranches and bungalows on unusually GENEROUS, irregular lots for an inner-ring suburb — and the reason is agricultural, not architectural. Wheat Ridge began as a Gold Rush rest stop in the late 1850s, became truck-farm and greenhouse country, and earned the nickname 'Carnation City' from its mid-twentieth-century carnation industry. Because market-garden and greenhouse parcels were subdivided piecemeal rather than laid out as uniform tracts, lot sizes are irregular and many backyards are notably deep compared with same-era housing in Arvada or Denver. The city did not incorporate until 17 June 1969, long after most of its housing was built. 32,398 residents (2020 census) across 9.58 sq mi at 3,470 people per square mile. HOA prevalence is LOW — this is one of the least HOA-encumbered municipalities in the batch. Median home value cited at $237,500 for 2013 — badly stale, refresh before publishing. Cost of living index 108.5 against a national 100.
facts.who_lives_there: 32,398 residents (2020 census). Median age 41.1 — the oldest in this batch and notably older than Golden's 34.1. 74.5% white, 22.3% Hispanic or Latino. Long-tenured owner-occupiers on the old farm-lot streets, with steady infill and redevelopment pressure along the 38th and 44th Avenue corridors bringing in younger buyers. Notable natives: NASA astronaut Matthew Dominick and Olympic cyclist Linda Brenneman. Jeffco Public Schools.
facts.golf: No golf course inside the city limits — a real finding, not a gap. The relevant course is Applewood Golf Course, immediately west at 14001 W. 32nd Avenue, Golden, CO 80401: public, par-71, operating since the 1960s, managed by KemperSports, repeatedly voted Best Value, Best Ego-Booster and Best Course for Families, Women and Seniors in the CAGGYs, with Bunkers Taproom and The Vista at Applewood wedding and events venue on site. The Applewood neighbourhood straddling the Wheat Ridge/Golden boundary is the affluent, large-lot pocket of this corridor and is where the backyard putting-green market actually lives. Also in range: Indian Tree and West Woods in Arvada, Fox Hollow and Homestead in Lakewood.
facts.commercial_targets: Wheat Ridge Recreation Center (leisure pool and climbing wall). Anderson Park and Anderson Pool. Prospect Park. Randall Park. The Green at 38th. The Active Adult Center. Parks and Recreation operates publicly as Rooted in Fun (rootedinfun.com), which is the brand to approach rather than a generic city department. Schools (Jeffco Public Schools): Wheat Ridge High School, plus Everitt Middle School — confirm the full elementary list with the district before naming. The surviving commercial greenhouse and garden-centre operations along the 38th and 44th Avenue corridors are a distinctive local B2B target that exists nowhere else in this batch. Applewood Golf Course just over the line, including Bunkers Taproom and The Vista at Applewood events venue. The Lutheran hospital campus area businesses.
facts.landmarks: The James H. Baugh House, an 1860 hand-hewn log cabin listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The annual Carnation Festival, which celebrates the city's floriculture heritage with free family activities. The Green at 38th. Clear Creek and the Clear Creek Trail. Crown Hill Park on the southern edge. Anderson Park, Prospect Park and Randall Park. The 38th Avenue Main Street corridor. The Applewood neighbourhood on the western boundary. Interstate 70 and Colorado 391 meet in the city.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE FINE SCHEDULE — nobody else in this batch has one. Arvada is the only town here with published, escalating penalties (warning, then $100, then $250, then $500) attached to a two-day watering calendar that a neighbour can report you for 24 hours a day through Ask Arvada. And the single most persuasive line in the whole ordinance is that new sod and seed get NO establishment grace period: they must follow the same two assigned days a week. So in 2026, re-sodding an Arvada lawn means asking new grass to root on two waterings a week under a $500 ceiling and a hard 1 October shutoff. That is a sharper, more urgent and more specific lead than anything available in Lakewood, Wheat Ridge or Golden, and it should be the first thing on the page. Then split east/west, because they are two different businesses. Olde Town and east Arvada: small post-war lots, mostly no HOA, long-tenured owners, old celery-farm ground — the buyer is a homeowner tired of the calendar and the water bill, and the job is a straightforward small-yard or pet-turf install. West Arvada, Candelas and the McIntyre Street corridor: this is the $10-12/sq ft 'upper echelon' target, and the closing argument is HB21-1229 — state law says your HOA cannot prohibit nonvegetative turf grass in your backyard — with two caveats you must get right or you will burn trust: the protection covers only detached single-family homes, so Candelas townhome and patio-home owners are not covered, and HOA COMMON AREAS are now caught by SB24-005 from 1 January 2026. Against Wheat Ridge next door, the contrast is stark: Arvada leads with enforcement and a fine schedule, Wheat Ridge leads with big un-HOA'd market-garden lots. Cannibalisation watch: check nocoturf.com for an existing Arvada or Westminster page before publishing.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Arvada's Land Development Code landscaping provisions could NOT be read (Municode blocks automated access) — verify with the city at 720-898-7000 before publishing any municipal code claim. The strong, checkable law is state law. C.R.S. 38-33.3-106.5(1)(i.5), from HB21-1229 (2021): an HOA may NOT prohibit the use of nonvegetative turf grass in the BACKYARD; may not unreasonably require hardscape on more than twenty percent of the landscaping area; must allow an at-least-80%-drought-tolerant plantings option; may not prohibit vegetable gardens in front, back or side yards; and must pre-approve at least three preplanned water-wise garden designs for front yards. It applies ONLY to single-family DETACHED homes — which matters enormously in west Arvada, because Candelas includes patio homes and townhomes that are NOT covered. Separately and importantly, SB24-005 (signed 15 March 2024) prohibits installing nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF or invasive species on commercial, institutional or industrial property, common-interest-community (HOA) property, and street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors, applying to local governments from 1 JANUARY 2026 — with artificial turf on ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY expressly EXEMPT. West Arvada's metro-district and HOA common areas are precisely the property class this catches, so the common-area pitch that would otherwise be obvious in Candelas needs legal review before it is made.
facts.water_and_rules: The City of Arvada runs its OWN water utility, and in 2026 it operates the strictest and most enforceable regime in this batch. Arvada declared a drought and imposed STAGE 1 MANDATORY RESTRICTIONS effective 15 APRIL 2026, targeting roughly a 20% reduction in water use, with lawn watering ending 1 OCTOBER 2026. Two assigned days per week and NO watering between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m.: even-numbered single-family homes Sunday and Thursday; odd-numbered single-family homes Wednesday and Saturday; ALL other properties — multifamily, commercial and HOA — Tuesday and Friday. Trees, shrubs and gardens may be watered any day by handheld hose or drip irrigation outside the restricted hours. Pools may be filled; outdoor fountains are discouraged; car washing at home is still allowed with a bucket or handheld hose (note this is LOOSER than Golden, which bans home car washing outright). THE MOST QUOTABLE PROVISION FOR THIS BUSINESS: newly installed sod or seed must follow the same two-day schedule — there is no establishment grace period. PENALTIES ESCALATE: first violation a warning notice, second $100, third $250, fourth $500. Residents can report violations 24/7 through the city's Ask Arvada platform. No artificial-turf rebate was found; do not imply one exists.
facts.soil_and_yard: Front Range expansive clay throughout — montmorillonite and bentonite, up to 30,000 psf swelling pressure per the Colorado Geological Survey, with driveway, sidewalk and basement-slab cracking the signature failure. The two halves of the city behave differently. West Arvada rises toward the hogback and the Ralston Valley with more slope, shallower bedrock and view lots — base depth and drainage dominate. East Arvada is flatter former celery-farm bottomland along Ralston Creek with heavier, more organic topsoil sitting over clay, plus the legacy of a century of flood irrigation — expect old ditch laterals and inconsistent fill on redeveloping parcels. Standley Lake and Ralston Reservoir govern the western drainage.
facts.housing_stock: A clean east-west split that should structure the entire page. EAST: Olde Town and east Arvada — the original townsite platted 1 December 1870 plus dense post-war ranch tracts on small lots, largely WITHOUT HOAs, owner-occupied and ageing. WEST: roughly west of Ward Road out toward the foothills — 1990s-2020s master-planned HOA and metro-district product. Candelas alone is a nearly 1,500-acre master-planned community at 9371 McIntyre Street, organised into six villages (TownView, SkyView, ValleyView, CanyonView, MountainView, ParkView) with single-family detached homes, patio homes, townhomes and custom residences by builders including Tri Pointe Homes, plus resort-style amenities, parks, trails, recreation centres and a community garden. 124,402 residents at the 2020 census (2024 estimate 121,873), seventh-largest city in Colorado, 39.57 sq mi across Jefferson (~98%) and Adams (~2%) counties. The town was the 'Celery Capital of the World' in the early twentieth century before suburbanising after WWII — which is why east-side ground is old irrigated bottomland.
facts.who_lives_there: 124,402 residents (2020 census). 76.36% white non-Hispanic, 14.98% Hispanic or Latino, 2.49% Asian. Median household income $66,125 — that is a 2010 figure and is STALE; refresh from current ACS before publishing. Served by RTD commuter rail with three stations, giving west-side professionals a downtown Denver commute. The demographic story is bimodal to match the housing: long-tenured older owners in the east, higher-income young families in the Candelas/McIntyre corridor in the west.
facts.golf: West Woods Golf Club, 6655 Quaker Street, Arvada, CO 80007 — operated by the City of Arvada, with three distinct nines: The Sleeping Indian, The Cottonwood and The Silo. Indian Tree Golf Club — operated by the Apex Park and Recreation District, not the city. Apex also runs the Lake Arbor Center and Outdoor Pool; confirm the current operating status of the Lake Arbor golf course itself before naming it on the page. Standley Lake sits in the west of the city.
facts.commercial_targets: The Apex Park and Recreation District is the single richest commercial target list in this batch — headquartered at 13150 W. 72nd Avenue, Arvada, it operates the Apex Center, the APEX FIELD HOUSE (indoor sports — a direct fit for the indoor sports facility line), the Apex Tennis Center, the Arvada Aquatics Center, a Racquetball and Fitness Center, the Community Recreation Center, Fitzmorris Recreation Center, Lake Arbor Center and Outdoor Pool, Secrest Recreation Center, Simms Street Recreation Center, Indian Tree Golf Club, and multiple athletic fields available for rental. West Woods Golf Club (City of Arvada). Schools (Jeffco Public Schools): Arvada High School, Arvada West High School, Ralston Valley High School, North Arvada Middle School, with Standley Lake High School nearby. Candelas' recreation centres and community garden. Olde Town Arvada's breweries, winery and hospitality tenants — outdoor patio and dog-friendly turf is a natural fit for that district.
facts.landmarks: Olde Town Arvada, 7307 Grandview Avenue — a restored turn-of-the-century Main Street district with restaurants, breweries and a winery, a designated drinking zone, ghost-story tours, the Olde Town Shindig in September and Trick or Treat Street in October. Standley Lake. Ralston Creek and the site of Lewis Ralston's 1850 gold discovery, the event that seeded the whole Front Range gold rush. The Arvada Center. Candelas. RTD G Line stations. The 'Celery Capital of the World' agricultural heritage.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE LAW, HONESTLY — Boulder is the one town in this batch where the city has restricted the product, and pretending otherwise will destroy credibility with the most code-literate customers in Colorado. Open the page with: 'Since 7 March 2026, Boulder prohibits artificial turf in new development unless it is FUNCTIONAL turf. Here is exactly what that means, when it applies to you, and what we can still legally build.' Then convert it into an authority play no competitor will bother to make, by naming the three markets that remain wide open: (1) existing homeowners in the 1960s-80s Martin Acres/Table Mesa/Frasier Meadows belt replacing a back lawn without a permit-triggering redevelopment — the manual is triggered by landscape/irrigation plan requirements, not by a homeowner swapping turf; (2) the explicitly exempted FUNCTIONAL categories — playgrounds, sports fields, picnic grounds, amphitheatres, park areas and 'the playing area of a golf course', which is a written invitation to pitch BVSD, CU Boulder and the city itself; and (3) indoor sports and climbing/fitness facilities, of which Boulder has an unusual concentration. Then meet the audience where it is: this city will ask about heat, microplastics, drainage and end-of-life recycling, so answer those on the page rather than deflecting. And do NOT over-index on water savings — Boulder's restrictions are merely voluntary, the mildest in the batch, so the water argument is genuinely weaker here than in Denver or Lafayette. Why it differs from next door: Louisville and Lafayette, four miles away, have no such prohibition at all — which is itself a useful line for readers on the boundary. Boulder's page is a compliance-and-competence page; Broomfield's is an HOA page; Denver's is a shade-and-dogs page. NOCO OVERLAP: none — nocoturf.com has no Boulder page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE HEADLINE, AND IT IS RESTRICTIVE. Boulder's water-wise landscape standards took effect 7 MARCH 2026 and state: 'Artificial turf is prohibited in all new development, unless it is functional artificial turf.' FUNCTIONAL turf is defined as 'turf that is located in a recreational use area or other space that is regularly used for civic, community, or recreational purposes, which may include a playground, a sports field, a picnic ground, an amphitheater, a portion of a park, and the playing area of a golf course.' NON-FUNCTIONAL turf is prohibited on residential lots with more than three dwelling units, on commercial/industrial/public/institutional properties, in any public right-of-way, and in new common areas within common interest communities. Residential lots of three units or fewer are limited to 'no more than 25% of the lot or parcel area or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less' as functional and/or non-functional turf. Installations made before 7 March 2026 are exempt unless modifications trigger compliance. CRITICALLY, the manual applies when a project requires a landscape or irrigation plan under the Boulder Revised Code — building permits for new development or redevelopment meeting thresholds, and Site Review, Use Review or Form-Based Code Review. A homeowner simply replacing an existing back lawn will generally NOT trigger it. Layered on top: SB24-005 (statewide, from 1 Jan 2026) and CRS 38-33.3-106.5's backyard protection, though the latter matters less here given low HOA density in the older belt. Get this section legally precise — Boulder customers will check.
facts.water_and_rules: City of Boulder water utility. Boulder entered a DROUGHT WATCH on 1 April 2026 — VOLUNTARY, not mandatory — asking residents to limit irrigation to a maximum of two times per week. Separately, Boulder's outdoor landscaping code makes it a permanent requirement from 1 May to 30 September that watering happens before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m. Boulder is therefore the LEAST coercive water regime in the batch (Denver and Lafayette are mandatory; Broomfield has a permanent ordinance) — so the water-scarcity argument is genuinely weaker here and the page should not overplay it. REBATES via Resource Central: lawn replacement up to $750 for converting at least 200 sq ft to water-wise landscaping, Garden-in-a-Box (with a $100 discount for Food Tax Rebate households), and free irrigation audits. Artificial turf does not qualify for any of them — these programmes require live water-wise plantings with 50%+ plant coverage at maturity.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA Soil Data Access for the Table Mesa / Martin Acres area returns Valmont ('Clayey over loamy-skeletal, MONTMORILLONITIC, mesic Aridic Argiustolls'), Nunn ('Fine, SMECTITIC'), Kutch ('Fine, montmorillonitic') and Hargreave as dominant components — plus, distinctively, mapped 'Terrace escarpments' at 12-60% slope and 'Gravel pits and mine dumps'. The Valmont profile is the operative one and it is different from Broomfield's: expansive clay OVER a loamy-skeletal (cobble and gravel) substrate, because south Boulder sits on old alluvial terraces shed off the Flatirons. Practical consequences unique to Boulder: excavation frequently hits cobble at shallow depth (slower digs, broken teeth, hand work), the terrace edges give genuinely steep grade breaks where mesa neighbourhoods drop away, and the clay-over-gravel contact perches water. Drainage design and realistic excavation pricing are the local competence signals.
facts.housing_stock: Median year built 1977, and unusually concentrated: of 47,465 units, 21% were built 1970-79, 17% 1960-69 and 15% 1980-89 — 53% of the entire city dates from 1960-1989. That is the Martin Acres / Table Mesa / Frasier Meadows / Gunbarrel belt of ranches, tri-levels and split-levels on flat-to-gently-sloping lots. A further 8% predates 1940 — Mapleton Hill, Whittier and Newlands Victorians and bungalows on small, tree-heavy lots. Only 8% has been built since 2010. Just 38.7% of units are single-family detached and only 47.2% are owner-occupied, both the lowest in the batch, because roughly a third of the population is CU students in multifamily. Average household 2.12 people and only 17% of households have children under 18 — by far the lowest child density here. Practical read: the addressable market is the owner-occupied 1960s-80s single-family belt, not the city as a whole.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 106,433. Median household income $87,493 — the LOWEST of the five — but median owner-occupied home value $1,039,500, the highest by a mile, and the only one above $1M. That gap is the whole story: the income figure is deflated by roughly 35,000 CU Boulder students, while the actual homeowner is wealthy. Per capita income $63,074. Do not lead a Boulder page with the median income number; lead with the home value. Highly educated, environmentally engaged, and unusually likely to interrogate the product's sustainability, microplastics, heat-island and recyclability claims — the page must meet that head-on rather than dodge it.
facts.golf: Flatirons Golf Course — City of Boulder-owned, at 57th and Arapahoe, built in 1938 with WPA support, designed by Willie Tucker, recertified as a Certified Audubon Cooperative Sanctuary by Audubon International, and hosting more than 50,000 rounds a year (over 1,000,000 since the city took over operations in 1986). Boulder Country Club, private, in Gunbarrel. Lake Valley Golf Club to the north near Niwot. Adjacent and easily referenced: Indian Peaks in Lafayette and Coal Creek in Louisville. Note the code angle: 'the playing area of a golf course' is explicitly named in Boulder's definition of FUNCTIONAL turf — golf is one of the few uses where synthetic turf remains permissible in new development.
facts.commercial_targets: This is where Boulder's restriction turns into opportunity, because the exempted 'functional' categories are exactly the institutional buyers. CU Boulder: Folsom Field, Potts Field, the Ford Practice Facility, Dal Ward Athletic Center, CU Events Center, CU Student Recreation Center, Buffalo Ranch. Boulder Valley School District playgrounds and fields. City facilities: North Boulder Recreation Center, South Boulder Recreation Center, East Boulder Community Center, Flatirons Golf Course practice areas. Private fitness and climbing, an outsized Boulder sector with heavy indoor-turf demand: The Spot Bouldering Gym, Boulder Rock Club, Movement Boulder Climbing and Fitness, Flatiron Athletic Club, Boulder Pickleball, the YMCA. Dog: Valmont Dog Park, East Boulder Dog Park, Foothills Community Dog Park, Bowhaus Boulder, scenthound, Only Natural Pet, Whole Pets, Woof Gang Bakery & Grooming, Arapahoe Animal Hospital. Preschools: Sunflower Preschool, Boulder Waldorf Kindergarten & Preschool, ScuttleBugs, Homestar Child Development Center, Off Broadway Preschool.
facts.landmarks: Pearl Street Mall, Chautauqua Park and the Flatirons, CU Boulder and Folsom Field, the NCAR Mesa Laboratory, NIST, the Boulder Creek Path, Valmont Bike Park, Boulder Reservoir, Scott Carpenter Pool, Table Mesa and the south Boulder mesas, Gunbarrel.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE OCTOBER 1 WATERING BAN ON A 1950s-70s RANCH BACKYARD. Sherrelwood is the batch's volume play and its cleanest single story: 80.5% of the housing went up between 1950 and 1979, 73.6% is detached single-family, 71.7% is owner-occupied, and the lots are uniform, flat, fenced and grid-platted — one repeatable job, sold thousands of times. On top of that sits the most urgent, most checkable fact available to any turf marketer in Colorado this month: Crestview Water and Sanitation District, a Denver Water master-meter distributor, has been under MANDATORY two-day-a-week watering since March 25, 2026, and from October 1, 2026 no outdoor watering is allowed at all, with fines. Combine that with a 70-year-old lawn under mature shade trees on slow-draining Platner clay — bluegrass that was already failing in dry shade and now legally cannot be watered — and the page writes itself. The technical proof point is the clay: linear extensibility 5.6 and 33% clay means the whole job is the base and the drainage plan, and saying so out loud separates a real installer from a roll-it-out competitor. This is a different lead from Federal Heights (manufactured-home pads, voluntary Westminster drought watch, no fines), from Welby (quarter-acre and acreage lots, split flat-clay/steep-bluff drainage), from Berkley (gravel-pit and made-ground subgrade lottery), and from Derby (sandy loam, the easiest install in the metro).
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Sherrelwood is UNINCORPORATED Adams County, so there is no city code — Adams County's rules apply. Adams County Code Compliance cites 'blight' violations that expressly include 'tall, overgrown grass, weeds and brush (12 inches)' — a 12-inch height limit, enforced by Neighborhood Services (720.523.2792).
