That is a directly usable hook: an owner who cannot water two days a week and cannot water at all after October 1 still faces a 12-inch weed-and-grass citation, and artificial turf removes the exposure entirely. State law: HB21-1229 means a common interest community may regulate but not prohibit artificial turf in a unit's backyard; SB24-005 bans new artificial turf on commercial, institutional, industrial, common-interest-community, right-of-way, parking-lot and median property from January 1, 2026 for local governments, exempting athletic fields of play only. HOAs are in any case rare in this 1950s-70s stock. I could not retrieve the text of Adams County's landscaping standards (the county code is at adamscounty.municipalcodeonline.com behind a JavaScript app), so no claim should be made about county landscape-material standards without a direct check with CEDD at 720.523.6800.
facts.water_and_rules: Crestview Water and Sanitation District (EPA PWS ID CO0101040, offices at 7145 Mariposa St, Denver 80221) serves roughly 23,756 people on 4,491 connections and is a Denver Water MASTER METER distributor. Parts of the area are also served by North Pecos Water and Sanitation District (CO0116553, 6900 Pecos St, ~2,500 people, 402 connections), also a Denver Water master-meter distributor. That means Denver Water's rules apply directly. As checked 2026-09-07, Crestview's own drought page states it follows Denver Water's MANDATORY watering rules effective March 25, 2026: no more than two days per week on assigned days — even-numbered addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd-numbered addresses Wednesday and Saturday, multi-family/commercial/HOA/government Tuesday and Friday; watering only between 6 pm and 10 am; Denver Water has issued a drought declaration seeking a 20% reduction in water use; and 'Beginning October 1, 2026, NO OUTDOOR WATERING IS ALLOWED. FINES FOR OUTDOOR WATERING WILL BE APPLIED.' Rebates: Crestview states plainly that 'Denver Water processes all of the water related fixture rebates for Crestview Water and Sanitation District Customers.' Denver Water's current published residential rebates are toilets (up to $100) and qualifying sprinkler nozzles; its yard-remodel programme is ColoradoScaping, which is about replacing Kentucky bluegrass with water-wise PLANTING. Nothing on Denver Water's rebate or remodel pages offers or mentions artificial turf. Position artificial turf as NOT rebate-eligible — the payback story here is the eliminated water bill and the October ban, not a rebate cheque.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO (CO001) sampled at two points: Platner loam, 0 to 3 percent slopes at 84th/Pecos and Platner loam, 3 to 5 percent slopes at 80th/Zuni — both 85% Platner, taxonomic class 'Fine, smectitic, mesic Aridic Paleustolls'. Smectitic means expansive clay. Measured top-30 cm values for Platner: linear extensibility 5.6 (moderate-to-high shrink-swell), 33% clay, saturated hydraulic conductivity 8.4 µm/s. Slopes are gentle throughout, 0-5%. So the local problem is not grade, it is a clay loam that swells wet, cracks dry, and drains slowly — plus a shallow argillic (clay-rich) horizon beneath. Practical consequence: flat lots with slow-percolating clay hold water at the base interface. The install spec that matters is over-excavation, a compacted aggregate base of adequate depth, a deliberate 1-2% fall or a French drain to a discharge point, and permeable backing — a turf laid straight onto Platner clay will pond and ripple. This is the most consistent, most predictable subgrade in the batch, which is exactly why it suits a standardised install and standardised pricing.
facts.housing_stock: The purest postwar tract suburb in the batch, and the highest-volume ordinary-backyard opportunity. ACS 2024 5-yr (B25034): of 6,742 housing units, 27.8% were built 1950-59, 28.2% in 1960-69 and 24.5% in 1970-79 — 80.5% of the entire stock went up between 1950 and 1979, with only 4.2% built since 2000. B25024: 73.6% single-family DETACHED, 8.8% in 10-19 unit buildings, and essentially no manufactured housing (0.7%, just 48 units) — the exact opposite of Federal Heights two miles north. 71.7% owner-occupied. ACS median value $432,200. The Census Bureau first defined Sherrelwood as a CDP in 1970 with 18,868 residents and it counted 19,228 in 2020 — the place was fully built out by 1970 and has been demographically flat for half a century. Yard reality: uniform rectangular ranch-house lots on a grid at roughly 2,750 units per square mile across 2.453 sq mi; expect conventional 6,000-8,000 sq ft lots with real, rectangular, fully fenced backyards of roughly 1,200-2,500 sq ft. I do not have parcel-level lot data for Sherrelwood, so treat those lot figures as an estimate from density and era, not a measured number. HOAs are rare — these are 1950s-70s platted subdivisions predating the HOA era, so almost every job is a direct homeowner decision with no architectural committee.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 19,228 (2020 census), 18,692 in the 2024 ACS — the largest of the five. Median household income $75,327. 63.4% Hispanic, 29.7% White, median age 32.4, 25.2% under 18. 42.7% married-couple households. Long-tenured owner-occupiers in starter-to-mid houses; a family-heavy, kid-heavy, dog-heavy market where the backyard is actively used and bluegrass under mature trees is failing.
facts.golf: Willis Case Golf Course (Vrain Street, Denver) is the closest full course. The Greg Mastriona Golf Courses at Hyland Hills (Westminster) and its North Par 3, Indian Tree Golf Club (Arvada), and Adventure Golf (miniature golf, Sheridan Blvd, Westminster) are all within about 8 km. There is no golf course inside the CDP and no golf-course residential community — golf is a backyard-putting-green story here, not a course-community story.
facts.commercial_targets: Schools (a mix of Westminster Public Schools, Adams 12 Five Star and Mapleton): Sherrelwood Elementary, Metz Elementary, Skyline Vista Elementary, Fairview Elementary, Valley View Elementary (W 70th Ave), Francis Day Elementary, M. Scott Carpenter Middle School (Lipan St), Iver C. Ranum Middle School (W 80th Ave), Orchard Park Academy (Zuni St, Westminster), The New America School (Washington St), Pinnacle Charter School, Global Campus. Sports: Highland Hills Sports Complex, Eminence Barbell Club, Orchard Park Outdoor Roller Rink, Federal Heights Skate Park. Childcare: A New Generation 3. Pet: The Vets Animal Hospital (Elati St, Thornton). Remember SB24-005 — school ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY are the one exempt commercial category, so the district athletic directors are the highest-value commercial call in this town; school landscape beds and parking-lot medians are now off-limits.
facts.landmarks: Sherrelwood Elementary School (Westminster Public Schools) — the CDP is named for the subdivision the school serves. Sherrelwood Park. Metz Park and Metz Elementary (Sherrelwood Drive). Iver C. Ranum Middle School (W 80th Ave), a name every long-time local knows from its years as Ranum High School. Twin Lakes Park. Orchard Park and the Orchard Park Outdoor Roller Rink (W 72nd Ave). City View Park. Waddell Park. Bell Roth Park. Northstar Park. Carmenisch Park. Sandhofer Open Space.

name: Denver

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE SHADED, DOG-WRECKED, 800-SQUARE-FOOT ALLEY-LOT BACKYARD — not with water savings. Denver is the only town in this batch where the customer's problem is that grass physically cannot grow: a 1910 bungalow on a 25-ft-platted lot, a detached alley garage eating a third of the yard, an 80-year-old elm or honeylocust throwing full shade, and a dog on the remaining patch. That is a shade-and-wear problem, not an irrigation-bill problem. It is also the batch's best margin story: at 600-1,500 sq ft, a $10-12/sq ft premium install is a $7,000-18,000 job the homeowner can actually say yes to, where the same rate across a 4,000 sq ft Broomfield yard is not. Secondary lead, and the one that serves the 'Cherry Creek types' ambition: Cherry Creek North, Country Club, Hilltop and Bonnie Brae are the metro's only genuinely urban luxury enclaves, and there the sell is a designed, small, perfect back garden — not a lawn replacement. Third, the technical authority play unique to Denver: the soil survey maps these neighbourhoods as SPOLIC fill over smectitic clay, so lead the process section with 'we don't know what's under your yard until we open it, and here's how we handle that' — buried clinker, ash, rubble and unpredictable dig depth. Why this differs from next door: Broomfield has no shade, no fill and near-universal HOAs; Boulder has an actual city prohibition; Louisville is a fire-rebuild market; Lafayette is a price-and-mandatory-restriction market. Denver alone is small, shaded, urban, un-HOA'd and dog-first. NOCO OVERLAP: none — nocoturf.com has no /areas/denver-co page (Denver appears only as generic 'Denver metro' copy on its homepage), so Denver is clean to claim.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No Denver-specific artificial turf ordinance was verifiable (denvergov.org refused all connections this session — flag for a follow-up check on the Denver Zoning Code landscape provisions). Two statewide rules govern instead. (1) COLORADO SB24-005: from 1 January 2026 local governments must prohibit installing nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF and invasive species on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common interest community (HOA common) property, street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors. Artificial turf on athletic fields of play is exempted. Single-family residential property is not among the listed property types. This substantially closes the commercial and HOA-common-area landscape market in Denver as of this year — sports fields and indoor facilities remain open. (2) CRS 38-33.3-106.5(1)(i.5)(I)(A) requires an association to 'Not prohibit the use of nonvegetative turf grass in the backyard of a unit owner's property', and (1)(i.5)(I)(B) bars unreasonably requiring hardscape on more than 20% of the landscaping area. Matters less in Denver than in the suburbs because HOA coverage is thin outside Central Park and Lowry.
facts.water_and_rules: Denver Water. The Board of Water Commissioners declared a STAGE 1 DROUGHT on 25 March 2026 with MANDATORY restrictions: single-family addresses ending even water Sunday and Thursday, odd water Wednesday and Saturday — two days per week, down from the normal three. All other customers (multifamily, commercial, HOAs, government) may water ONLY Tuesdays and Fridays. No watering between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. Summer rules run 1 May - 1 Oct. Temporary DROUGHT PRICING is in effect through 30 April 2027, putting a premium on high-volume outdoor use — this is the sharpest ROI hook in the metro. REBATES: Denver Water's Landscape Transformation Assistance Program pays $0.50/sq ft to HOAs/commercial, and Resource Central's residential lawn replacement gives up to $750 for removing 200+ sq ft. ARTIFICIAL TURF IS EXPLICITLY INELIGIBLE for both. Denver Water states it will not fund 'Designs that include artificial turf, landscape fabrics/weed barriers or hardscapes. These do not benefit the environment.' The same page cites SB24-005 approvingly. Be honest on the page: there is no rebate for this product anywhere in the metro — the money argument is the eliminated water bill plus drought pricing avoidance, not a subsidy.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA Soil Data Access for the Wash Park/Congress Park core returns Urban land, Elyria family and Racas as the dominant components — and the taxonomic classes are the story. Elyria is 'Fine-loamy, SPOLIC, mixed... Anthroportic Ustorthents' and Racas is 'Fine, SPOLIC, SMECTITIC... Torrertic Ustorthents'. 'Spolic' means human-transported material: Denver's inner neighbourhoods are literally mapped as fill, not natural soil, and the fill sits over smectitic (swelling) clay. Slopes are gentle, 0-6%. Practical consequence: unknown and variable fill depth, buried brick, clinker and coal ash from century-old furnaces, old privy pits and demolition rubble, over expansive clay. Excavation depth is unpredictable, compaction testing matters, and the drainage plane has to be engineered rather than assumed. Elyria family is also mapped 'somewhat poorly drained'.
facts.housing_stock: Median year built 1975, but that median hides a strongly bimodal stock (ACS 2020-24 5-yr, 359,581 units): 17% pre-1940, 5% 1940s, 12% 1950s — then a trough — then 16% 2010-19 and 4% since 2020. Practically: pre-war bungalows, Denver Squares and Four Squares (Wash Park, Congress Park, Baker, Park Hill, Highlands/LoHi), post-war brick ranches (Virginia Village, Harvey Park, Mar Lee, Athmar), and a large modern layer (Central Park/former Stapleton, RiNo, Sloan's Lake slot homes and duplexes). Only 40.5% of units are single-family detached and just 48.8% are owner-occupied — the lowest detached share of the five. Avg household 2.10 people; 22% of households have kids under 18. LOT/BACKYARD (characterised, not sourced — denvergov.org was unreachable all session, so verify against the Denver Zoning Code before publishing): Denver's older grid was platted in 25-ft lots; most single-family homes occupy two or three of them, giving roughly 37.5x125 (~4,690 sq ft) to 50x125 (~6,250 sq ft). With a ~1,200 sq ft footprint, an alley-loaded detached garage and mature street trees, the usable back yard is typically only ~600-1,500 sq ft — small, enclosed and heavily shaded. HOA prevalence is LOW across the historic neighbourhoods and high only in Central Park (master community association) and Lowry.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 718,877. Median household income $94,718; per capita income $64,163; median owner-occupied home value $616,000; 48.8% owner-occupied (ACS 2020-2024 5-year). Renter-heavy, small households, professional. The 'upper echelon' the owner wants is concentrated and geographically tight: Cherry Creek North, Country Club, Hilltop, Bonnie Brae, Washington Park, Belcaro — not spread across the city.
facts.golf: City-owned municipal courses: City Park Golf Course, Kennedy Golf Course (18-hole plus a 9-hole regulation course), Harvard Gulch (par 3), Overland Park, Wellshire, Willis Case, and Evergreen Golf Course (Denver-owned but located in Evergreen). Private/other in Denver: Denver Country Club (Country Club neighbourhood), Green Valley Ranch Golf Club (far NE Denver). Immediately adjacent and highly recognisable: Cherry Hills Country Club in Cherry Hills Village (US Open host), CommonGround Golf Course (Aurora), Broken Tee (Englewood), Meadow Hills and Aurora Hills (Aurora), Lakewood Country Club. Golf-adjacent housing is limited inside Denver proper — the putting-green pitch here is a backyard-amenity pitch, not a golf-community pitch.
facts.commercial_targets: Dog daycare/boarding is the strongest commercial vertical here: Camp Bow Wow (the first location opened in Denver in 2000, founded by Heidi Ganahl — a genuinely local origin story), Wag Hotels, City Bark Doggie Day Care, Hounds On The Hill, Woofhaus Dog Daycare, The Sniff Shack, Happy Dog Daycare, K-9 Castle, Daily Wag!. Off-leash parks: Lowry Dog Park, Fuller Dog Park, Kennedy Dog Park, First Creek Off-Leash Dog Park, Central Park/Stapleton Off-Leash. Sports: All City Stadium, Evie Garrett Dennis Stadium, Bladium Sports and Fitness Center (Central Park), Big Bear Ice Arena. Schools/childcare: Denver Public Schools; Bright Horizons, La Petite Academy, Mile High Montessori Early Learning, Paddington Station Preschool, Bethany Early Childhood Center. Pet retail with grooming floors: Kriser's Natural Pet, Chuck and Don's, Bentley's Pet Stuff, Only Natural Pet. Note: SB24-005 now blocks landscape artificial turf on commercial property — pitch these as INTERIOR/pet-relief-area and play-surface work, which is where the exemptions and the physical reality actually sit.
facts.landmarks: Cherry Creek North, Washington Park, Cheesman Park, City Park and Denver Zoo, Sloan's Lake, Union Station, Larimer Square, RiNo Art District, Denver Botanic Gardens, Coors Field, Empower Field at Mile High, Ball Arena, Central Park (formerly Stapleton), the Highland/Lohi pedestrian bridge, Denver Country Club.

sources: https://api.censusreporter.org/1.0/data/show/latest (ACS 2020-2024 5-year: B01003, B19013, B19301, B25003, B25010, B25024, B25034, B25035, B25077)

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: 'Meridian doesn't have back yards. It has 2,600 rental doors, three Fortune 500 headquarters and a golf course — and one of the strictest private design-review regimes in Douglas County.' This page should be written for a facilities director or a multifamily asset manager, not a homeowner, and should say so in the first line. The three arguments: (1) 85.9% of Meridian households rent — the product is amenity turf: dog runs, pet relief areas, courtyard lawns, pool decks, leasing-office frontage, corporate putting greens and hotel event lawns, all of them heavy-traffic surfaces where live bluegrass fails and gets re-sodded annually. (2) Meridian's DCC covenants bind every parcel 'regardless of ownership' and 'independent of the zoning and land use regulations of local governments,' require written approval before any work starts, and are backed by periodic site inspections — so the installer's value is that it submits DCC-ready plans and doesn't get a client red-tagged. (3) Be the firm that is straight about Colorado SB24-005: since January 1, 2026 new artificial turf on commercial, institutional and common-interest property is restricted, with ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY exempt. Publishing that honestly on the page is a trust weapon — every competitor is quietly hoping nobody asks. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Meridian is the only one of the five with a median household income under $100k, the only one where fewer than one in seven households owns their home, the only one with three-days-a-week watering and no drought stage, and the only one where the governing state law actively restricts the product. Every other page in this batch sells a back yard. This one sells a permitted commercial scope of work.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: TWO REAL CONSTRAINTS, BOTH UNUSUAL. (1) The Meridian Design Control Committee. Meridian's Protective Covenants 'legally apply to all land that is part of Meridian, regardless of ownership and are independent of the zoning and land use regulations of local governments.' Any proposal to construct, modify or demolish improvements — explicitly including maintenance activities and changes in property use — must obtain DCC plan approval BEFORE work begins, and the DCC performs periodic site inspections during and after development to ensure compliance. Covenant documents are separated by sub-area: Meridian International Business Center, Meridian North, Meridian Commons, Meridian Village. (2) Colorado SB24-005 (signed March 15, 2024; effective for local governments January 1, 2026) prohibits installing nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF, or invasive plant species on commercial, institutional and industrial property, common interest community property, street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors — with artificial turf on ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY expressly EXEMPT. Residential yards are not covered. HONEST CAVEAT: the bill summary does not spell out how far 'common interest community property' reaches, and the applicability to private commercial redevelopment versus publicly-funded projects needs legal confirmation before the page makes a flat claim. This is the single most important compliance question in the whole batch and it lands squarely on Meridian.
facts.water_and_rules: Meridian Metropolitan District (meridiandistrict.com, 12111 E. Belford Ave, Englewood CO 80112, 303-790-0345), created in 1980. Supplies drinking water, wastewater AND reclaimed water for irrigation. CURRENT STATUS (checked 2026-09-07): no mandatory drought stage declared; MMD says its primary supply is groundwater and 'remains reliable,' it is a member of the WISE (Water Infrastructure and Supply Efficiency) partnership, and it holds two emergency interconnects with neighbouring utilities — it calls itself 'drought resilient.' Its 2026 Summer Watering Requirements: don't start irrigating until May 1; water before 6 a.m. or after 6 p.m.; THREE days per week by address parity — even-ending addresses and odd-ending addresses each get three assigned days. MMD states it 'reuses 100% of our water,' with treated effluent irrigating parks and open space. Reclaimed water is NOT delivered directly to residential customers. TURF REBATE: none offered by MMD; the state CWCB program closed March 2025 and funds living landscape only. Note that Meridian is the ONLY place in this batch with three-days-a-week watering and no drought stage — which means the 'save water' argument is weaker here and the argument has to be maintenance cost, appearance under heavy foot traffic, and dog/pet durability instead.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 5,932 ft, described in its own geography as 'naturally rolling hills and grassland' — the I-25 corridor between Inverness Parkway and Lincoln Avenue in northern Douglas County. Dawson Formation-derived plains soils; expansive clay is a general Front Range hazard per the Colorado Geological Survey, and the same CGS warning about irrigation water entering soil next to foundations applies to building perimeters and courtyard planters here. The real site conditions to design for in Meridian are commercial ones: compacted subgrade around structures, heavy concentrated foot traffic on amenity lawns, dog-run urine loading and drainage/odour management in multifamily pet areas, shaded north-facing courtyards where live grass never fills in, and rooftop/podium deck weight and drainage limits.
facts.housing_stock: THIS IS NOT A SINGLE-FAMILY YARD MARKET AND THE PAGE MUST NOT PRETEND IT IS. 2,621 housing units on 0.509 sq miles with a 6.4% vacancy rate — and HOMEOWNERSHIP IS ONLY 14.1% (national average 65.2%). About 46% of the 2,453 households are single individuals. In plain terms: Meridian is an office park with apartment and townhome communities wrapped around it, built largely from the late 1980s through the 2000s and still infilling. There are almost no private back yards to sell. What there IS: large multifamily communities with shared courtyards, dog runs, pool decks and amenity lawns; corporate campuses with entry plazas and courtyards; hotels; and district-maintained parks, greenbelts and trails. Any 'typical lot and backyard size' framing is simply wrong for Meridian.
facts.who_lives_there: ~4,786-5,634 residents; median age 32.0 — the youngest in the batch by three years; only 9.3% aged 65+ and 18.6% under 18. Median household income $89,877 — roughly HALF of Roxborough Park's and about a third of Castle Pines Village's — and it declined 0.7% year over year. Most racially mixed of the five: 66.6% White, 17.4% Asian, 11.2% Hispanic, 3.7% Black. Commute just 19.2 minutes; 77.3% drive alone. Employment base 3,505 and growing ~5%/yr. Renters, young professionals and corporate staff. The buyer here is a property manager, an asset manager, a facilities director or a GM — never a homeowner.
facts.golf: Meridian Golf Club sits inside the development (Meridian Blvd, Englewood 80112) — and per the Meridian Metropolitan District's own FAQ, the district's reclaimed irrigation water 'is currently used on the golf course, commercial properties, parks, and common areas.' Adjacent: Inverness Golf Club (Englewood/Centennial, immediately north across I-25), Lone Tree Golf Club & Hotel, and The Ridge at Castle Pines North a short run south. Meridian Golf Club is the single most credible commercial golf target in this batch — a practice/short-game or tee-line synthetic project at a club that already irrigates with reclaimed water is an easy conversation.
facts.commercial_targets: DISH Network campus, Liberty Media and Qurate Retail Group headquarters (entry plazas, courtyards, executive putting greens, rooftop and terrace amenity areas). Toyota, American Family Insurance and Jacobs Engineering offices. Meridian Golf Club (practice green, tee line, clubhouse surrounds — already on reclaimed irrigation). The hotel properties along Meridian Blvd (courtyards, event lawns). The large apartment and townhome communities that produce the 85.9% renter share — dog runs, pet relief areas, pool decks, courtyard lawns and leasing-office frontage are the highest-volume repeatable product in Meridian. Corporate-serving daycares and childcare centres in the office park. MMD parks, greenbelts, open space and trail heads. IMPORTANT: screen every one of these against SB24-005 before quoting; the athletic-fields-of-play exemption is the clean lane.
facts.landmarks: Meridian International Business Center. DISH Network headquarters, Liberty Media and Qurate Retail Group — three Fortune 500 headquarters inside 0.5 sq miles. Toyota, American Family Insurance and Jacobs Engineering offices. Meridian Golf Club. I-25 at Lincoln Avenue and at Inverness Parkway. Meridian Boulevard. 'Spin at Meridian' — the district's own recreation program. Park Meadows, Sky Ridge Medical Center and RidgeGate are the neighbouring reference points everyone uses. ZIP 80112.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE RULE, VERBATIM: 'In Stonegate, artificial turf is approved for the REAR YARD ONLY — and the rest of that back yard can be no more than 30% non-living material.' Nowhere else in this batch is there a written, dated, quotable HOA sentence about synthetic turf, and quoting it does three things at once: it proves the installer actually knows Stonegate, it pre-empts the #1 objection ('will my HOA let me?'), and it converts the page from a sales pitch into a compliance service. Build the whole page as PERMIT NAVIGATION: we design to the 30% rule, we lay out the turf as smaller shaped areas with living beds around it exactly the way the Standards recommend, we don't touch your builder grading (the Standards forbid altering lot drainage), our base excavation stays under the 18-inch 'excavation' threshold, and we prepare your Modifications Committee packet — including the neighbour signatures — for the up-to-45-day review. Add the practical hook: this is the highest-kid-density place in the batch (28.7% under 18) with small fenced back yards, so the job is almost always 'the whole back lawn, once, done.' WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Meridian next door is a corporate campus with no meaningful residential yard market; Castle Pines Village's gate is a price tier and a DRC calendar, not a front-yard prohibition; Roxborough's gate is a drought order from Aurora; Sterling Ranch's gate is a new-build approved-vendor list. Stonegate is the only page that should read like an HOA submittal guide.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THIS IS THE BEST-DOCUMENTED TURF RULE IN THE ENTIRE BATCH. SVOA Community-Wide Standards dated October 2, 2023, under 'Landscaping': 'Committee approval is required... The use of artificial turf as a xeric option may be submitted for approval by the Committee IN THE REAR YARD ONLY. If artificial turf is being requested for the rear yard, all remaining portions of the rear yard not covered with artificial turf may have no more than thirty percent (30%) non-living material.' Separately, the general xeric cap: 'no more than thirty percent (30%) of either the front, side or rear yard can be covered with non-living material.' Front yards: 'The appearance of the ground plane of a front yard in Stonegate shall be predominantly sod or a combination of sod and shrubs, unless the owner has submitted and received approval by the Committee for a complete or partial xeriscape design plan' — and front yard landscaping must be installed before initial occupancy, with a sprinkler system required in all front yards and two trees (one on cul-de-sac bulbs). Side yards on corner lots require irrigated sod held back no more than 5 feet from the foundation. The Standards even give design direction: 'outlining smaller areas of the yard with the artificial turf and incorporating bedded living plant material around the site.' PROCESS: the Modifications Committee requires a submitted plan, NEIGHBOUR SIGNATURES on modification requests, and takes up to 45 days. Pre-approved xeriscape plans exist on svoacommunity.com but still require formal submission and approval before installation. Note also Colorado SB24-005 restricts new artificial turf on common-interest-community property (athletic fields of play exempt) — an open question for SVOA/SVMD COMMON AREAS that should be checked before quoting any common-area job here.
facts.water_and_rules: Stonegate Village Metropolitan District IS the water and wastewater utility (svmd.org, 10252 Stonegate Parkway, Parker CO 80134, 303-858-9909). CURRENT STATUS (checked 2026-09-07): Stage 1 Drought Restrictions & Water Conservation Guidelines in force, effective April 22, 2026, adopted under the District's Water Conservation Plan. Rules: even-numbered addresses (0,2,4,6,8) may water Sunday, Tuesday, Friday; odd-numbered (1,3,5,7,9) Monday, Thursday, Saturday; multi-family, commercial and irrigation accounts Monday, Thursday, Saturday; NO WATERING WEDNESDAYS; watering only before 10:00 a.m. or after 6:00 p.m. The District warns that continued dry conditions may trigger Stage 2 with more restrictive requirements. It also offers a 21-Day Watering Exemption Permit (the new-sod establishment variance) — useful competitive intel: a live-sod installer has to apply for a permit, a turf installer does not. The District also irrigates its own parks with treated effluent and has a stated goal to 'identify areas that can be converted to low water use plant materials.' TURF REBATE: none. SVMD offers no turf-replacement rebate, and the state CWCB Turf Replacement Grant Program closed to applications in March 2025 and funds living water-wise landscape, not synthetic. There is no rebate story in Stonegate — the story is the covenant and the schedule.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 5,896 ft on the rolling Cherry Creek-drainage plains of north-eastern Douglas County — flat to gently sloping, nothing like Roxborough's grades. Soils are the clay-rich Dawson/Denver Formation-derived plains soils where expansive (bentonite/montmorillonite) clay is a well-known Front Range problem; the Colorado Geological Survey specifically identifies inadequate surface drainage and irrigation water entering soil next to foundations as a landscaping-caused damage mechanism. This matters operationally because SVOA's own Community-Wide Standards state: 'The proper drainage of the Lot is the responsibility of the Owner and should not be altered from the original grading completed by the builder. Any landscape modifications must not alter the drainage of the Lot.' Also relevant: the Standards define 'excavation' as any surface disturbance deeper than 18 inches and require approval for it — a normal 3-4 inch turf base excavation stays well inside that, which is a genuinely reassuring point to put in writing on the page.
facts.housing_stock: 3,184 housing units on just 1.844 sq miles — the densest of the five and effectively fully built out. Dominant era is early-1990s through mid-2000s production suburbia: two-story tract homes and some ranches, mostly 1,800-3,200 sq ft, on conventional 5,000-9,000 sq ft lots. Typical BACK YARD is small and rectangular — roughly 900-2,000 sq ft of usable turf behind the house, fully fenced, which is exactly the size band where a synthetic install prices cleanly at $7-12/sq ft and where a whole-yard conversion is a realistic single-day-or-two job. HOA prevalence 100%: every lot is in the Stonegate Village Owners Association (SVOA, managed by PCMS / Property Management Systems, 303-224-0004, portal svoacommunity.com) AND in the Stonegate Village Metropolitan District. Homeownership 91.2%; median property value $641,600; homeowner vacancy 0.2% — nobody leaves.
facts.who_lives_there: 8,906-9,072 residents. Median household income $159,086; median age 39.1 — the classic peak-family stage. 28.7% under 18 (highest child share in the batch), 66.3% married-couple households, only 9.4% aged 65+. Top sectors: Professional/Scientific/Technical, Healthcare, Education. Commute 26.8 minutes and 27.1% work from home. This is the dog-and-kids demographic: worn-out bluegrass, a muddy back door, a trampoline dead-spot, and a home office window looking at it all day.
facts.golf: Stonegate itself has no course inside its boundary. Adjacent/nearby: Blackstone Country Club (private, Aurora, immediately north-east across E-470), The Pinery Country Club (Parker), Pradera (Parker), Colorado Golf Club (Parker), and Cherry Creek State Park's surrounds to the north. Practically, the golf sell in Stonegate is NOT a club adjacency story — it is the backyard practice green for a member who plays at Blackstone, Pinery or Pradera and has 900 sq ft to work with.
facts.commercial_targets: Stonegate Village Metro District Community Center (rentable facilities). Stonegate North Pool and Stonegate South Pool surrounds and deck areas. The Gazebo and District parks. District tennis and pickleball court surrounds. SVOA common-area entry monuments and medians (check SB24-005 first). Nearby DCSD schools: Mammoth Heights Elementary, Prairie Crossing Elementary, Sierra Middle School, Chaparral High School. Parker-corridor daycares and dog daycares/boarding along Parker Road and Lincoln Ave. Cottonwood Water & Sanitation District's Community Demonstration Gardens in Parker (8334 Sandreed Cir) is a visible neighbouring-district xeriscape showcase worth knowing about.
facts.landmarks: E-470 forms the northern edge with access at Exits 3 and 4. Stonegate Parkway. The Gazebo and its picnic/BBQ facilities. Stonegate North Pool and Stonegate South Pool. The District's tennis and pickleball courts (access code is on your water bill — a detail only a local knows). The Stonegate Community Center. Cherry Creek. Grand View Estates to the west, the Town of Parker immediately east. ZIP 80134.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE MANDATE AND THE MATH — Lafayette is the value town, and it is the only town in this batch where a MANDATORY restriction lands on a genuinely price-sensitive household. The opening should be blunt and specific: on 10 April 2026 Lafayette moved to a mandatory Stage 1 drought response demanding up to a 17% cut in outdoor watering with increased enforcement, its water comes from two watersheds that both had historically poor snowpack, and the city's entire outdoor rebate offering is three dollars a sprinkler nozzle and fifty dollars of drip line — there is no turf removal rebate here at all. That is a much harder, more concrete argument than Louisville can make (still voluntary) or Boulder can make (voluntary, plus a municipal prohibition), and it is aimed at a household earning $119,040 against Louisville's $147,319 and Superior's $159,434, so the page must talk total cost of ownership, payback period and phased installation rather than assuming a blank cheque. Second beat, and the local pride hook nobody else can use: Indian Peaks is a HALE IRWIN-designed municipal course, opened 1993, with the Continental Divide on the horizon and a neighbourhood built around it — in a town whose golf identity is that strong, backyard putting greens are the natural premium upsell and the honest route toward the $10-12/sq ft ambition. Third beat, the technical differentiator: Lafayette's soils are flatter and WETTER than its neighbours' — poorly drained Calkins and Loveland bottomland around Coal Creek and Waneka Lake, under expansive clay — so drainage design, not slope or cobble, is what separates a good Lafayette install from a swampy one. Why it differs from next door: Louisville is the fire-rebuild, top-income, most-children town with only voluntary water rules; Lafayette is the mandatory-restriction, no-rebate, more affordable, drainage-problem town with a signature golf course. Same county, four miles apart, genuinely different pages. NOCO OVERLAP: none — nocoturf.com has no Lafayette page, though it does hold Erie next door.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No Lafayette-specific ordinance regulating artificial turf was found, and Lafayette's own outdoor water efficiency rebate page does not mention artificial or synthetic turf at all. The governing rules are Lafayette's mandatory Stage 1 drought restrictions (above) and the two state laws: SB24-005, prohibiting installation of artificial turf on commercial, institutional, industrial and common interest community property, rights-of-way, parking lots and medians from 1 January 2026, with athletic fields of play exempted; and CRS 38-33.3-106.5(1)(i.5)(I)(A), which bars an association from prohibiting nonvegetative turf grass in a unit owner's BACKYARD, plus the 20% hardscape ceiling at (1)(i.5)(I)(B). The HOA statute is worth a solid section here because much of the 1990s-2010s stock is association-governed, but it should not be the lead the way it is in Broomfield.
facts.water_and_rules: City of Lafayette water utility, sourced from the Boulder Creek and Upper Colorado River watersheds — both of which hit peak snowpack nearly a month early this year, with Boulder Creek at less than half its historical average. Lafayette entered STAGE 1 MODERATE DROUGHT RESPONSE effective 10 APRIL 2026: MANDATORY, targeting a 10% overall demand reduction and up to 17% reduction in outdoor watering, with increased enforcement. Irrigation systems limited to a maximum of two days per week ('only add a third day when absolutely necessary'), NO watering of outdoor landscaping between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m., no runoff onto sidewalks, driveways or streets, and no hose or power-washer cleaning of paved surfaces. REBATES: rotary/high-efficiency sprinkler nozzles at $3 per nozzle (10-50 per residence, once per 10 years), drip equipment up to $50, and free smart controllers and rain sensors for customers who complete a Resource Central Slow the Flow evaluation. THERE IS NO TURF REPLACEMENT OR LAWN REMOVAL REBATE AT ALL in Lafayette — and nothing for artificial turf.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA Soil Data Access around the Indian Peaks area returns a genuinely different mix from Louisville's: Colby ('Fine-silty, mixed, calcareous, mesic Ustic Torriorthents') is dominant, alongside Heldt (fine, montmorillonitic), Nunn (fine, smectitic), Manter and Hargreave — and, importantly, TWO POORLY DRAINED units, Calkins ('Cumulic Haplaquolls') and Loveland ('Fine-loamy over sandy or sandy-skeletal... Typic Haplaquolls'). Slopes are gentle, mostly 0.7-6%. The distinguishing local problem is therefore not slope or cobble but DRAINAGE: Lafayette has more low-lying, poorly drained bottomland — the Coal Creek corridor and the ground around Waneka Lake and Baseline Reservoir — sitting alongside expansive montmorillonitic and smectitic clays. Flat plus clay plus a high water table is the combination that produces standing water, soft spots and odour complaints under poorly built turf. Sub-base drainage and positive fall are the competence signals here, where Boulder's are cobble excavation and terrace grades.
facts.housing_stock: Median year built 1994. Of 12,939 units: 27% built in the 1990s, 21% in 2010-19, 18% in the 1980s and 9% in 2000-09 — so roughly three-quarters of the town is 1980-2019, spread more evenly across four decades than Louisville's tight 1980s-90s spike. Only 3% predates 1940: Old Town Lafayette's coal-miner cottages on small lots along and around Public Road. 55.1% single-family detached and 65.7% owner-occupied — noticeably more attached housing and more renters than Louisville (66.2%/71.7%), reflecting a deliberate run of townhome, duplex and affordable development. Average household 2.41 with 30% of households having children under 18 — family-heavy, second only to Louisville. Named subdivisions include Indian Peaks (wrapped around the golf course), Silver Creek, Coal Creek Village, Beacon Hill and the newer Willoughby Corner. HOA coverage is common in the 1990s-2010s subdivisions and absent in Old Town.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 30,602. Median household income $119,040; per capita income $62,261; median home value $686,500; 65.7% owner-occupied. Read this comparatively, because that is where the insight is: Lafayette sits $28,000 below Louisville ($147,319), $40,000 below Superior ($159,434) and $54,000 below Erie ($173,349) on median household income, with a median home value nearly $200,000 below Louisville's. Lafayette is the affordable, more socioeconomically mixed, more diverse town in the Boulder County ring — comfortable and family-heavy, but genuinely price-sensitive in a way Louisville is not. A page written in Louisville's register will misjudge this audience.
facts.golf: Indian Peaks Golf Course, 2300 Indian Peaks Trail — owned by the City of Lafayette, opened in 1993, DESIGNED BY HALE IRWIN (three US Opens, two US Senior Opens). Six sets of tees from 4,916 to 7,088 yards, with views of the Indian Peaks range and the Continental Divide, and eight named peaks visible from the course. The Indian Peaks residential neighbourhood is built around it, so there is a genuine golf-course-frontage housing cohort in town. Waneka Lake Park also has a disc golf course. Coal Creek Golf Course in Louisville is minutes away. A Hale Irwin municipal course is an unusually strong, checkable local hook for a putting-green pitch — no other town in this batch has a signature-designer public course.
facts.commercial_targets: Bob L. Burger Recreation Center, Great Outdoors Water Park, Waneka Lake Park, and the city's athletic fields. The Great Bark Dog Park — the city even runs a compost programme there, which makes it a natural conversation about surfacing and odour management. Pet businesses: Dogtopia, The Divine Canine, Lafayette Companion Animal Hospital, Bark Avenue Pet Boutique, Natural Pet Food, Little Groomer Pet Salon. Childcare and schools: Hope Montessori Academy, the YMCA, and Boulder Valley School District sites including Centaurus High School, Angevine Middle School and Peak to Peak Charter. Indian Peaks Golf Course itself is a live commercial prospect for practice-green and tee-line work — and note that golf course playing areas and athletic fields of play sit inside the SB24-005 exemption.
facts.landmarks: Waneka Lake Park (and its disc golf course), the Great Outdoors Water Park, the Bob L. Burger Recreation Center, Old Town Lafayette and Public Road, The Great Bark Dog Park, the Coal Creek Trail, Indian Peaks Golf Course, Baseline Reservoir, and the Lafayette Peak to Peak corridor. Centaurus High School and Angevine Middle School are the local school landmarks; Peak to Peak Charter is nearby.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: 'No city hall, no covenant committee — the largest unincorporated backyard market on the west side.' Dakota Ridge is 33,892 people who voted down incorporation in 1988 and answer to no municipality. Where Ken Caryl one mile south makes you file an application with an Architectural Committee that meets twice a month, a great many Dakota Ridge homeowners can simply decide and book. That permission-free speed is the hook, and it is genuinely differentiating. Then earn the price with the second half of the page: the hogback. This community is literally named for the ridge it is built against, its western flank sits on bedrock dipping at roughly 45 degrees, and the Colorado Geological Survey names heaving bedrock as a hazard causing 'exceptional damage' along exactly this piedmont. Sell the base build — depth, compaction, sub-drainage, seam placement on slope — as the reason a Dakota Ridge install costs more than a flatland install and lasts. That combination, freedom plus engineering, is the pitch that moves this town from a $7-8 job to a $10-12 job. WHY THIS DIFFERS: Ken Caryl sells covenant fluency, Applewood sells easy ground and golf, Fairmount sells a water bill, West Pleasant View sells small-job affordability. Dakota Ridge alone sells autonomy plus difficult terrain — the 1980s tract house on a tilted edge with nobody to ask.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No municipal ordinance — Dakota Ridge is unincorporated and governed by Jefferson County; residents voted incorporation down in 1988. There is no city permit counter and no city landscaping code, which is a real and sellable contrast with Lakewood immediately north. Where an HOA does exist, Colorado HB21-1229 (signed 2 July 2021, effective 7 September 2021) applies: artificial turf is a protected drought-tolerant landscaping material that an association 'may regulate but not prohibit in the backyard area of a unit.' For any approach to the Foothills Park & Recreation District or a school, Colorado SB24-005 now governs: since 1 January 2026 artificial turf may not be installed on local government property, commercial/institutional/industrial property or HOA common areas — with an explicit carve-out for ATHLETIC FIELDS OF PLAY. HONEST GAP: Jefferson County's own building and zoning pages could not be reached this session; confirm whether any grading or drainage permit threshold is triggered by large installs before making a 'no permit needed' claim in print.
facts.water_and_rules: Primary provider for much of the area: Southwest Metropolitan Water and Sanitation District (303-979-2333), which serves 18,017 residences and businesses across western Arapahoe, eastern Jefferson and northern Douglas counties. It is currently passing through Denver Water's declared STAGE 1 DROUGHT with mandatory restrictions in force. Other districts operating in and around the 80127/80465 area whose sites were confirmed live: Lakehurst Water and Sanitation District, Green Mountain Water and Sanitation District. Because the CDP is unincorporated and spans two ZIPs, the provider genuinely varies by address — the page should say so and offer to check. Applicable Denver Water Stage 1 rules: two days per week only, even addresses Sunday and Thursday, odd addresses Wednesday and Saturday, multifamily and commercial Tuesday and Friday; nothing between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m.; penalties escalating to $1,000; and all spray irrigation of grass banned after 30 September. REBATE ANSWER: no rebate applies to artificial turf — the Denver Water and state programmes fund vegetative water-wise landscaping only.
facts.soil_and_yard: Dakota Ridge is defined by its western boundary: the community 'is bordered to the west by the Dakota Hogback, a sharp hogback ridge that to the north near Morrison is also known as Dinosaur Ridge.' The hogback is Cretaceous Dakota Group sandstone over softer shales, formed in the Laramide orogeny about 50 million years ago, with the western edge tilting at roughly 45 degrees. That means the whole western flank of this CDP is built on or against steeply dipping bedrock — the exact setting the Colorado Geological Survey identifies for HEAVING BEDROCK, a hazard it describes as 'capable of causing exceptional damage to houses, roads, and utilities' and responsible for 'tens of millions of dollars worth of damage along the Front Range piedmont.' Add general Front Range expansive clay, which can swell 20% by volume and exert 30,000 psf. Lots east toward Kipling flatten out; lots against the hogback carry slope, rock and drainage complexity. This is the town page where an engineered base and sub-drainage section genuinely belongs in the body copy.
facts.housing_stock: 33,892 people (up 5.9% from 32,005 in 2010) in 13,182 housing units, only 2.3% vacant with a 0.5% homeowner vacancy rate — the tightest owner market in this batch. Median age 40.2; 58.2% married-couple households. Area 9.685 sq mi (about 6,198 acres), giving a gross density of 2.13 units/acre — very close to Ken Caryl's, but WITHOUT Ken Caryl's 4,800 acres of open space absorbing the land, so real lots here are on average more generous than the raw number suggests. The stock is predominantly late-1970s through 1990s Jefferson County tract subdivision: ranch, split-level, tri-level and two-storey production homes on the bench between Bear Creek and Ken Caryl Avenue, west of Kipling and running up against the hogback. ZIP codes 80127 (Littleton) and 80465 (Morrison). Voters rejected incorporation in 1988, so this is genuinely county-governed, not a city. HONEST GAP: subdivision-level HOA prevalence could not be verified. The era and product type strongly imply a mix of no-HOA and light-touch HOA subdivisions, unlike Ken Caryl next door, but that should be spot-checked against a few named subdivisions before the page asserts it.
facts.who_lives_there: Median age 40.2, 21.7% under 18, 14.9% aged 65+, 81.5% white and 13.1% Hispanic or Latino. 58.2% married-couple households and a 0.5% homeowner vacancy rate paint a settled, family, move-up-once-and-stay market — people who have been in the same house long enough to be replacing an original 1980s lawn and irrigation system rather than a builder-grade new one. Rental vacancy is 5.8%, the highest of the two big CDPs, so there is a modest rental segment. HONEST GAP: current income unverified for the same reason as Ken Caryl — the Census API now requires a key and the usual aggregator sites blocked access.
facts.golf: The Foothills Park & Recreation District, whose headquarters at 6612 S. Ward St, Littleton 80127 sits in this community's own ZIP, operates TWO courses: Foothills Golf Course and Meadows Golf Club. Raccoon Creek Golf Course is at 7301 W. Bowles Ave, Littleton 80123. Red Rocks Country Club is in Morrison, immediately over the hogback to the west. This is the best-served golf catchment in the batch on a public-course basis, which cuts both ways: plenty of golfers to sell practice greens to, but less scarcity value than Ken Caryl's zero-course situation.
facts.commercial_targets: Dakota Ridge High School. The Foothills Park & Recreation District is the single biggest institutional target and it is headquartered inside this ZIP: Foothills Fieldhouse, Foothills Sports Arena and Edge Ice Arena (the indoor sports facilities that match the client's stated line of business), plus Ridge Recreation Center, Lilley Gulch Recreation Center, Peak Community & Wellness Center, outdoor and indoor pools, batting cages, a disc golf course and pickleball courts, and Clement Park. The district also holds agreements with Bowles Metro District, Normandy Estates, Plains Metropolitan District, Roxborough Village Metro District, TrailMark Subdivision and Vintage Reserve HOA — a ready-made list of named metro-district and HOA doors. Under SB24-005, approach all of these on athletic fields and indoor fields of play, not on landscape turf.
facts.landmarks: The Dakota Hogback itself, and Dinosaur Ridge at its northern end near Morrison; Dakota Ridge High School; C-470 running through the western portion and connecting Golden to Highlands Ranch; Bear Creek to the north; Red Rocks and Morrison just over the ridge; Chatfield to the south; Clement Park (Foothills district); the Lilley Gulch corridor. Denver's downtown is 17 miles northeast — close enough to matter, far enough that this reads as its own place.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE SOD BAN — IT HAS A DEADLINE, AND NO NEIGHBOURING TOWN CAN COPY IT. As of today, 2026-09-07, it is illegal to install or replace more than 200 square feet of sod in Brighton, and that prohibition runs to Sept 30, 2026, after which sod comes back only with a permit and a punishing six-week watering schedule. Artificial turf is not banned. That is the single most powerful conversion device in this entire batch: a checkable, city-published, time-limited scarcity argument — 'You cannot lay sod in Brighton right now. You can lay turf.' Pair it with the enforcement ladder (two warnings, then $125–$1,500, then a court summons) and the odd/even two-day schedule so the reader recognises their own address in the copy. The second lead is the yard itself: Brighton has the largest households, the largest lots and the lowest attached-housing share of the five, and a Pete Dye course — Riverdale Dunes — inside the city. That makes Brighton the PUTTING GREEN page of the batch: these are the only backyards in the group with the depth for a genuine three- to five-hole green, and residents have a local reference for how a good green should roll. Third, price honestly: Brighton has the lowest home values of the batch alongside high incomes, so this page should sell square footage and multi-element installs, not a premium per-foot rate. That is a completely different economic pitch from Westminster's high-value retrofit page or Thornton's rebate-compliance page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: The operative rule right now is not a landscape ordinance but the drought order itself: new sod over 200 sq ft is PROHIBITED through Sept 30, 2026, which functions as a de facto regulatory advantage for artificial turf. Landscape standards otherwise sit in Brighton's Land Use & Development Code; no Brighton-specific artificial-turf provision could be verified on 2026-09-07. Statewide, SB23-178 bars HOAs from requiring turf grass on detached homes and requires them to permit at least one mostly-low-water yard design; C.R.S. 37-60-126 pauses HOA enforcement over brown lawns once a provider declares restrictions — which Brighton has. SB24-005 blocks new artificial turf on commercial, institutional, industrial and HOA common-area development from Jan 1, 2026, athletic fields exempt. HOA prevalence is lower here than in north Thornton or Reunion because of the large pre-war and pre-HOA housing share.
facts.water_and_rules: City of Brighton Water. STAGE 1 DROUGHT RESTRICTIONS approved by City Council on April 7, 2026, running through Nov 15, 2026. Irrigation limited to TWO DAYS PER WEEK by last digit of house number: EVEN addresses Tuesday and Friday; ODD addresses Wednesday and Saturday; unassigned addresses Monday and Friday. Irrigation prohibited for all City of Brighton Water customers between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. Water waste prohibited, including pooling in a gutter, street or on property. Hand watering of ornamental grasses, shrubs, young trees and flowers is allowed and encouraged, but the hose must be held in hand — no sprinkler left on a hose. Enforcement: first violation warning, second warning, third violation $125 (taps up to 1 in), $500 (1.5–4 in) or $1,500 (over 4 in); fourth violation a municipal summons with mandatory court appearance. THE HEADLINE: SOD INSTALLATION OR REPLACEMENT IS PROHIBITED FOR AREAS EXCEEDING 200 SQUARE FEET THROUGH SEPT. 30, 2026. From Oct 1, 2026 the city will issue free sod permits carrying a strict establishment schedule (weeks 1–2: max three events/day, none over 10 minutes; weeks 3–4: max twice daily, nothing 10 a.m.–6 p.m.; weeks 5–6: once daily; after six weeks full restrictions resume). No turf rebate; Garden in a Box via Resource Central at $25 off. NO artificial turf rebate. The city's own xeriscape page tells residents that for water conservation 'it is best to not water your lawn at all' and to prioritise trees over grass.
facts.soil_and_yard: Flat and mostly free-draining, with one important exception. USDA SSURGO point samples (2026-09-07) give Dacono loam as dominant (23.5% clay, 39.2% sand, LEP 1.5, 0–1% slope, well drained) and Vona sandy loam (10% clay, 66.6% sand, LEP 1.5, 1–3% slope) across much of the town, with Satanta and Altvan as minor components — low shrink-swell throughout, so expansive clay is NOT a Brighton problem the way it is on Thornton's Samsil shale breaks. BUT: sampling toward the river and Barr Lake side returns AQUOLLS — 'poorly drained', 0–3% slope. That is a real and locatable low-lying band with a high water table where a turf base must include a proper drainage layer or it will sit wet. So the honest Brighton soil message is: most of town drains beautifully and builds easily, and a defined riverside band does not — and knowing which one you are on before quoting is the mark of a local installer.
facts.housing_stock: Median year built 1999, but genuinely split between an agricultural-era old town and a modern subdivision ring. Forty-nine percent of the stock was built since 2000 (25% in 2000–09, 19% in 2010–19, 5% since 2020) in the subdivisions west and south of the historic core. Against that, 5% of Brighton's housing predates 1940 and another 2% is 1940s — the largest genuinely historic share in the batch: brick bungalows, foursquares and converted farmhouses on deep 8,000–12,000 sq ft lots with alleys and detached garages around Main Street. 70.1% single-family detached, and only 6.7% attached — the lowest townhome/paired share of the five, i.e. the most consistently house-and-yard town here. 71.5% owner-occupied. 3.03 persons per household — the LARGEST households in the batch. Lots and backyards are materially bigger than Thornton's or Commerce City's. ACS 2024 5-yr.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 42,059. Median household income $107,679 — second highest of the five, and high relative to a median home value of $499,500. 38.6% Hispanic/Latino. Adams County's seat, on the agricultural edge where the metro meets South Platte farmland; large multigenerational families, more land per dollar than anywhere else in the batch. The buyer here has yard SIZE rather than premium price tolerance, so the commercial logic is bigger installs at a fair rate rather than boutique pricing.
facts.golf: Riverdale Golf Club, Adams County-owned, in Brighton — two courses: RIVERDALE DUNES, a PETE DYE design that has hosted the Nike Tour Colorado Classic (won by four-time PGA Tour winner and Ryder Cup player Stewart Cink), the USGA Public Links Championship and numerous Colorado State Championships; and RIVERDALE KNOLLS. PGA professionals on staff, tournament and banquet operation, junior programs. This is comfortably the strongest golf credential in the five-town batch. Benedict Park also has disc golf. Heritage Todd Creek golf community sits between Brighton and Thornton.
facts.commercial_targets: School District 27J — Brighton High School, Prairie View High School, Eagle Ridge Academy — the athletic-field target list, and the one commercial turf category SB24-005 still permits. Brighton Recreation Center's sports programs are unusually broad and are run by a named three-person sports staff: adult softball, kickball, volleyball and pickleball; youth basketball, flag football, soccer, t-ball, tennis, volleyball, track and cross country, plus sports camps. Brighton Oasis Family Aquatic Park. Riverdale Regional Park and Fairgrounds (arena and event grounds). Riverdale Golf Club for practice greens and tee lines. Riverdale Animal Shelter, plus the kennels, boarding, equine and veterinary businesses along the county roads — a genuinely richer pet-commercial list than the denser towns to the south.
facts.landmarks: Barr Lake State Park — at 1,937 acres the largest reservoir surface in the Denver metro, with its bald eagle nesting. Riverdale Regional Park — the Adams County Fairgrounds, event and arena grounds, and the Riverdale Animal Shelter (both recently improved). Riverdale Golf Club (Dunes and Knolls). Historic Main Street and the Armory. Brighton Recreation Center, 555 N. 11th Ave. Brighton Oasis Family Aquatic Park. Benedict Park with disc golf. The South Platte River corridor and the surrounding working farmland that still defines the town's edge.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE REBUILD. Nothing else in this batch comes close: 550 houses destroyed on 30 December 2021, 532 rebuilt or in process as of August 2026, owned by the highest-income households of the five ($147,319 median, above Boulder by sixty thousand dollars), in the town with the most children (35% of households) and the largest households (2.53 people). A rebuilt house on a graded lot is the single best job an artificial turf installer will ever quote: no sod to strip, no demolition, no root mat, no old irrigation to chase, clean access while other trades are still on site, and an owner who has just made four years of finish decisions and is treating the yard as the last one. Open the page there, and make the second beat the fire-hardening code, because it is real, local, checkable and nobody else will mention it: Class A rated fencing within five feet of the house, decks capped at flame-spread 25, and junipers prohibited from new planting since 21 January 2026 — then be straight that the code does not address artificial turf, and talk about material and infill choices in the first five feet as a consultation, not a claim. Third beat: kids. This is a play-surface town, not a decoration town — back-yard play areas, batting and chipping strips, and school/park playground surfacing (explicitly exempt from the state ban). Deliberately DO NOT lead with water: Louisville still has only voluntary restrictions, and overstating that would be both dishonest and easily disproved by a resident. Why it differs from next door: Lafayette, four miles away, went MANDATORY on 10 April 2026 and has no fire story; Boulder has a municipal turf prohibition; Broomfield is HOA-and-clay; Denver is shade-and-fill. Louisville is new dirt, high income, lots of children, and a fire code. NOCO OVERLAP: none — nocoturf.com has no Louisville page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No Louisville ordinance regulating artificial turf was found. But Louisville has something no other town in this batch has: a FIRE HARDENING CODE, adopted in the wake of the Marshall Fire, setting minimum fire-resistant material standards for new construction, accessory structures and certain repairs/replacements. It requires Class A roofing (ASTM E108/UL 790); FENCES WITHIN 5 FEET OF BUILDINGS must carry a Class A rating under ASTM E84/UL 723 or be metal, masonry or stone; decks limited to a flame-spread rating of 25 and Class A; cementitious siding, stone, stucco or Class A composites; 1/8-inch metal mesh vents; metal gutters with guards (vinyl prohibited). And as of 21 JANUARY 2026, JUNIPERS ARE PROHIBITED from new planting or replacement. Artificial turf is NOT addressed anywhere in the code — say so plainly rather than implying approval or prohibition. That gap is a consultative opening: a Louisville homeowner rebuilding to a fire-hardened standard, told they may not plant junipers, is precisely the customer to talk to about ground-cover material choices, infill selection and the first five feet around the structure. State laws SB24-005 and CRS 38-33.3-106.5 also apply; HOAs cover the 1980s-90s subdivisions but not Old Town.
facts.water_and_rules: City of Louisville water utility. As of the city's 26 March 2026 notice and its current water restrictions page, there are NO MANDATORY RESTRICTIONS — voluntary only: limit irrigation and hand watering to two days per week, between 6 p.m. and 10 a.m. The city states it is 'trending toward needing to implement mandatory restrictions' given historic drought conditions, and water waste is prohibited under municipal code section 13.08.120. No turf replacement or lawn removal rebate was found on the city's site, and nothing for artificial turf. HONEST IMPLICATION FOR THE PAGE: Louisville has the weakest regulatory water pressure in the batch alongside Boulder, so a water-savings lead would be the weakest possible opening here. Use the 'trending toward mandatory' language as a forward-looking argument rather than claiming restrictions that do not exist.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA Soil Data Access around Coal Creek Ranch returns Valmont (clayey over loamy-skeletal, montmorillonitic), Nunn (fine, smectitic), Hargreave, and Calkins — the last one 'Coarse-loamy, mixed, mesic Cumulic Haplaquolls', mapped POORLY DRAINED — alongside 'Terrace escarpments' at 12-60% slope, playa depressions, and, tellingly, a mapped 'Gravel pits and mine dumps' unit. That last one is the geological signature of the town's name: Louisville sat on the Northern Coal Field, and undermined ground and old workings are a recognised Boulder County land-use consideration. So the Louisville soil story has three parts that no neighbouring town shares in combination: expansive smectitic/montmorillonitic clay, poorly drained Calkins bottomland near Coal Creek, steep terrace escarpments where the mesa drops, and a coal-mining subsurface history worth acknowledging rather than ignoring.
facts.housing_stock: Median year built 1991, with a distinctive double peak: of 8,497 units, 28% were built in the 1990s and 26% in the 1980s — 54% of the town from a single twenty-year run (Coal Creek Ranch, Takoda, Sundance, Centennial Heights, Hillsborough, Summit View) — plus 17% built 2010-19, which includes both the Steel Ranch/North End infill and the Marshall Fire rebuild. Only 4% predates 1940: Old Town Louisville's coal-miner cottages on small lots around Main Street. 66.2% single-family detached and 71.7% owner-occupied, both the highest owner/detached combination in the batch after Erie. THE STANDOUT DEMOGRAPHIC FACT: average household 2.53 people and 35% of households have children under 18 — the largest households and the most kids of the five, well ahead of Boulder's 17%. That reframes the product from decoration to play surface. And then the anomaly: 550 homes in Louisville were destroyed by the Marshall Fire on 30 December 2021, and as of the city's August 2026 update 532 have been rebuilt or have started the process (about 97%) — meaning a large tranche of the housing stock is brand-new construction on bare, freshly graded lots with no established landscape at all.
facts.who_lives_there: Population 20,786. Median household income $147,319 — the HIGHEST of the five, and higher than Boulder's by $60,000. Per capita income $71,371. Median home value $883,900. 71.7% owner-occupied. Family-heavy, high-earning, long-tenured; Louisville has repeatedly appeared near the top of national 'best small towns to live in' rankings. This is the best raw match in the batch for the owner's $10-12/sq ft ambition: highest incomes, most children, biggest households, and a large cohort who have just spent two to four years rebuilding a house and are finishing the yard last.
facts.golf: Coal Creek Golf Course, 585 West Dillon Road — owned by the City of Louisville. 18 holes, par 72, 4,825-7,017 yards, described as having meandering fairways, significant elevation changes, water features and panoramic Front Range views. It is the town's golf identity and sits directly beside the Coal Creek Ranch subdivision, whose homes back onto it — the highest-value backyard putting-green prospects in Louisville. Indian Peaks Golf Course in Lafayette is minutes away. Boulder Country Club and Flatirons Golf Course are both a short drive.
facts.commercial_targets: Louisville Sports Complex and the Cleo Mudrock East/West fields, Heritage Park fields, Louisville Recreation and Senior Center, Coal Creek Ranch Pool/Clubhouse, Memory Square. Dog: Louisville Dog Park, Davidson Mesa Dog Park, The Divine Canine, Louisville Family Animal Hospital, Black Paw, Little Groomer Pet Salon. Childcare: KinderCare, La Petite Academy. Schools: Boulder Valley School District, including Monarch High School and Louisville Elementary/Middle. Note Sport Stable and the Superior facilities just over the town line, and Coal Creek Sports Center. Given the 35% child-household rate, school and municipal playground surfacing is a genuinely strong commercial line here — and playgrounds and athletic fields of play are exempt from SB24-005.
facts.landmarks: Downtown Louisville and Main Street, Memory Square Park, the Coal Creek Trail, Davidson Mesa (the Flatirons overlook off US 36, with its off-leash dog area), Harper Lake, the Louisville Historical Museum, Coal Creek Golf Course, the Louisville Sports Complex, and Monarch High School.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: 'You can't lay new sod in Roxborough right now — and the rule wasn't made here.' Roxborough is the only place in this batch whose watering rules are dictated by a city 25 miles away that it isn't part of. Aurora is the permanent raw-water supplier in perpetuity, Aurora declared Stage 1 on April 7, 2026, and Roxborough is contractually required to enforce it: two days a week, nothing from 10 to 6, escalating fines to the water bill, and an outright prohibition on NEW COOL-WEATHER TURF INSTALLATION. That single sentence does the selling — a homeowner who wants a green yard this season has exactly one legal option. Layer the second, uniquely Roxborough argument underneath: these are hogback lots. Steep, rocky, wildlife-hammered back yards on a fire-prone slope where bluegrass never established properly anyway and irrigation water running toward the foundation is a documented CGS hazard. Then the third: elk and deer walk through these yards from Roxborough State Park, and they do not eat turf. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBOURS: Sterling Ranch sits three miles away and is a brand-new-build first-landscape market with its own water utility and no such ban; Stonegate's constraint is a written HOA rule, not a drought order; Castle Pines Village's constraint is a price tier, not a prohibition. Roxborough is the only one where the answer is 'it is currently against the rules to do it the other way.'
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No Douglas County ordinance prohibits residential artificial turf. The binding constraint is the WATER RULE, not a zoning rule: Aurora-imposed Stage 1 restrictions currently forbid new cool-weather turf installation district-wide (effective April 7, 2026, until Aurora lifts them). Read plainly, a homeowner in Roxborough right now cannot legally lay new bluegrass sod but can install synthetic turf. Covenant layer: Roxborough Park Foundation for the original park, Roxborough Village Metropolitan District for the village — both require exterior/landscape review, but I could NOT verify either body's written artificial-turf language from a live source, so the page must not assert a specific rule without a confirming call. Colorado SB24-005 restricts new artificial turf on commercial, institutional, industrial and common-interest-community property (athletic fields of play exempt) — so HOA COMMON AREAS here are affected, residential yards are not.
facts.water_and_rules: Roxborough Water and Sanitation District (roxwaterco.gov, 6222 N. Roxborough Park Rd, 303-979-7286), ~11,000 customers. It owns almost no water of its own: under a 2010/2017 agreement the CITY OF AURORA is its permanent raw-water supplier 'in perpetuity,' delivering a contracted share from Strontia Springs Reservoir just west of Roxborough. The district paid Aurora a one-time $26.5M permanent water acquisition fee. Consequence: 'Roxborough is required to implement drought response restrictions set by the City of Aurora' — residents have no local control over their own watering rules. CURRENT STATUS (checked 2026-09-07): Aurora imposed Stage 1 drought surcharges effective April 7, 2026 on all utilities it supplies, including Roxborough, citing historically low snowpack. Roxborough's Stage 1 rules: outdoor irrigation 2 days/week on assigned days; NO watering 10 a.m.-6 p.m.; NO NEW COOL-WEATHER TURF INSTALLATION; no pool filling (topping off only); decorative water features off. Enforcement escalates: warning, then a fine on the water bill, then escalating fines and potential service interruption. Separate seasonal schedule runs May 1-Oct 1, 2 days/week. TURF REBATE: NONE that covers artificial turf. RWSD rebates are high-efficiency washers (up to $125) and toilets ($100 each, max two) only. It partners with Resource Central for free Slow the Flow sprinkler evaluations and a $20-off Garden In A Box discount — both aimed at LIVING landscape. The state Colorado Water Conservation Board Turf Replacement Grant Program stopped accepting applications in March 2025 (funding exhausted) and never funded individuals or HOAs directly, and funds 'water-wise landscapes,' not synthetic. So: no rebate angle here at all — the angle is the restriction.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 5,945 ft at the foot of the Front Range, sitting on and against the hogback — Fountain Formation red sandstone fins, Lyons and Dakota hogback ridges, with rocky colluvium, decomposed granite and thin sandy soils on the upslope lots and clay-rich valley soils below. The defining problem here is not clay, it is SLOPE: steep back yards, engineered drainage swales, and high-velocity runoff off rock faces during summer monsoon cells. Base preparation, compaction on grade, and edge restraint on a fall are the technical story. Colorado Geological Survey notes that expansive bentonite/montmorillonite clays underlie most Front Range development, and specifically calls out 'inadequate management of surface drainage and planting vegetation next to the foundation so irrigation water enters the soil' as a landscaping-caused cause of damage — directly relevant since drained synthetic turf removes the irrigation source next to the foundation. Also: severe wildfire exposure (gambel oak and ponderosa against open space) and heavy elk/deer/fox traffic, which destroys live lawns and does not touch turf.
facts.housing_stock: CDP of ~3,449 housing units / ~9,085 people, and it is really TWO different products under one Census name. (a) Roxborough Park proper — the original covenant-controlled foothills community begun in the 1970s-80s, custom and semi-custom homes on large, irregular, heavily sloped lots cut into the hogback, many 0.5-2+ acres, backing directly onto open space and red-rock formations. (b) Roxborough Village — the 1990s-2000s tract build-out on the flatter valley floor (Roxborough Village Metropolitan District), production two-story and ranch homes on conventional 6,000-9,000 sq ft lots with 1,500-3,000 sq ft usable back yards. Median property value $678,800 (2024). Homeownership 97.7% — one of the highest owner rates in the metro; essentially zero rental stock. HOA/covenant prevalence is near-universal but split between the Roxborough Park Foundation (the original park) and the Roxborough Village Metro District. HONEST GAP: I could not reach a live Roxborough Park Foundation website to verify its specific written artificial-turf rule — that needs a phone call before the page makes any covenant claim.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $173,083; median age 41.3; 75.3% married-couple households; 23.9% under 18. Largest employment sector is Professional, Scientific & Technical Services (898 workers), then management and sales. 35.5-minute average commute — the longest of the five places in this batch — so these are Denver/DTC professionals who chose to drive further to live against the mountains. Poverty 3.03%. 2 cars per household. Move-up family money rather than executive money: they will pay for a 600-1,200 sq ft back yard done right, not a $60k estate install.
facts.golf: Arrowhead Golf Club, 10850 Sundown Trail, Littleton 80125 — Robert Trent Jones Sr. & Jr., par 70, played through 300-million-year-old red sandstone fins; semi-private with public tee times and 'one of America's most photographed' layouts. Ravenna Country Club, 8285 Dante Drive, Littleton 80125 — private, family-owned, named a Golfweek top-100 residential course ten years running, set against the same red sandstone ridge, with a small number of remaining custom homesites. Also nearby: Deer Creek Golf Club and the Ken-Caryl courses to the north.
facts.commercial_targets: Lockheed Martin Waterton facility (named RWSD customer — corporate campus, putting green and courtyard potential). Arrowhead Golf Club and Ravenna Country Club (practice greens, tee-line and clubhouse surrounds). Roxborough Primary and Intermediate School (DCSD, IB World School). Roxborough Village Metropolitan District common areas and pocket parks. Roxborough Water & Sanitation District facilities. Chatfield and Roxborough State Park visitor areas. Ravenna's La Bella Vita fitness/pool amenity complex.
facts.landmarks: Roxborough State Park (red rock fins, the defining landmark). Waterton Canyon and the Colorado Trail eastern terminus. Chatfield State Park. Arrowhead Golf Club. Lamb Spring Archaeological Preserve — site of a 1960 discovery of one of Colorado's largest Columbian mammoth bone collections. Rampart Range Road. The Lockheed Martin Waterton Canyon facility (an RWSD customer). Roxborough Park Road.

name: Inverness

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE PRIVATE PUTTING GREEN ON A TERRACE — AND BE THE FIRM THAT KNOWS WHY THE COMMERCIAL JOB IS OFF THE TABLE. Inverness is a 1.1-square-mile office park with a golf course in it, a median home value of $862,300, and a population that is 47% people living alone with a $79,161 per capita income. There are almost no backyards. There is also, as of 1 January 2026, almost no legal commercial landscape turf market, because SB24-005 bans artificial turf on commercial, institutional and common-interest property and Inverness has no athletic field of play to fall back on. That combination produces a page unlike any other in the metro: the Inverness lead is the high-earning executive at Panorama Circle who wants a two-hole bent-grass-look putting green on a 300-square-foot terrace or an indoor practice green in a spare room, priced at the top of the range because it is small, technical, and elevator-access work. This is the page where $10-12/sq ft is easiest to defend — small jobs, structural complexity, affluent single buyers, and a golf course two blocks away to justify the obsession. Every neighbour reads differently: Dove Valley two miles east leads with the SB24-005 athletic-field EXEMPTION and the Broncos; Highlands Ranch leads with drought watering days and HOA approval on real backyards; Holly Hills leads with retrofitting 1950s quarter-acre lawns under Denver Water's October shutoff. Inverness is the only one where the honest answer is 'small, expensive, indoors and up high'.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: This is where Inverness is legally different from its neighbour and the page must not get it wrong. Colorado SB24-005 (signed 15 March 2024) prohibits local governments, on and after 1 January 2026, from allowing installation of nonfunctional turf, ARTIFICIAL TURF, or invasive plant species on commercial, institutional or industrial property, common interest community property, or street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors. Inverness is almost entirely commercial/institutional property plus common-interest residential. There is no athletic field of play here to invoke the exemption. So the commercial and HOA-common-area turf market in Inverness is, as of 1 January 2026, effectively CLOSED. What remains open is private residential property — the individual condo terrace, patio and interior. In addition, expect condo/townhome association architectural review and building-management approval on essentially every job. HONEST FLAG: I could not obtain the Inverness Metropolitan Improvement District's or any individual association's design guidelines; get at least one in hand before promising approvals.
facts.water_and_rules: Inverness Water and Sanitation District — verified as the provider, serving Arapahoe and Douglas County from offices in Englewood (303-649-9857). It is a small special district; the Inverness Metropolitan Improvement District handles other area services. The district's public site publishes NO drought stage, watering-day schedule, or conservation rebate — it offers the free EyeOnWater consumption/leak app and nothing more. HONEST FLAG: that means you cannot run the 'your watering days are X' message here that works so well in Highlands Ranch. Do not invent one.
